<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
\label{Def:IdealTriangulation}
Suppose that $(t_i)$ is a disjoint collection of tetrahedra.
Suppose that $(\phi_j)$ is a collection of linear homeomorphisms between the faces of the $t_i$ that pairs every face with exactly one other face.
Let $\mathcal{T}$ be the result of quotienting the disjoint union of the $(t_i)$ by the face pairings $(\phi_j)$.

Suppose that $M$ is a three-manifold with boundary.
If $M - \partial M$ is homeomorphic to $\mathcal{T}$ minus its vertices, then we say that $\mathcal{T}$ is an \emph{ideal triangulation} of $M$.
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
\label{Def:Taut}
Suppose that $\mathcal{T}$ is an ideal triangulation with tetrahedra $(t_i)$.
Let $E$ be the collection of all edges of all tetrahedra (six per tetrahedron).
Let $\alpha \colon E \to \{0,\pi\}$ be a map such that
\begin{itemize}
\item for each vertex $v$ of each tetrahedron $t_i$, the sum of the values assigned to the edges of $t_i$ incident to $v$ is $\pi$, and
\item for each collection of edges that are identified together in the quotient, the sum of the assigned values is $2\pi$.
\end{itemize}
Then we say that $\alpha$ is a \emph{taut angle structure} on $\mathcal{T}$.
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- definition-3: body_md -->
\label{Def:Layered}
Suppose that $\mathcal{T}$ is a transverse taut triangulation of a manifold $M$.
We say that $\mathcal{T}$ is \emph{layered} if the branched surface equations for $\mathcal{B}$ have a positive solution.
<!-- end definition-3 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{Lem:CommensurablePreservesLayered}
Suppose that $(M, \mathcal{S})$ and $(N, \mathcal{T})$ are commensurable.
Then $\mathcal{S}$ is layered if and only if $\mathcal{T}$ is.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Let $(P, \mathcal{R})$ be the common finite-sheeted cover.
Suppose that $\mathcal{S}$ is layered.
By definition, the horizontal branched surface $\mathcal{B}_\mathcal{S}$ admits a positive weighting. 
Lifting, we find that $\mathcal{B}_\mathcal{R}$ admits a positive weighting.
We find a positive weighting for $\mathcal{B}_\mathcal{T}$ by, for any fixed face, adding the weights of its finitely many preimages.
Thus $\mathcal{T}$ is layered.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- definition-4: body_md -->
\label{Def:Veering}
Suppose that $\mathcal{T}$ is a transverse taut ideal triangulation of an oriented manifold $M$.
We pull back the orientation of $M$ to obtain orientations on the tetrahedra $t_i$.
We say that $\mathcal{T}$ is \emph{transverse veering} if there is a two-colouring, in red and blue, of the edges of the one-skeleton of $\mathcal{T}$ with the following property.
We pull the colouring back to the edges of each tetrahedron $t_i$.
For every vertex $v$ of $t_i$, the edges of $t_i$ incident to~$v$, taken in anticlockwise order as viewed from $v$, have
\begin{itemize}
\item angle $\pi$,
\item the colour blue, and
\item the colour red. \qedhere
\end{itemize}
<!-- end definition-4 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
\label{Rem:LocallyVeering}
                                                                                                                     
Throughout most of the paper we will simply refer to transverse veering triangulations as veering triangulations.
However, when the need arises, we consider taut triangulations (possibly not transverse) on three-manifolds (possibly not orientable).
We call such a taut triangulation \emph{locally veering} if it becomes transverse veering in a finite cover.
See~\cite[Definition~10.2]{FSS22}.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{Lem:VeeringHyperbolic}
Suppose that $\mathcal{V}$ is a finite locally veering triangulation of a three-manifold $M$.
Then the interior of $M$ admits a complete finite-volume hyperbolic metric.
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
It suffices to show the interior of some finite-sheeted cover of $M$ admits a complete finite-volume hyperbolic metric;
see~\cite[Theorem~8.36]{Kapovich10}.
Since $M$ admits a locally veering triangulation, there is a finite-sheeted cover $M' \to M$ which admits a veering triangulation.  
Appealing to~\cite[Theorem~1.5]{HRST11}, and the sentence immediately after it, we obtain the desired hyperbolic structure on this cover.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
\label{Rem:VeeringHyperbolic}
With Lemma~\ref{Lem:VeeringHyperbolic} in hand, for the remainder of the paper, whenever $M$ is a manifold with a finite (locally) veering triangulation we fix an identification between the universal cover of $M - \partial M$ and hyperbolic three-space $\mathbb{H}^3$.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{Lem:Laminations}
\leavevmode
\begin{enumerate}
\item
\label{Itm:CrownZZ}
The leaves in a crown associated to a cusp $c$ accumulate on $c$ from both sides.
Also, $c$ is the unique accumulation point of any sequence of distinct leaves in the crown.
\item
\label{Itm:NoCusps}
No leaf of either lamination has an ideal point at any cusp. 
\item
\label{Itm:Adjacent}
Distinct leaves $\lambda$ and $\lambda'$ have a common ideal point $x$ if and only if 
they are adjacent boundary leaves of a common crown.
\item
\label{Itm:Approach}
Every leaf of either lamination is the limit of both boundary and interior leaves of that lamination.  
Interior leaves are limits from both sides while boundary leaves are only approached from the side opposite their associated cusp.
\item
\label{Itm:NoEndpoints}
No leaf $\lambda \in \Lambda^\mathcal{V}$ shares an ideal point with any leaf $\mu \in \Lambda_\mathcal{V}$. 
\item
\label{Itm:Interleave}
For any cusp $c$, the crowns $\Lambda^c$ and $\Lambda_c$ \emph{interleave}:
any pair of (non-cusp) ideal points of one crown is linked by some pair of (non-cusp) ideal points from the other.  \qed
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- definition-5: body_md -->
\label{Def:DecompositionElementsCircle}
A \emph{decomposition element} in $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$ is one of the following subsets of $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$. 
\begin{enumerate}
\item
Suppose that $c \in \Delta_\mathcal{V}$ is a cusp.  
Then $c$, together with the ideal points of $\Lambda^c$ and the ideal points of $\Lambda_c$ (its thorns) is a decomposition element.
We refer to this decomposition element as the \emph{clamshell boundary} associated to $c$.
\item
Suppose that $\lambda$ is an interior leaf of $\Lambda^\mathcal{V}$ or of $\Lambda_\mathcal{V}$.  
Then the pair of points $\lambda$ is a decomposition element.
\item  
Suppose that $x \in \mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$ is not contained in one of the above.
Then the singleton set $\{x\}$ is a decomposition element.
\end{enumerate}
The decomposition element containing $x$ is denoted $[x]_{S^1}$.
<!-- end definition-5 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{Cor:CircleDecomposition}
The decomposition elements partition $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$. \qed
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
We abuse notation slightly and refer to $x \in \mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$ as a \emph{singleton} if it is neither a cusp nor an ideal point of a leaf.
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- definition-6: body_md -->
\label{Def:VeeringSphere}
We denote the quotient of $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$ by the decomposition elements as $\mathcal{S}^2(\mathcal{V})$.
We denote the quotient map by $\Psi_\mathcal{V} \colon \mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V}) \to \mathcal{S}^2(\mathcal{V})$.
We call $\mathcal{S}^2(\mathcal{V})$ the \emph{veering two-sphere}.
<!-- end definition-6 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{Thm:Sphere}
The veering two-sphere $\mathcal{S}^2(\mathcal{V})$ is a two-sphere.  
Furthermore, the action of $\pi_1(M)$ on $\mathcal{S}^2(\mathcal{V})$ is continuous, faithful, and orientation preserving. 
Finally, if $\mathcal{V}$ is finite then the action has dense orbits.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- definition-7: body_md -->
\label{Def:PreSphere}
Let $S^2$ be the unit sphere in $\mathbb{R}^3$;
let $Z = \{ z = 0 \}$ be the horizontal plane.
We identify $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$ with the intersection $S^2 \cap Z$.
The orientation of $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$ is anticlockwise as viewed from above.
Let $D^\mathcal{V}$ and $D_\mathcal{V}$ be the (closed) upper and lower hemispheres of $S^2$.
Using the hemisphere model of $\mathbb{H}^2$ we identify their interiors with $\mathbb{H}^2$.
We call this copy of $S^2$ the \emph{pre-sphere}.
<!-- end definition-7 -->
<!-- definition-8: body_md -->
\label{Def:DecompositionElementsSphere}
Suppose that $x$ is a point of $S^2$.
We construct its decomposition element, $[x]_{S^2}$, as follows. 
\begin{enumerate}
\item 
If $x$ lies in $D^c$ or $D_c$, for some cusp $c \in \Delta_\mathcal{V}$, then we take $[x]_{S^2} = D^c \cup D_c$. 
\item
If $x$ lies in $[\lambda]^D$ for some interior leaf $\lambda$ of $\Lambda^\mathcal{V}$, then we take $[x]_{S^2}  = [\lambda]^D$. 
\item
If $x$ lies in $[\lambda]_D$ for some interior leaf $\lambda$ of $\Lambda_\mathcal{V}$, then we take $[x]_{S^2}  = [\lambda]_D$. 
\item
If $x$ lies in $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$, and is not a cusp or a leaf ideal point, then we take $[x]_{S^2}  = \{x\}$. 
\end{enumerate}
We call these decomposition elements \emph{clamshells}, \emph{upper leaves}, \emph{lower leaves}, and \emph{singletons}, respectively.
<!-- end definition-8 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{Lem:Slice}
For any point $x$ in the pre-sphere, we have that $[x]_{S^2}$ meets the veering circle $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$.
Also, for a point $x \in \mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$ we have $[x]_{S^2} \cap \mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V}) = [x]_{S^1}$.
This induces a bijection between the quotient of the pre-sphere and the veering two-sphere $\mathcal{S}^2(\mathcal{V})$. \qed
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{Lem:Equiv}
The decomposition elements of Definition~\ref{Def:DecompositionElementsSphere} form a closed equivalence relation on the pre-sphere.
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
We show that the decomposition elements cover the pre-sphere.
Suppose that $x$ is a point of the pre-sphere.
By Corollary~\ref{Cor:CircleDecomposition}, if $x$ lies in $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$ then $x$ is either a cusp, a point in the boundary of a leaf (of $\Lambda^\mathcal{V}$ or of $\Lambda_\mathcal{V}$), or a singleton.
In all cases, $[x]_{S^2}$ is a decomposition element.
Suppose instead, breaking symmetry, that $x$ lies in the interior of $D^\mathcal{V}$.
If $x$ lies in $[\lambda]^D$ for some $\lambda \in \Lambda^\mathcal{V}$ then we are done.
Suppose not.
Let $E$ be the closure of the component of $D^\mathcal{V} - [\Lambda^\mathcal{V}]^D$ containing $x$.
By Lemma~\ref{Lem:Laminations}(\ref{Itm:Approach}) the disc $E$ meets only boundary leaves of $[\Lambda^\mathcal{V}]^D$ and these boundary leaves are all associated to a single cusp, say $c$.
We deduce that $E = D^c$ and thus $x \in [c]_{S^2}$.
Thus the decomposition elements cover the pre-sphere.

We now show that decomposition elements partition the pre-sphere.
Fix $x$ and $y$ in the pre-sphere.  
Suppose that $[x]_{S^2} \cap [y]_{S^2}$ is non-empty.  
Since all decomposition elements meet $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$, we may assume that the representatives $x$ and $y$ lie in $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$.  
Applying Corollary~\ref{Cor:CircleDecomposition} and Lemma~\ref{Lem:Slice}, we conclude that the decomposition elements partition the pre-sphere. 

                                                                
We now show that the resulting equivalence relation is closed.
Suppose that $(x_n, y_n)$ is a sequence in $S^2 \times S^2$ so that $[x_n]_{S^2} = [y_n]_{S^2}$ for all $n$.
Suppose that the sequence converges to $(x_\infty, y_\infty)$.
We must show that $[x_\infty]_{S^2} = [y_\infty]_{S^2}$.
Taking subsequences if necessary, we may assume that all decomposition elements $[x_n]_{S^2}$ are of the same type. 

Suppose that $[x_n]_{S^2}$ is a singleton for all $n$.
Thus $x_n = y_n$ for all $n$.
Thus $x_\infty = y_\infty$.
Therefore $[x_\infty]_{S^2} = [y_\infty]_{S^2}$.

Suppose now that $[x_n]_{S^2}$ is a leaf for all $n$.
Passing to a further subsequence and breaking symmetry if needed, we may assume that $[\lambda_n]^D =  [x_n]_{S^2}$ is a leaf of the lamination $[\Lambda^\mathcal{V}]^D$ in the upper hemisphere $D^\mathcal{V}$.
Passing to a further subsequence, we may assume that the $[\lambda_n]^D$ Hausdorff converge to either a single point $z_\infty$ in $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$ or a leaf $[\lambda_\infty]^D$ of $[\Lambda^\mathcal{V}]^D$.
                                            
In the first case $x_\infty = z_\infty = y_\infty$ and we are done.
                                                                                             
In the second case, $[\lambda_\infty]^D$ contains both $x_\infty$ and $y_\infty$.
Since $[\lambda_\infty]^D \subset [\lambda_\infty]_{S^2}$ we are done.
                                                                              

Finally, suppose that $[x_n]_{S^2} = C_n$ is a clamshell for all $n$.
Pass to a subsequence so that the $C_n$ Hausdorff converge to $L$. 

We write $D^n = C_n \cap D^\mathcal{V}$ and $D_n = C_n \cap D_\mathcal{V}$. 
Each of $D^n$ and $D_n$ is an infinity-gon.
These Hausdorff converge to $L^\infty$ and $L_\infty$, respectively.

\begin{claim*}
Each of $L^\infty$ and $L_\infty$ is either a point of $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$, a leaf of $[\Lambda^\mathcal{V}]^D$ or $[\Lambda_\mathcal{V}]_D$, or an infinity-gon.
\end{claim*}

\begin{proof}
It suffices to consider $L^\infty$.
Note that $L^\infty$ is convex in the upper hemisphere metric on $D^\mathcal{V}$ since the approximating infinity-gons $D^n$ are.
If $L^\infty$ has interior then the $D^n$ eventually contain a small disc of the interior, hence they meet each other, hence the sequence is eventually constant.
In this case $L^\infty$ is an infinity-gon.

Set $\partial_\infty D^n = D^n \cap \mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$.
Note that $\partial_\infty L^\infty$ is the Hausdorff limit of $\partial_\infty D^n$.
If $\partial_\infty L^\infty$ is a single point then by convexity, $L^\infty$ is a single point and we are done.
If $\partial_\infty L^\infty$ contains three or more points then by convexity $L^\infty$ has interior and we are in the previous case.
So suppose that $\partial_\infty L^\infty$ consists of exactly two points, $u$ and $v$ in $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$.
Thus $L^\infty$ is a geodesic.
For large $n$, the vertices of $D^n$ are partitioned by being close to either $u$ or $v$.
Thus there are exactly two boundary leaves, of $D^n$, each of which has its ideal points close to $u$ and $v$.
                                     
Thus $L^\infty$ is a Hausdorff limit of leaves, and so is itself a leaf.
                                            
\end{proof}

Note that the $C_n$ are connected.
Thus, $L = L^\infty \cup L_\infty$ is also connected.
We now consider cases.
\begin{itemize}
\item
Suppose that both $L^\infty$ and $L_\infty$ are points. 
Then $L$ is a point and we are done.

\item
Suppose that neither $L^\infty$ nor $L_\infty$ is an infinity-gon and at least one is a leaf.
Then the other is not a leaf by Lemma~\ref{Lem:Laminations}(\ref{Itm:NoEndpoints}).
Thus $L$ is a leaf of either $[\Lambda^\mathcal{V}]^D$ or $[\Lambda_\mathcal{V}]_D$, so is contained in a decomposition element, and we are done.

\item
Finally, breaking symmetry, suppose that $L^\infty$ is an infinity-gon.
Since infinity-gons have non-empty interiors, we deduce that the sequence $D^n$ is eventually constant.
Thus the sequence $D_n$ is eventually constant.
Thus $L$ is a clamshell and we are done. 
\end{itemize}
This completes the proof of Lemma~\ref{Lem:Equiv}.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- claim--1: body_md -->
Each of $L^\infty$ and $L_\infty$ is either a point of $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$, a leaf of $[\Lambda^\mathcal{V}]^D$ or $[\Lambda_\mathcal{V}]_D$, or an infinity-gon.
<!-- end claim--1 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
It suffices to consider $L^\infty$.
Note that $L^\infty$ is convex in the upper hemisphere metric on $D^\mathcal{V}$ since the approximating infinity-gons $D^n$ are.
If $L^\infty$ has interior then the $D^n$ eventually contain a small disc of the interior, hence they meet each other, hence the sequence is eventually constant.
In this case $L^\infty$ is an infinity-gon.

Set $\partial_\infty D^n = D^n \cap \mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$.
Note that $\partial_\infty L^\infty$ is the Hausdorff limit of $\partial_\infty D^n$.
If $\partial_\infty L^\infty$ is a single point then by convexity, $L^\infty$ is a single point and we are done.
If $\partial_\infty L^\infty$ contains three or more points then by convexity $L^\infty$ has interior and we are in the previous case.
So suppose that $\partial_\infty L^\infty$ consists of exactly two points, $u$ and $v$ in $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$.
Thus $L^\infty$ is a geodesic.
For large $n$, the vertices of $D^n$ are partitioned by being close to either $u$ or $v$.
Thus there are exactly two boundary leaves, of $D^n$, each of which has its ideal points close to $u$ and $v$.
                                     
Thus $L^\infty$ is a Hausdorff limit of leaves, and so is itself a leaf.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{Lem:Homeo}
The bijection of Lemma~\ref{Lem:Slice} is a homeomorphism.
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
We prove that both directions of the bijection are closed maps.

Suppose we have a closed subset $A$ of the quotient of the pre-sphere.
The preimage $B$ of $A$ in the pre-sphere is closed and saturated in the pre-sphere.
                                 
Therefore $C$, the intersection of $B$ with the circle, is closed and saturated in the circle.
Therefore $D$, the image of $C$ in the quotient of the circle, is closed.
                                                    

Suppose that we have a closed subset $D$ of the quotient of the circle, $\mathcal{S}^2(\mathcal{V})$.
Thus $C$, the preimage of $D$ in the circle, is closed and saturated in the circle.
                                 
Extend $C$ by taking its union with all leaves and clamshells it meets. 
Call the resulting extension $B$; this is saturated by construction.
We now prove that $B$ is closed.
Suppose that $x_n \in B$ is a sequence with limit $x_\infty$ in the pre-sphere.
For each $n$, applying Lemma~\ref{Lem:Slice} we choose $c_n \in [x_n]_{S^2} \cap \mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$.
Since $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$ is compact, we pass to a subsequence so that $c_n \to c_\infty$.
Note that $c_\infty$ lies in $C$.
So $[c_\infty]_{S^2}$ lies in the extension $B$.
Note that $[x_n]_{S^2} = [c_n]_{S^2}$. 
By Lemma~\ref{Lem:Equiv}, the equivalence relation on the pre-sphere is closed.
Thus it is sequentially closed. 
Thus $[x_\infty]_{S^2} = [c_\infty]_{S^2}$.
Thus $x_\infty$ lies in $B$, so $B$ is closed.
Thus $A$, the image of $B$ in the quotient of the pre-sphere, is closed.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{Lem:ConnNonSep}
For each $x$ in the pre-sphere, the decomposition element $[x]_{S^2}$ is connected and non-separating.
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
This is because $[x]_{S^2}$ is either a single point, an embedded arc, or a one-point union of a pair of embedded discs.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
Lemmas~\ref{Lem:Equiv} and~\ref{Lem:ConnNonSep} verify the hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{Thm:Moore}.  
Thus the quotient of the pre-sphere is homeomorphic to a two-sphere.  
By Lemma~\ref{Lem:Homeo}, we have that $\mathcal{S}^2(\mathcal{V})$ is a two-sphere.

We now analyse the action of $\pi_1(M)$ on the veering two-sphere $\mathcal{S}^2(\mathcal{V})$.  
By~\cite[Theorem~7.1]{FSS22}, the action of $\pi_1(M)$ on $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$ has all of the properties listed in the conclusions of Theorem~\ref{Thm:Sphere}.
This implies that the action on $\mathcal{S}^2(\mathcal{V})$ is continuous and, when $\mathcal{V}$ is finite, has dense orbits.
                                                                 
                                                                    
                                                                
                                 
                                                                    
                                                                
                
             
The action of $\pi_1(M)$ on the cusps $\Delta_\mathcal{V}$ is faithful;
these embed in $\mathcal{S}^2(\mathcal{V})$.
Thus the action on $\mathcal{S}^2(\mathcal{V})$ is faithful.

                             
We now show that the action on $\mathcal{S}^2(\mathcal{V})$ is orientation preserving.
Let $d^\mathcal{V}$ be the interior of the upper hemisphere $D^\mathcal{V}$, in the pre-sphere.
The image of $d^\mathcal{V}$ in $\mathcal{S}^2(\mathcal{V})$ is a countably branching dendrite. 
                                                                                                                         
                                                               
The action of $\pi_1(M)$ preserves the dendrite and the circular order of the arcs emanating from any branch point.
Thus the action is orientation preserving.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
\label{Lem:DecompositionElementsRecover}
The collection of infinite decomposition elements in $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$ recovers the upper and lower laminations $\Lambda^\mathcal{V}$ and $\Lambda_\mathcal{V}$, up to swapping the two laminations.
<!-- end lemma-8 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
Suppose that $[c]_{S^1} \in \mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$ is an infinite decomposition element.
By Corollary~\ref{Cor:CircleDecomposition}, we deduce that there is exactly one element $c \in [c]_{S^1}$ which is an accumulation point; 
this is the cusp.
Up to choosing a basepoint, this gives a unique order isomorphism between $[c]_{S^1} - \{c\}$ and $\mathbb{Z}$.
Using this isomorphism, pairs of points differing by two are the ideal points of boundary leaves of the upper and lower laminations $\Lambda^\mathcal{V}$ and $\Lambda_\mathcal{V}$.

However, leaves that link belong to opposite laminations.
Since the link space is a plane, under the relation of linking, the boundary leaves form a connected bipartite graph.
                                                
                                                                                
This allows us to separate the boundary leaves of $\Lambda^\mathcal{V}$ from the boundary leaves of $\Lambda_\mathcal{V}$.
Since they are the closures of their boundary leaves (see Section~\ref{Sec:Dynamics}), the upper and lower laminations $\Lambda^\mathcal{V}$ and $\Lambda_\mathcal{V}$ are thus determined. 
However, we do not learn which lamination is which.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- definition-9: body_md -->
\label{Def:Rectangle}
Suppose that $f_R \colon (0, 1)^2 \to \mathcal{L}$ is an embedding with image $R$.  
We call $R$ a \emph{rectangle} if $f_R$ sends arcs parallel to the $y$--axis ($x$--axis) to arcs of $F^\mathcal{L}$ (of $F_\mathcal{L}$).
<!-- end definition-9 -->
<!-- definition-10: body_md -->
\label{Def:CuspRect}
A rectangle $R$ is a \emph{south-west cusp rectangle} if there is a continuous extension of $f_R$ to a homeomorphism 
\[
{\overline{f}}_R \colon [0,1]^2 - \{(0,0)\} \to {\overline{R}}
\]
See Figure~\ref{Fig:CuspRect}.
We define cusp rectangles with the other intercardinal directions similarly.
The two sides (see~\cite[Definition~2.6]{SchleimerSegerman24}) of a cusp rectangle which are not closed intervals are called \emph{cusp sides}.
<!-- end definition-10 -->
<!-- definition-11: body_md -->
\label{Def:TetRect}
A rectangle $R$ is a \emph{tetrahedron rectangle} if there are $a, b, c, d \in (0,1)$ and a continuous extension of $f_R$ to a homeomorphism 
\[
{\overline{f}}_R \colon [0,1]^2 - \{(a,0), (1,b), (c,1), (0,d)\} \to {\overline{R}} \qedhere
\]
<!-- end definition-11 -->
<!-- definition-12: body_md -->
\label{Def:Loom}
We say that $\mathcal{L}$ is a \emph{loom space} if its rectangles satisfy the following axioms.
\begin{enumerate}
\item 
\label{Itm:Cusp}
For every cusp side $s$ of every cusp rectangle, some initial open interval of $s$ is contained in some rectangle.
(See Figure~\ref{Fig:CuspSide}.)
\item 
\label{Itm:Tet}
Every rectangle is contained in some tetrahedron rectangle. \qedhere
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end definition-12 -->
<!-- definition-13: body_md -->
\label{Def:Cusp}
A \emph{cusp} $c$ of a loom space $\mathcal{L}$ is an equivalence class of the transitive closure of the following relation.
Two cusp rectangles of $\mathcal{L}$ are \emph{adjacent} if some cusp side of one is contained in some cusp side of the other.
<!-- end definition-13 -->
<!-- definition-14: body_md -->
\label{Def:CuspNonCuspLeaves}
A leaf of either foliation $F^\mathcal{L}$ or $F_\mathcal{L}$ is a \emph{cusp leaf} if it contains some cusp side of some cusp rectangle.
We say that the leaf \emph{belongs to} the cusp containing the cusp rectangle.
<!-- end definition-14 -->
<!-- lemma-9: body_md -->
\label{Lem:NoTriangles}
Suppose that $\ell$ and $\ell'$ are distinct cusp leaves of the same foliation, belonging to a common cusp $c$.
Then any leaf $m$ of the opposite foliation meets at most one of $\ell$ and $\ell'$.
<!-- end lemma-9 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
Since $\ell$ and $\ell'$ belong to a common cusp there is a chain of cusp rectangles with $\ell$ containing a cusp side of the first and $\ell'$ containing a cusp side of the last.
Since $\ell$ and $\ell'$ are distinct and in the same foliation, this implies that there is a cusp leaf $m'$ of the opposite foliation which
\begin{itemize}
\item
contains a cusp side of one of the cusp rectangles and
\item
separates $\ell$ from $\ell'$ in the plane $\mathcal{L}$.
\end{itemize}
The leaf $m$ cannot cross $m'$ since they belong to the same foliation.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- definition-15: body_md -->
\label{Def:BiLeaf}
Suppose that $\ell$ and $\ell'$ are cusp leaves of the same foliation.  
Suppose that $c$ is the cusp of both $\ell$ and $\ell'$.  
Suppose further that $\ell$ and $\ell'$ are separated (in $\mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V})$) by exactly one cusp leaf $m$ in the other foliation.  
Note that $m$ necessarily also has its cusp at $c$.  
We call the union 
\[
k = \ell \cup \{c\} \cup \ell'
\]
a \emph{bi-leaf}.
In an abuse of notation, we say that $k$ \emph{belongs to} the foliation that contains $\ell$ and $\ell'$. 
We call $c$ the \emph{centre} of $k$.
We call the leaf $m$ the \emph{divider} of $k$.
<!-- end definition-15 -->
<!-- remark-4: body_md -->
\label{Rem:NonCuspLeavesDense}
There are countably many cusps and countably many cusp leaves emanating from each.
(Cusp leaves come from boundary leaves, which come from branch lines; see~\cite[Lemma~6.10(2) and Definition~8.14]{FSS22}.)
So there are countably many cusp leaves in total.
In particular, non-cusp leaves are dense.
<!-- end remark-4 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{Thm:LinkIsLoom}
Suppose that $\mathcal{V}$ is a veering triangulation of a three-manifold $M$.  
Then the link space $\mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V})$, equipped with the foliations $F^\mathcal{V}$ and $F_\mathcal{V}$, is a loom space.
A leaf is a cusp leaf (in the sense of the link space) if and only if it is a cusp leaf of the loom space structure.
Furthermore, $\mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V})$ has a canonical orientation.
The fundamental group $\pi_1(M)$ acts on $\mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V})$ by orientation-preserving homeomorphisms preserving the loom space structure. \qed
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- definition-16: body_md -->
\label{Def:IdealPoints}
Suppose that $\ell$ is a leaf of $F^\mathcal{V}$.
If $\ell$ is the non-cusp leaf associated to an interior leaf $\lambda$ in $\Lambda^\mathcal{V}$ then the \emph{ideal endpoints} of $\ell$ are the (ideal) points of $\lambda$.
If $\ell$ is the cusp leaf associated to adjacent boundary leaves $\lambda$ and $\lambda'$ of the crown $\Lambda^c$ then the \emph{ideal endpoints} of $\ell$ are the cusp $c$ and the common ideal point of $\lambda$ and $\lambda'$.
In this case we say that $\ell$ \emph{emanates} from $c$.
We make similar definitions when $\ell$ is a leaf of $F_\mathcal{V}$.
See Figure~\ref{Fig:HypRectStyles}.
<!-- end definition-16 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{Cor:OnlyAsymptotics}
Suppose that $\ell$ and $m$ are distinct leaves in $\mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V})$ (in either of the foliations).
Suppose that $\ell$ and $m$ share a common ideal point.
Then $\ell$ and $m$ are both cusp leaves and the shared point is a cusp.
\qed
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- definition-17: body_md -->
\label{Def:Polygonal}
A \emph{polygonal path} $\rho$ in $\mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V})$ is an oriented arc, loop, ray, or line with the following properties. 
\begin{itemize}
\item
The path $\rho$ is a finite union $(\rho_i)_{i = 0}^{n-1}$ of \emph{segments}: oriented closed connected subsets of leaves of $F^\mathcal{V}$ and $F_\mathcal{V}$.  
(When $\rho$ is a loop, all indices are taken modulo $n$.)
\item 
The segment $\rho_i$ lies in $F^\mathcal{V}$ if and only if $\rho_{i+1}$ lies in $F_\mathcal{V}$. 
\item
The terminal point of $\rho_i$ equals the initial point of $\rho_{i+1}$.
\end{itemize}
The intersection points $\rho_i \cap \rho_{i+1}$ are called the \emph{material corners} of $\rho$.
<!-- end definition-17 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
\label{Cor:TransverseOmnibus}
\leavevmode
\begin{enumerate}
\item
\label{Itm:PreCompactBasis}
The precompact rectangles form a basis for the topology on $\mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V})$. 
\item
\label{Itm:PreCompactBoundary}
The boundary $\partial R$ of a precompact rectangle $R$ is an embedded polygonal loop with exactly four segments. 
\item
\label{Itm:Ascending}
Every rectangle is an ascending union of precompact rectangles.
\item
\label{Itm:Proper}
Suppose that $\rho \subset \mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V})$ is an embedded polygonal line.  
Then $\rho$ is properly embedded in $\mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V})$.  
\item
\label{Itm:DiscUnion}
Suppose that $\rho$ is an embedded polygonal loop in $\mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V})$.  
Then the open disc bounded by $\rho$ is a finite union of (necessarily precompact) rectangles. \qed
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- definition-18: body_md -->
\label{Def:Ideal}
Suppose that $\rho$ is a polygonal ray or a line in $\mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V})$.  
We define $\partial_\infty \rho$ to be the ideal points of those segments $\rho_i$ which are non-compact.  
There are at most two of these. 
See Figure~\ref{Fig:PolygonalPath}.
<!-- end definition-18 -->
<!-- lemma-10: body_md -->
\label{Lem:LeftIsLeft}
Suppose that $\ell \subset \mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V})$ is a leaf of either foliation, and similarly for $m$ and $m'$. We have the following.
\begin{enumerate}
\item
\label{Itm:TwoEndpoints}
The two ideal points $\partial_\infty \ell$ are distinct.
\item
\label{Itm:CrossIFFLinked}
The leaves $\ell$ and $m$ cross if and only if $\partial_\infty \ell$ and $\partial_\infty m$ are linked in $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$. 
\item
\label{Itm:LeftIsLeft}
Let $\{x, y\} = \partial_\infty \ell$.
Suppose that $m$ and $m'$ are distinct leaves that cross $\ell$ at $q$ and $q'$, respectively.
Then $q$ separates $q'$ from the end of $\ell$ associated to $x$ if and only if, in $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$, the ideal points $\partial_\infty m$ separate $\partial_\infty m'$ from $x$ (see Figure~\ref{Fig:LeftIsLeft}).
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-10 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
Conclusions~(\ref{Itm:TwoEndpoints}) and~(\ref{Itm:CrossIFFLinked}) follow directly from the definition of $\mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V})$ (see~\cite[Section~10]{FSS22}).
 
Suppose that $\ell$ is a non-cusp leaf.
Let $\lambda$ be the interior leaf of $\Lambda^\mathcal{V}$ giving $\ell$.
Let $\Lambda_\lambda \subset \Lambda_\mathcal{V}$ be the set of leaves that link $\lambda$.
As in the proof of~\cite[Lemma~8.24]{FSS22}, the set $\Lambda_\lambda$ is linearly ordered and locally has the topology of the Cantor set.
As in the proof of~\cite[Theorem~10.51]{FSS22}, a copy of the set $\Lambda_\lambda$ collapses to give the leaf $\ell$;
the order on $\Lambda_\lambda$ orients $\ell$.

The collapsing map preserves order as follows.
Suppose that $\mu$ and $\mu'$ are leaves of $\Lambda_\lambda$ with images containing $m$ and $m'$, respectively.
Then $\mu < \mu'$ in $\Lambda_\lambda$ if and only if $q < q'$ along $\ell$.
By Lemma~\ref{Lem:NoTriangles}, the ideal points of $m$ and $m'$ are distinct.
Conclusion~(\ref{Itm:LeftIsLeft}) now follows when $\ell$ is a non-cusp leaf.
The proof is similar when $\ell$ is a cusp leaf.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- lemma-11: body_md -->
\label{Lem:NoDoubleCusps}
A leaf $\ell$, in either foliation, has at most one ideal point at a cusp.  \qed
<!-- end lemma-11 -->
<!-- remark-5: body_md -->
\label{Rem:Fenley}
Our result and parts of its proof are inspired by a result of Fenley~\cite[Theorem~3.31]{Fenley12}.  
We follow him in relying on Zippin's characterisation of the two-disc, stated above as Theorem~\ref{Thm:Zippin}.

Our task is easier than Fenley's in some respects but harder in others.
On the one hand, our task is easier because we begin with the veering circle; 
indeed we used it to build the link space.  
Fenley instead begins with the \emph{leaf space} and then gives a delicate construction of a circle at infinity. 
                                                             
On the other hand, our task is more difficult; 
unlike Fenley, our three-manifold $M$ has torus boundary.  
Thus our proof must contend with the cusp points in $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$.
<!-- end remark-5 -->
<!-- remark-6: body_md -->
There are at least two other approaches to proving Theorem~\ref{Thm:Disc}.

                         
Modelled on the construction of the veering two-sphere, we form the pre-sphere out of hemispheres $D^\mathcal{V}$ and $D_\mathcal{V}$, glued along $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$.
As before, we build a copy of $[\Lambda^\mathcal{V}]^D$ in $D^\mathcal{V}$.
Now we build a (reflected) copy of $[\Lambda_\mathcal{V}]_D$ also in $D^\mathcal{V}$.
We denote this copy by $[\Lambda_\mathcal{V}]^D$.
We define a partition of the pre-sphere as follows.
\begin{itemize}
\item Each point of $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$ is its own equivalence class.
\item Each point of the interior of $D_\mathcal{V}$ is its own equivalence class.
\item Two points of the interior of $D^\mathcal{V}$ are equivalent if they are connected by an arc in $D^\mathcal{V}$ that does not strictly cross any leaf of either $[\Lambda^\mathcal{V}]^D$ or $[\Lambda_\mathcal{V}]^D$.
\end{itemize}
These give a closed equivalence relation on the pre-sphere, satisfying the hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{Thm:Moore}.
Taking the quotient, we obtain a two-sphere.
The image of $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$ is a Jordan curve and bounds the image of $D^\mathcal{V}$.
This is the desired disc $\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{V})$.

                         
Alternatively one could follow~\cite{Mather82}. 
The exact formulation required can be found as~\cite[Theorem~1.2]{Bonatti26}. 
Note, however, that for this approach one would need to carefully check that $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$ places the same circular order on the cusps as Mather's circle.
<!-- end remark-6 -->
<!-- definition-19: body_md -->
\label{Def:Set}
The underlying set for the \emph{veering disc} $\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{V})$ is the disjoint union of the link space $\mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V})$ and the veering circle $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$.
<!-- end definition-19 -->
<!-- definition-20: body_md -->
\label{Def:Action}
We equip $\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{V})$ with an action by $\pi_1(M)$ by taking the ``disjoint union'' of its actions on $\mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V})$ and on $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$.
<!-- end definition-20 -->
<!-- definition-21: body_md -->
\label{Def:HalfDisc}
Suppose that $\rho \subset \mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V})$ is an oriented embedded polygonal line.  
Let $u$ and $v$ be the initial and terminal ideal points of $\rho$, respectively. 
So $\partial_\infty \rho = \{u, v\}$. 
Throughout this definition we assume that $u \neq v$.  
By Corollary~\ref{Cor:TransverseOmnibus}(\ref{Itm:Proper}) the line $\rho$ is properly embedded.  
Thus Theorem~\ref{Thm:Schoenflies} implies that $\rho$ separates $\mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V})$ into two connected components.  

\begin{itemize}
\item
Let $H^\circ(\rho)$ be the component of $\mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V}) - \rho$ to the left of $\rho$.  
                                                                           
We call $H^\circ(\rho)$ the \emph{half-plane} associated to $\rho$.   
\item
Let $H(\rho) = H^\circ(\rho) \cup (v, u)^{\rotatebox[origin=c]{-90}{\scalebox{0.7}{$\curvearrowleft$}}}$.  
We call $H(\rho)$ the \emph{half-disc} associated to $\rho$.  
When $\rho$ is a cusp leaf, we call $H(\rho)$ a \emph{cusp half-disc}.
\item
We call $\partial_\infty \rho = \{u, v\}$ the \emph{ideal corners} of $H(\rho)$.
\item
We call the material corners of $\rho$ the \emph{material corners} of $H(\rho)$.  
\item
At every material corner we say that $\rho$ \emph{turns left} or \emph{turns right} as it turns towards or away from $H^\circ(\rho)$.  
\item
We call $\partial_\infty H(\rho) = (v, u)^{\rotatebox[origin=c]{-90}{\scalebox{0.7}{$\curvearrowleft$}}}$ the \emph{ideal boundary} of $H(\rho)$.
\item
We call $\partial_\textrm{mat} H(\rho) = \rho$ the \emph{material boundary} of $H(\rho)$.
\qedhere
\end{itemize}
<!-- end definition-21 -->
<!-- remark-7: body_md -->
Note that $\rho \cup \partial_\infty \rho$ is disjoint from $H(\rho)$.
<!-- end remark-7 -->
<!-- definition-22: body_md -->
\label{Def:Topology}
The topology on $\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{V})$ is defined to be the smallest topology where the cusp half-discs $H(\ell)$ are open, as $\ell$ ranges over oriented cusp leaves of $F^\mathcal{V}$ and of $F_\mathcal{V}$.
<!-- end definition-22 -->
<!-- remark-8: body_md -->
\label{Rem:SubBasis}
The cusp half-discs give a \emph{sub-basis}~\cite[page~4]{SteenSeebach95}.
<!-- end remark-8 -->
<!-- lemma-12: body_md -->
\label{Lem:Action}
The $\pi_1(M)$--action on $\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{V})$ is by homeomorphisms.
<!-- end lemma-12 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
The action preserves the set of cusp leaves;
thus it preserves the given sub-basis.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- lemma-13: body_md -->
\label{Lem:LeafHalfDisc}
Suppose that $\ell$ is an oriented leaf in $\mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V})$.  
Then $H(\ell)$ is open in $\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{V})$.
<!-- end lemma-13 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
Suppose that $\ell$ is a leaf of either foliation.  
If $\ell$ is a cusp leaf then $H(\ell)$ is a cusp half-disc; 
thus it is open by Definition~\ref{Def:Topology}.

Suppose instead that $\ell$ is a non-cusp leaf.
Fix a point $p$ on $\ell$.
We build, as in Section~\ref{Sec:Astroid}, the staircase $S$ about $p$ to the left of $\ell$ containing the initial end of $\ell$. 
See Figure~\ref{Fig:ApproachLeaf}.
Let $(c_i)$ be the cusps of $S$. 
Each $c_i$ has two cusp leaves $\ell_i$ and $m_i$ meeting the interior of $S$. 
By the astroid lemma~\cite[Lemma~4.10]{SchleimerSegerman24} the intersection points $\ell \cap m_i$ exit the initial end of $\ell$. 
Again applying the astroid lemma, we deduce that the cusp leaves $\ell_i$ approach $\ell$ from the left. 
Thus $H(\ell) = \mathbin{\scalebox{1.5}{\ensuremath{\cup}}}_i H(\ell_i)$ is open.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- lemma-14: body_md -->
\label{Lem:Rectangle}
Suppose that $R$ is a rectangle in $\mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V})$.  
Then $R$ is open in $\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{V})$.
<!-- end lemma-14 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
Applying Corollary~\ref{Cor:TransverseOmnibus}(\ref{Itm:Ascending}), it suffices to consider the case where $R$ is precompact.  
We give $\partial R$ its induced orientation.  
By Corollary~\ref{Cor:TransverseOmnibus}(\ref{Itm:PreCompactBoundary}), there are four oriented leaves $\{\ell_i\}_{i = 0}^3$ so that 
\begin{itemize}
\item
$R$ is to the left of $\ell_i$ and 
\item
one segment of $\partial R$ lies in $\ell_i$. 
\end{itemize}
Thus $R = \mathbin{\scalebox{1.5}{\ensuremath{\cap}}}_i H(\ell_i)$ and we are done by Lemma~\ref{Lem:LeafHalfDisc}.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- lemma-15: body_md -->
\label{Lem:SubspaceL}
The subspace topology for $\mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V}) \subset \mathcal{D}(\mathcal{V})$ has the following properties.
\begin{enumerate}
\item
\label{Itm:Sub}
It agrees with the original topology on $\mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V})$; 
thus it is homeomorphic to $\mathbb{R}^2$. 
\item
\label{Itm:Open}
$\mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V})$ is open as a subset of $\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{V})$.  
\item
\label{Itm:Arc}
$\mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V})$ is path-connected by embedded polygonal arcs. 
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-15 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
By Lemma~\ref{Lem:Rectangle}, rectangles are open in the subspace topology on $\mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V})$.  
By Corollary~\ref{Cor:TransverseOmnibus}(\ref{Itm:PreCompactBasis}), precompact rectangles give a basis for the original topology. 
Thus the subspace topology has at least as many open sets as the original topology.   

Now suppose that $\ell$ is an oriented cusp leaf.  
The half-plane $H^\circ(\ell) = H(\ell) \cap \mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V})$ is a union of rectangles; thus the subspace topology on $\mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V})$ has no more open sets than the original topology on $\mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V})$.  
This proves (\ref{Itm:Sub}).

Since $\mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V})$ is a union of rectangles it is open in $\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{V})$.  
This gives (\ref{Itm:Open}).

Finally, suppose that $p$ and $q$ are points of $\mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V})$.  
Since $\mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V})$ is homeomorphic to $\mathbb{R}^2$ it is path-connected.  
Let $s$ be an arc from $p$ to $q$.  
Since $s$ is compact, we can cover it by finitely many rectangles.  
There is an embedded polygonal arc $\sigma$ from $p$ to $q$ contained in the union of these rectangles.  
This proves (\ref{Itm:Arc}).
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- lemma-16: body_md -->
\label{Lem:HalfDiscOpen}
Suppose that $\rho$ is an embedded polygonal line in $\mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V})$.  
Then $H(\rho)$ is open. \qed
<!-- end lemma-16 -->
<!-- lemma-17: body_md -->
\label{Lem:Span}
Suppose that $c$ and $d$ are cusps.  
Then there is an embedded polygonal line $\rho$ with ideal points at $c$ and $d$.
<!-- end lemma-17 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
Suppose that $\ell$ and $m$ are distinct cusp leaves ending at $c$ and $d$, respectively.  
Lemma~\ref{Lem:SubspaceL}(\ref{Itm:Arc}) gives us an embedded polygonal arc $\beta$ running from a point of $\ell$ to a point of $m$.  
We extend $\beta$ by subrays of $\ell$ and $m$ towards $c$ and $d$, respectively. 
Finally, we delete loops and backtracking.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- lemma-18: body_md -->
\label{Lem:SubspaceS}
The subspace topology on $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$ agrees with its original topology.
<!-- end lemma-18 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
By construction, the subspace topology on $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$ has no more open sets than the original topology.  

By Lemmas~\ref{Lem:Span} and~\ref{Lem:HalfDiscOpen} the subspace topology also contains a basis for the original topology, namely the open intervals ending at cusps.  
Thus the subspace topology has no fewer open sets than the original topology.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- definition-23: body_md -->
\label{Def:Basic}
A \emph{basic} set $H = \mathbin{\scalebox{1.5}{\ensuremath{\cap}}}_i H(\ell_i)$ is a finite intersection of cusp half-discs.
We extend the notations of Definition~\ref{Def:HalfDisc} to basic sets.  
We orient the components of its material boundary, $\partial_\textrm{mat} H$, so that $H$ is (locally) to the left of each. 
We define $H^\circ = H \cap \mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V})$.
<!-- end definition-23 -->
<!-- remark-9: body_md -->
\label{Rem:Basis}
By Remark~\ref{Rem:SubBasis}, the basic sets form a \emph{basis}~\cite[page~4]{SteenSeebach95} for the topology on $\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{V})$.
<!-- end remark-9 -->
<!-- lemma-19: body_md -->
\label{Lem:BasicOmnibus}
Suppose that $H$ is a basic set.
\begin{enumerate}
\item
\label{Itm:TurnsLeft}
Suppose that $\rho$ is a component of $\partial_\textrm{mat} H$ and suppose that $q$ is a material corner of $\rho$.  
Then $\rho$ turns left at $q$. 
\item
\label{Itm:Loop}
Suppose that $\rho$ is a component of $\partial_\textrm{mat} H$ which is a loop.
Then $H$ is a precompact rectangle. 
\item
\label{Itm:PathConnected}
The intersection $H^\circ = H \cap \mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V})$ is path-connected by embedded polygonal arcs. 
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-19 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
Suppose that $H$ equals $\mathbin{\scalebox{1.5}{\ensuremath{\cap}}}_{i = 1}^n H(\ell_i)$ where the $\ell_i$ are cusp leaves. 

Suppose that $\rho$ is a component of $\partial_\textrm{mat} H$ and suppose that $q$ is a material corner of $\rho$.  
The segments of $\rho$ lie in the leaves $\ell_i$.  
Let $\ell$ and $m$ be the leaves of the two foliations through $q$.  
Let $R$ be a small rectangle about $q$.  
Then $\ell$ and $m$ cut $R$ into four subrectangles.  
Since $H \subset H(\ell) \cap H(m)$, the basic set $H$ only contains one of the four subrectangles.  
Finally, since $\rho$ is oriented so that $H$ lies to its left, we deduce that $\rho$ turns left at $q$.  
This proves (\ref{Itm:TurnsLeft}).  

Suppose that $\rho$ is a component of $\partial_\textrm{mat} H$ which is a loop.  
By our orientation convention, $H$ locally lies to the left of $\rho$. 
By the Jordan curve theorem (Theorem~\ref{Thm:Schoenflies}), the loop $\rho$ cuts $\mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V})$ into a precompact piece (to its left) and a non-precompact piece (to its right).
Thus $H$ is a precompact open disc and $\partial_\textrm{mat} H = \rho$.  
By the previous paragraph, $\rho$ turns left at all material corners.  
An Euler characteristic argument (see~\cite[Section~3]{SchleimerSegerman20}) now shows that $H$ is a rectangle.  
This proves (\ref{Itm:Loop}).

Suppose that $p$ and $q$ are points of $H$.  
By Lemma~\ref{Lem:SubspaceL}(\ref{Itm:Arc}) there is an embedded polygonal arc $\beta \subset \mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V})$ connecting them.  
Since the segments of $\beta$ are compact, we can tile them by rectangles and so move $\beta$ (inside the rectangles) so that it is transverse to $\partial_\textrm{mat} H$.  
Surger $\beta$ off of $\partial_\textrm{mat} H$, discarding loops as they arise.
                                                                                                                                                          
This proves (\ref{Itm:PathConnected}).
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- lemma-20: body_md -->
\label{Lem:HalfDiscNeighBasis}
Suppose that $x$ is a point of $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$.  
The half-discs (as given in Definition~\ref{Def:HalfDisc}) containing $x$ give a neighbourhood basis for $x$ in $\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{V})$.
<!-- end lemma-20 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
Suppose that $H$ is a basic set containing $x$.  
                                                                 
Since $\partial_\infty H$ is an intersection of finitely many open intervals, 
                               
it is a disjoint union of finitely many open intervals.  
Let $(v, u)^{\rotatebox[origin=c]{-90}{\scalebox{0.7}{$\curvearrowleft$}}}$ be the component of $\partial_\infty H$ containing $x$.  
Let $\rho$ and $\sigma$ be the components of $\partial_\textrm{mat} H$ that start and end at $u$ and $v$, respectively. 
(Here we use the induced orientations coming from $H$.)
If $\rho = \sigma$ then the half-disc $H(\rho)$ equals $H$ and we are done.
                                                                                                      

Suppose instead that $\rho$ is not equal to $\sigma$.
By Lemma~\ref{Lem:BasicOmnibus}(\ref{Itm:PathConnected}) there is an embedded polygonal arc $\beta' \subset H$ connecting a point near $\rho$ to a point near $\sigma$.  
                            
We extend $\beta'$ to obtain an embedded polygonal arc $\beta$ so that $\beta$ connects a point of $\rho$ to a point of $\sigma$ and $\beta \cap \partial_\textrm{mat} H$ consists of those two points.
We orient $\beta$ from $\rho$ and towards $\sigma$.  
Let $\rho'$ be the component of $\rho - \beta$ with ideal point at $u$; 
let $\sigma'$ be the component of $\sigma - \beta$ with ideal point at $v$.  
Thus $\tau = \rho' \cup \beta \cup \sigma'$ is an embedded polygonal line.  
Note that the half-disc $H(\tau)$ is contained in $H$.
Furthermore, $\partial_\infty H(\tau) = (v, u)^{\rotatebox[origin=c]{-90}{\scalebox{0.7}{$\curvearrowleft$}}}$ contains $x$.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- lemma-21: body_md -->
\label{Lem:Triple}
Suppose that $\rho$ is a leaf of either $F^\mathcal{V}$ or $F_\mathcal{V}$.  
Let $q$ be a point of $\mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V})$ not lying on $\rho$.  
Let $\ell$ and $m$ be the leaves of $F^\mathcal{V}$ and $F_\mathcal{V}$ meeting $q$.  
Then $q$ lies in $H^\circ(\rho)$ if and only if at least three of the four ideal points of $\ell$ and $m$ lie in $\partial_\infty H(\rho)$.
<!-- end lemma-21 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
It suffices to prove the forward direction.
So, assume that $q$ lies in $H^\circ(\rho)$.

Lemma~\ref{Lem:SubspaceL}(\ref{Itm:Arc}) gives us an oriented embedded polygonal arc $\sigma \subset \mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V})$ running from $q$ to $\rho$, and meeting each only at its endpoints.  
By Corollary~\ref{Cor:TransverseOmnibus}(\ref{Itm:Proper}) and Theorem~\ref{Thm:Schoenflies}, and since $q$ lies in $H^\circ(\rho)$, the interior of $\sigma$ lies in $H^\circ(\rho)$.  
Suppose that $\{\ell_i\}_{i = 0}^{n-1}$ are the leaves which $\sigma$ runs along, with orientations induced by $\sigma$.  
We order the indices of the $\ell_i$ to increase with the orientation of $\sigma$. 
We will assume that $\ell_0 = \ell$, the leaf of $F^\mathcal{V}$ through $q$.
Set $\partial_\infty \ell = \{x, y\}$ with $\ell$ running from $x$ to $y$.  
Also, let $q_i$ and $q_{i+1}$ be the endpoints of $\sigma \cap \ell_i$.  
So $q_0 = q$ and $q_n$ lies in $\rho$.  
We will induct on $n$. 

Suppose that $n = 1$.  
By Lemma~\ref{Lem:LeftIsLeft}(\ref{Itm:CrossIFFLinked}), since $\rho$ and $\ell$ cross, their ideal points are linked in $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$.
So exactly one of $x$ and $y$ lies in $\partial_\infty H(\rho)$.
Since $q$ lies in $H^\circ(\rho)$, we find that $m$ is not equal to $\rho$.
Since $\ell$ is oriented from $q$ to $q_1$, we deduce that $q$ separates $q_1$ from the end of $\ell$ associated to $x$.
Applying Lemma~\ref{Lem:LeftIsLeft}(\ref{Itm:LeftIsLeft}), we find that $\partial_\infty m$ separates $\partial_\infty \rho$ from $x$.  
Thus when $n = 1$ the intersection $(\partial_\infty \ell \cup \partial_\infty m) \cap \partial_\infty H(\rho)$ equals $\{x\} \cup \partial_\infty m$.
This completes the base case.  

Suppose that $n > 1$.  
Thus $q_1$ lies in $H^\circ(\rho)$. 
Recall that $\ell_0$ and $\ell_1$ are the two leaves through $q_1$.
Thus, by induction, at least three of the four ideal points of $\ell_0$ and $\ell_1$ lie in $\partial_\infty H(\rho)$.  

We now have various subcases. 
\begin{itemize}
\item
Suppose that both $x$ and $y$ lie in $\partial_\infty H(\rho)$.  
Since $\ell = \ell_0$ and $m$ cross, their ideal points are linked.  
So at least one point of $\partial_\infty m$ also lies in $\partial_\infty H(\rho)$.
\item
Suppose that $x$, say, lies in $\partial_\infty H(\rho)$ while $y$ does not, and $y$ is not an ideal point of $\rho$.  
Thus $\ell$ and $\rho$ cross.
In this case we replace $\sigma$ by a segment of $\ell$, and appeal to the base case.
\item
Finally, suppose that $x$, say, lies in $\partial_\infty H(\rho)$ while $y$ is one of the two points of $\partial_\infty \rho$.  
By Corollary~\ref{Cor:OnlyAsymptotics}, and because $\rho$ is not equal to $\ell$, we find that $y$ is a cusp.                                      
Since $\{x, y\}$ links $\partial_\infty m$, at least one point of $\partial_\infty m$ lies in $\partial_\infty H(\rho)$.  
Let $z$ be the other point of $\partial_\infty m$.
There are three subcases.
\begin{itemize}
\item
If $z$ lies in $\partial_\infty H(\rho)$ then we are done.
\item
If $z$ lies in $\partial_\infty \rho$ then by Corollary~\ref{Cor:OnlyAsymptotics} and Lemma~\ref{Lem:Laminations}(\ref{Itm:NoCusps}), the leaf $m$ is a cusp leaf emanating from $z = y$.
Thus $\partial_\infty \ell$ does not link $\partial_\infty m$, a contradiction.
\item 
If $z$ lies outside of $\partial_\infty H(\rho) \cup \partial_\infty \rho$ then $\partial_\infty m$ links $\partial_\infty \rho$.
Thus $m$ and $\rho$ cross, and we reduce to the base case.
\qedhere
\end{itemize}
\end{itemize}
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- lemma-22: body_md -->
\label{Lem:Extension}
Suppose that $\ell$ is a leaf of either foliation.  
Suppose that $r$ is a subray of $\ell$.  
Then the union $r \cup \partial_\infty r$ is an arc in $\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{V})$.
<!-- end lemma-22 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
We define a function $\lambda \colon [0, 1] \to \mathcal{D}(\mathcal{V})$ by
\begin{itemize}
\item
taking $\lambda | [0, 1)$ to be an orientation-preserving homeomorphism from $[0, 1)$ to $r$ and
\item
setting $\lambda(1) = \partial_\infty r$.
\end{itemize}
Note that $\lambda$ is injective and its image meets $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$ only at $\partial_\infty r$.  
We must show that $\lambda$ is continuous.

Let $U \subset \mathcal{D}(\mathcal{V})$ be any open set.  
Lemma~\ref{Lem:SubspaceL}(\ref{Itm:Open}) implies that $U \cap \mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V})$ is open.  
Thus $\lambda^{-1}(U \cap \mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V}))$ is open.  
If $\partial_\infty r$ does not lie in $U$ then there is nothing left to prove.  
Suppose that $\partial_\infty r$ lies in $U$; thus $U$ is an open neighbourhood of $\partial_\infty r$.   

\begin{claim*}
For some $t \in (0, 1)$ we have $(t, 1) \subset \lambda^{-1}(U \cap \mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V}))$.
\end{claim*}

\begin{proof}
Applying Definition~\ref{Def:Topology} we may replace $U$ by a smaller neighbourhood of the form $V = \mathbin{\scalebox{1.5}{\ensuremath{\cap}}}_{i} H(m_i)$.  
Here $\{H(m_i)\}$ is a finite collection of cusp half-discs whose ideal boundaries each contains $\partial_\infty r$.

Fix $i$.
We now must show that a subray of $r$ lies in $H(m_i)$.

Recall that $\partial_\infty r$ lies in $\partial_\infty H(m_i)$.  
Thus $\ell$ is not equal to $m_i$.  
If $\ell$ lies in $H(m_i)$ then we are done.                                                              
So suppose that $\ell$ contains a point $q$ of $H^\circ(m'_i)$, where $m'_i$ is the leaf $m_i$ with the opposite orientation.
Let $m$ be the other leaf through $q$.  
Applying Lemma~\ref{Lem:Triple} (with $m'_i$ for $\rho$), at least three of the four ideal points $\partial_\infty m \cup \partial_\infty \ell$ lie in $\partial_\infty H(m'_i)$.  
However, $\partial_\infty r$ lies in $\partial_\infty H(m_i)$.
Therefore $\ell$ and $m_i$ cross, say at the point $q_i$.  
By Lemma~\ref{Lem:LeftIsLeft}(\ref{Itm:LeftIsLeft}) we find that $q_i$ separates $q$ from the end of $\ell$ associated to $\partial_\infty r$.  
Thus the end of $r$ lies in $H(m_i)$, proving the claim.
\end{proof}

Since $\partial_\infty r$ lies in $U$, we deduce that $(t, 1]$ lies in $\lambda^{-1}(U)$, proving that $\lambda$ is continuous.
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- claim--2: body_md -->
For some $t \in (0, 1)$ we have $(t, 1) \subset \lambda^{-1}(U \cap \mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V}))$.
<!-- end claim--2 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
Applying Definition~\ref{Def:Topology} we may replace $U$ by a smaller neighbourhood of the form $V = \mathbin{\scalebox{1.5}{\ensuremath{\cap}}}_{i} H(m_i)$.  
Here $\{H(m_i)\}$ is a finite collection of cusp half-discs whose ideal boundaries each contains $\partial_\infty r$.

Fix $i$.
We now must show that a subray of $r$ lies in $H(m_i)$.

Recall that $\partial_\infty r$ lies in $\partial_\infty H(m_i)$.  
Thus $\ell$ is not equal to $m_i$.  
If $\ell$ lies in $H(m_i)$ then we are done.                                                              
So suppose that $\ell$ contains a point $q$ of $H^\circ(m'_i)$, where $m'_i$ is the leaf $m_i$ with the opposite orientation.
Let $m$ be the other leaf through $q$.  
Applying Lemma~\ref{Lem:Triple} (with $m'_i$ for $\rho$), at least three of the four ideal points $\partial_\infty m \cup \partial_\infty \ell$ lie in $\partial_\infty H(m'_i)$.  
However, $\partial_\infty r$ lies in $\partial_\infty H(m_i)$.
Therefore $\ell$ and $m_i$ cross, say at the point $q_i$.  
By Lemma~\ref{Lem:LeftIsLeft}(\ref{Itm:LeftIsLeft}) we find that $q_i$ separates $q$ from the end of $\ell$ associated to $\partial_\infty r$.  
Thus the end of $r$ lies in $H(m_i)$, proving the claim.
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- corollary-4: body_md -->
\label{Cor:HalfDiscPathConnected}
Suppose that $\rho$ is an embedded polygonal line in $\mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V})$.  
Then $H(\rho)$ is path-connected. \qed
<!-- end corollary-4 -->
<!-- lemma-23: body_md -->
\label{Lem:ConnectedImpliesConnected}
Suppose that $H$ and $K$ are half-discs with $\partial_\infty H \cap \partial_\infty K$ non-empty.  
Then $H^\circ \cap K^\circ$ is also non-empty.
<!-- end lemma-23 -->
<!-- proof-22: body_md -->
Note that $\partial_\infty H$ and $\partial_\infty K$ are open intervals in $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$.  
Thus there is some cusp $c$ in their intersection.  
Let $r$ be a subray of a cusp leaf ending at $c$.  
Let $\lambda \colon [0, 1] \to \mathcal{D}(\mathcal{V})$ be the arc given by Lemma~\ref{Lem:Extension}.  
So $\lambda^{-1}(H)$ and $\lambda^{-1}(K)$ are open neighbourhoods of $1$; 
thus there is a point $t \in (0, 1)$ in both. 
Thus $\lambda(t)$ lies in $H^\circ \cap K^\circ$.
<!-- end proof-22 -->
<!-- lemma-24: body_md -->
\label{Lem:Hausdorff}
The space $\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{V})$ is Hausdorff.
<!-- end lemma-24 -->
<!-- proof-23: body_md -->
Suppose that $x$ and $y$ are distinct points.  
If both lie in $\mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V})$ then we appeal to Lemma~\ref{Lem:SubspaceL}(\ref{Itm:Sub}).

Suppose that $x$ and $y$ both lie in $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$.  
Let $c, d \in \Delta_\mathcal{V}$ be a pair of cusps that link the pair $(x, y)$.  
By Lemma~\ref{Lem:Span} there is an embedded polygonal line $\rho$ with ideal points $c$ and $d$.  
Thus $x$ and $y$ are contained in the left and right half-discs corresponding to $\rho$.  
By Lemma~\ref{Lem:HalfDiscOpen} these are open. 

Finally suppose that $x$ lies in $\mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V})$ while $y$ lies in $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$.  
Let $R$ be a rectangle which is precompact in $\mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V})$ and contains $x$; 
by Lemma~\ref{Lem:Rectangle} the rectangle $R$ is open.  

We orient the sides of $R$ anticlockwise.  
This induces orientations of the leaves $\{\ell_i\}_{i = 0}^3$ containing the sides of $R$.  
Note that $\ell_i$ and $\ell_{i+1}$ cross.  
By Corollary~\ref{Cor:OnlyAsymptotics} the leaves $\ell_i$ have no ideal points in common.  
Thus the half-discs $H(\ell_i)$ cover $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$; 
breaking symmetry suppose that $H(\ell_0)$ contains $y$; 
by Lemma~\ref{Lem:LeafHalfDisc} the half-disc $H(\ell_0)$ is open.  
Since $H(\ell_0)$ and $R$ are disjoint, and are open as above, we are done.
<!-- end proof-23 -->
<!-- lemma-25: body_md -->
\label{Lem:Compact}
The space $\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{V})$ is compact.
<!-- end lemma-25 -->
<!-- proof-24: body_md -->
Suppose that $\mathcal{U}_I = \{ U_i \}_{i \in I}$ is the given open cover.  
Since the $U_i$ are open, by appealing to Lemma~\ref{Lem:HalfDiscNeighBasis} for every $x \in \mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$ we may pick an embedded polygonal line $\rho_x$ so that 
$x \in H(\rho_x) \subset U_i$ for some $i \in I$.
                             
Set $V_x = H(\rho_x)$ and $\mathcal{V}_{S^1} = \{ V_x \}_{x \in S^1}$.  
So $\mathcal{V}_{S^1}$ covers $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$.  
Appealing to the compactness of $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$ there is a finite set $X \subset S^1$ so that $\mathcal{V}_X = \{ V_x \}_{x \in X}$ covers $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$.   

                                                                      
                                                                    
                                                                     
                 

\begin{claim*}
The set $C = \mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V}) - \mathbin{\scalebox{1.5}{\ensuremath{\cup}}}_X V_x$ is compact. 
\end{claim*}

\begin{proof}
Let $\Sigma$ be the closure of $C$ minus the interior of $C$.  
Each polygonal line $\rho_x$ is made up of a finite collection of segments lying in leaves from $F^\mathcal{V}$ and $F_\mathcal{V}$.  
Also, $\Sigma$ lies in the union $\cup_{x\in X} \rho_x$.
So $\Sigma$ is a union of finitely many segments in leaves.
For a contradiction, suppose that one of these segments contains a ray, say $\rho$.
Let $y \in \mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$ be the ideal point associated to $\rho$.
Since the intervals $\partial_\infty V_x$, for $x \in X$, cover $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$, the point $y$ lies in one of these.  
Thus, by Lemmas~\ref{Lem:Extension} and~\ref{Lem:HalfDiscOpen} the ray $\rho$ enters $V_x$, a contradiction.  
Thus all (finitely many) segments of $\Sigma$ are intervals.
So $\Sigma$ is a finite graph in the plane $\mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V})$.

For every loop $\sigma \subset \Sigma$, Theorem~\ref{Thm:Schoenflies} provides a unique disc $H(\sigma)$ in $\mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V})$ with $\partial H(\sigma) = \sigma$.   
Choose $\sigma$ so that $H(\sigma)$ does not contain any smaller such discs.
                                
Suppose for a contradiction that there is some $x \in X$ so that $H^\circ(\rho_x)$ lies in $H(\sigma)$.  
Then the points $\partial_\infty \rho_x$ are contained in the closure of $H(\sigma)$.  
Thus they are contained in $\mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V})$, the desired contradiction. 

We deduce that $C$ is contained in the union of the closures of the (finitely many) $H(\sigma)$, together with finitely many intervals in leaves. 
Thus $C$ is compact. 
\end{proof}

Applying the claim and recalling that $\mathcal{U}_I$ is an open cover, there is a finite subset $K \subset I$ so that $\mathcal{U}_K$ covers $C$.  
For each $x \in X$ choose some $j \in I$ so that $V_x \subset U_j$.
Collecting the finitely many indices $j$ into a set $J \subset I$, we find that $\mathcal{U}_{J \cup K}$ is a finite cover of $\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{V})$.
<!-- end proof-24 -->
<!-- claim--3: body_md -->
The set $C = \mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V}) - \mathbin{\scalebox{1.5}{\ensuremath{\cup}}}_X V_x$ is compact.
<!-- end claim--3 -->
<!-- proof-25: body_md -->
Let $\Sigma$ be the closure of $C$ minus the interior of $C$.  
Each polygonal line $\rho_x$ is made up of a finite collection of segments lying in leaves from $F^\mathcal{V}$ and $F_\mathcal{V}$.  
Also, $\Sigma$ lies in the union $\cup_{x\in X} \rho_x$.
So $\Sigma$ is a union of finitely many segments in leaves.
For a contradiction, suppose that one of these segments contains a ray, say $\rho$.
Let $y \in \mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$ be the ideal point associated to $\rho$.
Since the intervals $\partial_\infty V_x$, for $x \in X$, cover $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$, the point $y$ lies in one of these.  
Thus, by Lemmas~\ref{Lem:Extension} and~\ref{Lem:HalfDiscOpen} the ray $\rho$ enters $V_x$, a contradiction.  
Thus all (finitely many) segments of $\Sigma$ are intervals.
So $\Sigma$ is a finite graph in the plane $\mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V})$.

For every loop $\sigma \subset \Sigma$, Theorem~\ref{Thm:Schoenflies} provides a unique disc $H(\sigma)$ in $\mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V})$ with $\partial H(\sigma) = \sigma$.   
Choose $\sigma$ so that $H(\sigma)$ does not contain any smaller such discs.
                                
Suppose for a contradiction that there is some $x \in X$ so that $H^\circ(\rho_x)$ lies in $H(\sigma)$.  
Then the points $\partial_\infty \rho_x$ are contained in the closure of $H(\sigma)$.  
Thus they are contained in $\mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V})$, the desired contradiction. 

We deduce that $C$ is contained in the union of the closures of the (finitely many) $H(\sigma)$, together with finitely many intervals in leaves. 
Thus $C$ is compact.
<!-- end proof-25 -->
<!-- lemma-26: body_md -->
\label{Lem:Continuum}
The space $\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{V})$ is a Peano continuum.
<!-- end lemma-26 -->
<!-- proof-26: body_md -->
Since $\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{V})$ contains $\mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V})$, which is homeomorphic to $\mathbb{R}^2$, it has two distinct points.  
Thus $\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{V})$ is non-degenerate.

                                                                                            
The sub-basis for the topology, given in Definition~\ref{Def:Topology}, is countable.  
Taking finite intersections gives a basis (Remark~\ref{Rem:Basis}) which is still countable.  
Thus $\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{V})$ is second countable.

                                                                
Lemmas~\ref{Lem:Hausdorff} and~\ref{Lem:Compact} tell us that $\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{V})$ is Hausdorff and compact.  Thus, by~\cite[Theorem~1.27, page~74]{Wilder49}, the space $\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{V})$ is normal.

                   
Since $\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{V})$ is compact it is locally compact.
                                                  
                                                                                           

             
From Lemmas~\ref{Lem:SubspaceL}(\ref{Itm:Arc}) and~\ref{Lem:SubspaceS} we have that both $\mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V})$ and $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$ are path-connected.
Corollary~\ref{Cor:HalfDiscPathConnected} tells us that $H(\ell)$ is path-connected for any leaf $\ell$.
Thus $\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{V})$ is path-connected and so is connected.

                     
By Lemma~\ref{Lem:SubspaceL}(\ref{Itm:Sub}) we have that for all $x \in \mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V})$ the space $\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{V})$ is locally connected at $x$.  
Suppose instead that $x$ lies in $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$.  
Fix any open neighbourhood $U$ of $x$ in $\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{V})$.  
By Lemma~\ref{Lem:HalfDiscNeighBasis} there is some half-disc $H \subset U$ so that $x \in \partial_\infty H$.  
By Corollary~\ref{Cor:HalfDiscPathConnected} we have that $H$ is path-connected.  
Thus $\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{V})$ is locally connected at $x$.  
Thus $\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{V})$ is a Peano space. 

            
Finally, by Lemma~\ref{Lem:Compact}, we have that $\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{V})$ is compact. 
Thus it is a Peano continuum.
This completes the proof.
<!-- end proof-26 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{Thm:Disc}
Suppose that $\mathcal{V}$ is a transverse veering triangulation of a three-manifold $M$.
Then we have the following.
\begin{enumerate}
\item 
\label{Itm:Disc}
The veering disc $\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{V})$ is a disc, having the veering circle $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$ as its boundary and the link space $\mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V})$ as its interior. 
\item 
\label{Itm:Ends}
For any ray $r$ of any leaf of $F^\mathcal{V}$ or $F_\mathcal{V}$ we have that its closure in $\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{V})$ is ${\overline{r}} = r \cup \partial_\infty r$.
\item 
\label{Itm:Dense}
The endpoints of cusp leaves (respectively, non-cusp leaves) are dense in $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$.
\item 
\label{Itm:Unique}
Any other compactification of $\mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V})$ by a circle yielding a disc, with properties (\ref{Itm:Ends}) and (\ref{Itm:Dense}), is homeomorphic to $\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{V})$.
\item 
\label{Itm:Action}
Furthermore, the action of $\pi_1(M)$ on $\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{V})$ is by orientation-preserving homeomorphisms. 
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- remark-10: body_md -->
Note that here we do not assume that $\mathcal{V}$ is a finite triangulation.
<!-- end remark-10 -->
<!-- proof-27: body_md -->
To prove that $\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{V})$ is a disc, we verify the hypotheses of Zippin's characterisation (Theorem~\ref{Thm:Zippin}).  
Note that Lemma~\ref{Lem:Continuum} proves that $\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{V})$ is a Peano continuum.  
Our candidate boundary is the veering circle $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$.  

Suppose that $\ell$ is a leaf of $F^\mathcal{V}$ or $F_\mathcal{V}$.  
By Lemma~\ref{Lem:LeftIsLeft}(\ref{Itm:TwoEndpoints}) the leaf $\ell$ has two distinct ideal points.  
By Lemma~\ref{Lem:Extension} the union $\ell \cup \partial_\infty \ell$ is an arc in $\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{V})$.  
By construction, this union meets $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$ in exactly $\partial_\infty \ell$.  
Thus $\ell \cup \partial_\infty \ell$ is a spanning arc, giving hypothesis (\ref{Itm:Exists}) of Theorem~\ref{Thm:Zippin}.

Suppose that 
\[
(\gamma, \partial \gamma) \subset (\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{V}), \mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V}))
\]
is an oriented spanning arc.  Let $x$ and $y$ be the two points of $\partial \gamma$, with $\gamma$ oriented away from $x$.  Let $\delta = (y, x)^{\rotatebox[origin=c]{-90}{\scalebox{0.7}{$\curvearrowleft$}}}$ and $\epsilon = (x, y)^{\rotatebox[origin=c]{-90}{\scalebox{0.7}{$\curvearrowleft$}}}$; these are the two components of $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V}) - \partial \gamma$.  

We write $\gamma^\circ$ for $\gamma - \partial \gamma$; we call this the \emph{interior} of $\gamma$.  Note that $\gamma^\circ$ is an embedding of $(0, 1)$ into $\mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V})$.  

\begin{claim}
The interior $\gamma^\circ$ is a Jordan line in $\mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V})$.
\end{claim}

\begin{proof}
We must prove that $\gamma^\circ$ is properly embedded.  Fix a compact subset $K \subset \mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V})$.  Since $\gamma$ is continuous and $[0, 1]$ is compact, the preimage $\gamma^{-1}(K)$ is compact.  It is disjoint from $\{0, 1\}$ by assumption.  Note that $(\gamma^\circ)^{-1}(K) = \gamma^{-1}(K)$.  Thus the latter is compact in $(0, 1)$ and we are done. 
\end{proof}

Applying Theorem~\ref{Thm:Schoenflies}, we find that $\gamma^\circ$ separates $\mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V})$ into two open discs.  We denote these by $H$ and $K$.  

                
Fix $u \in \delta$.  
Since $\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{V})$ is normal, there is a basic open set $U$ containing $u$ and disjoint from $\gamma$.  
By Lemma~\ref{Lem:BasicOmnibus}(\ref{Itm:PathConnected}) the set $U^\circ = U \cap \mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V})$ is connected; 
thus $U^\circ$ is contained in $H$ or in $K$.  
Breaking symmetry, suppose that $U^\circ$ is contained in $H$.  

\begin{claim}
\label{Clm:DinD}
Suppose that $v$ lies in $\delta$.  
Suppose that $H_v$ is a half-disc neighbourhood of $v$ that misses $\gamma$.
Then $H_v \cap \mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V})$ lies in $H$.
\end{claim}

\begin{proof}
Let $\delta'$ be any compact subarc of $\delta$ containing both $u$ and $v$.  
Since $\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{V})$ is normal, and applying Lemma~\ref{Lem:HalfDiscNeighBasis}, 
for every $w \in \delta'$ we may pick a half-disc $H_w$ so that $w \in H_w$ and so that $H_w$ misses $\gamma$.  
The compactness of $\delta'$ gives us a finite subcollection of the $H_w$ that covers $\delta'$.  
By Lemma~\ref{Lem:ConnectedImpliesConnected}, if $H_w$ and $H_{w'}$ meet in $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$ then they meet in $\mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V})$.  
The connectedness of $\delta'$ now implies that all of the sets $H_w \cap \mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V})$ lie in $H$.  
We deduce that $H_v \cap \mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V})$ lies in $H$, as desired. 
\end{proof}

                                                                                                          
\begin{claim}
\label{Clm:EinE}
Suppose that $v$ lies in $\epsilon$.  
Suppose that $K_v$ is a half-disc neighbourhood of $v$ that misses $\gamma$.  
Then $K_v \cap \mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V})$ lies in $K$.
\end{claim}

\begin{proof}
Recall that $x$ and $y$ are the ideal points of $\gamma$ and that $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V}) - \{x, y\} = \delta \sqcup \epsilon$.  
Set $K_v^\circ = K_v \cap \mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V})$.  
For a contradiction, suppose that $K_v^\circ$ lies in $H$.  
Fix any cusp $d$ in $\delta$ and suppose that $H_d$ is a half-disc neighbourhood of $d$, disjoint from $\gamma$.  
By Claim~\ref{Clm:DinD}, the set $H_d^\circ$ lies in $H$.  
Let $e$ be any cusp in $\partial_\infty K_v$.  
As a bit of notation we take $K_e = K_v$. 
                                    
Since $v$ lies in $\epsilon$, which is connected, we deduce that $e$ also lies in $\epsilon$.  
Thus $(x, y)$ links $(d, e)$.

Pick rays $r_d$ and $r_e$ (contained in cusp leaves) ending at the cusps $d$ and $e$ and contained in $H_d$ and $K_e$, respectively.  
Since $H$ is path-connected, and since $H_d^\circ$ and $K_e^\circ$ both lie in $H$, there is a polygonal arc connecting a point of $r_d$ to a point of $r_e$.  
Deleting loops, we find that there is an embedded polygonal line $\rho$, contained in $H$, that has $d$ and $e$ as its ideal points.  

Note that $\gamma^\circ$ and $\rho$ are disjoint properly embedded lines in $\mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V})$.  
Thus $\rho$ divides $H$ into two components.  
We orient $\rho$ so that $H^\circ(\rho)$ is the component of $H - \rho$ that does not contain any point of $\gamma^\circ$ in its closure.  
Since $(x, y)$ links $(d, e)$, breaking symmetry, we have that $y$ lies in $\partial_\infty H(\rho)$.  
By Lemma~\ref{Lem:HalfDiscOpen} the half-disc $H(\rho)$ is open.  
Since $\gamma$ is an arc, thinking of it as a function we have that $\gamma^{-1}(H(\rho))$ is open and non-empty.                                  
So it contains an interval.  
Thus $\gamma^\circ$ meets $H^\circ(\rho)$, a contradiction.
\end{proof}

We extend our previous notation for half-discs and define $H(\gamma) = H \cup \delta$.
Let $\gamma'$ be $\gamma$ with the opposite orientation.
We take $H(\gamma') = K \cup \epsilon$.  
From the claims above, from Corollary~\ref{Cor:HalfDiscPathConnected}, 
and from the fact that $H$ and $K$ are open discs, we deduce that $H(\gamma)$ and $H(\gamma')$ are path-connected, disjoint, and open.   
Thus $\gamma$ separates, giving hypothesis (\ref{Itm:All}) of Theorem~\ref{Thm:Zippin}.

Suppose that $q$ is any point of $\gamma$.  If $q$ lies in $\mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V})$ then Theorem~\ref{Thm:Schoenflies} implies that $H \cup \{ q \} \cup K$ is path-connected.  
If $q$ lies in $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$ then $q$ is equal to one of $x$ or $y$: the ideal points of $\gamma$.  
Thus $\delta \cup \{ q \} \cup \epsilon$ is path-connected.  
In either case, $H(\gamma) \cup \{ q \} \cup H(\gamma')$ is path-connected, giving hypothesis (\ref{Itm:None}) of Theorem~\ref{Thm:Zippin}.

Thus $\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{V})$ is a closed disc with boundary $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$. 
It follows that $\mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V})$ is the interior of $\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{V})$.                                                                  
This proves property (\ref{Itm:Disc}).

        
Lemma~\ref{Lem:Extension} proves property (\ref{Itm:Ends}).

         
Cusps are dense in $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$ by construction~\cite[Theorem~7.1]{FSS22}.
Ends of non-cusp leaves are dense by Lemma~\ref{Lem:Laminations}(\ref{Itm:Approach}).
Together, these imply property (\ref{Itm:Dense}).

          
Properties (\ref{Itm:Ends}) and (\ref{Itm:Dense}) imply (with appropriate choices) the characterising properties of~\cite[Theorem~2.1]{Bonatti26}.
                                             
                                                             
                                                                                                                             
                                                          
                                                                                                                                                     
                                                                    
Property (\ref{Itm:Unique}) follows.

          
By Lemma~\ref{Lem:Action}, the action of $\pi_1(M)$ on $\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{V})$ is by homeomorphisms.  
The elements of $\pi_1(M)$ preserve the orientation of $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$~\cite[Theorem~7.1(1)]{FSS22} and of $\mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V})$~\cite[Theorem~10.8(6)]{FSS22}.  
Thus they preserve the induced orientation on $\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{V})$. 
This proves property (\ref{Itm:Action}).
<!-- end proof-27 -->
<!-- claim-1: body_md -->
The interior $\gamma^\circ$ is a Jordan line in $\mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V})$.
<!-- end claim-1 -->
<!-- proof-28: body_md -->
We must prove that $\gamma^\circ$ is properly embedded.  Fix a compact subset $K \subset \mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V})$.  Since $\gamma$ is continuous and $[0, 1]$ is compact, the preimage $\gamma^{-1}(K)$ is compact.  It is disjoint from $\{0, 1\}$ by assumption.  Note that $(\gamma^\circ)^{-1}(K) = \gamma^{-1}(K)$.  Thus the latter is compact in $(0, 1)$ and we are done.

Since $\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{V})$ is normal, and applying Lemma~\ref{Lem:HalfDiscNeighBasis},
