<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{Prop:LimitOfLeaves}
Suppose that $(\ell_i)$ is a sequence of non-cusp leaves and/or bi-leaves in $\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{V})$.
                                                            
Suppose that the closures $({\overline{\ell}}_i)$ Hausdorff converge to a set $L$.
Then $L$ is one of the following:
\begin{itemize}
\item
a point of $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$,
\item
the closure of a bi-leaf, or
\item
the closure of a non-cusp leaf. 
\end{itemize}
Furthermore, in the last two cases, let $F$ be the foliation containing $L$.
Then all but finitely many of the $\ell_i$ belong to $F$.
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- lemma-27: body_md -->
\label{Lem:TwoImpliesLeaf}
Suppose that $L$ contains two distinct points $x$ and $y$.
Then for one of the two foliations, say $F$, there is a leaf or bi-leaf $\ell_\infty$ contained in $F$ so that
\begin{itemize}
\item $L$ contains $\ell_\infty$ and 
\item both $x$ and $y$ lie in the closure of~${\ell}_\infty$.
\end{itemize}
<!-- end lemma-27 -->
<!-- proof-31: body_md -->
Since $x$ and $y$ are distinct, there is some cusp leaf $m$ that separates them.
                                                                                                           
                                                                                                              
                                                                                                       
                                                
                                                                     
Choose small basic neighbourhoods $U$ and $V$ of $x$ and $y$ disjoint from $m$.
Pass to a tail of the sequence $(\ell_i)$ so that all of the $\ell_i$ meet both $U$ and $V$.
All leaves in this tail cross $m$.
Therefore all $\ell_i$ in this tail are in one of the two foliations, say $F$.

By Theorem~\ref{Thm:Disc}(\ref{Itm:Disc}), the disc $\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{V})$ is normal and first countable.
Thus there are nested neighbourhood bases $(U_j)$ and $(V_j)$, about $x$ and $y$ respectively, so that ${\overline{U}}_j \cap {\overline{V}}_j$ is empty.

We now recurse on $j$, starting with the $j$th subsequence $(\ell_i)$ of the original sequence of leaves.
Pass to a further tail of $(\ell_i)$ whose members meet both $U_j$ and $V_j$.
We deduce that there are arcs, rays, or lines $m_x$ and $m_y$ in the boundaries of $U_j$ and $V_j$ respectively so that the leaves of an infinite subsequence
of $(\ell_i)$ cross $m_x$ and $m_y$. 
(This gives the $j+1$st subsequence of the original.)
We deduce that the leaves containing $m_x$ and $m_y$ are not in $F$.

                                      
Set $p_i = \ell_i \cap m_x$ and set $q_i = \ell_i \cap m_y$.
Note that $p_i \neq q_i$ because the closures of $U_j$ and $V_j$ are disjoint.
Set $\ell'_i = [p_i, q_i] \subset \ell_i$.

The arcs $\ell'_i$ between $m_x$ and $m_y$ all cobound rectangles (with appropriate subarcs of $m_x$ and $m_y$).
The union of these rectangles gives a rectangle $R$.
Since $\mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V})$ is a loom space (Theorem~\ref{Thm:LinkIsLoom}), 
by Definition~\ref{Def:Loom}(\ref{Itm:Tet}), we have that $R$ is contained in a tetrahedron rectangle $R'$.  
Let $\lambda_i = \ell_i \cap R'$.
Let $\lambda^j$ be the Hausdorff limit of the (closures of the) $\lambda_i$.
Thus $\lambda^j$ is either one leaf, or two leaves and a cusp, of $F \cap {\overline{R}}'$.
Note that $\lambda^j$ lies in the Hausdorff limit $L$.
This completes the recursive step.

Now let $\lambda_\infty \subset L$ be the ascending union of the $\lambda^j$.
Note that $\lambda_\infty$ accumulates (in $\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{V})$) on both $x$ and $y$.
The ascending union $\lambda_\infty$ either has no cusps, and so is contained in a leaf of $F$, or has a cusp, and so is contained in a bi-leaf of $F$.
Call this leaf or bi-leaf $\ell_\infty$.
Thus $\ell_\infty$ accumulates (in $\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{V})$) on both $x$ and $y$.

We now show that $\ell_\infty \subset L$. 
Let $p$ be any point of $\ell_\infty$.
Let $q$ be a point of $\lambda_\infty$, chosen so that $q$ and $p$ are in the same component of $\ell_\infty$.
Let $[p, q]$ be the interval of $\ell_\infty$ with endpoints $p$ and $q$.  
Let $Q$ be a rectangle containing $[p, q]$ in its interior. 
Since the leaves $\ell_i$ approach $q$, they eventually enter $Q$ and thus approach $p$.
This proves that $\ell_\infty \subset L$.
<!-- end proof-31 -->
<!-- lemma-28: body_md -->
\label{Lem:OneInteriorImpliesLeaf}
Suppose that $L$ contains a point $p$ of $\mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V})$.
Then $L$ contains the leaf $\ell_p$ of $F$ through $p$.
<!-- end lemma-28 -->
<!-- proof-32: body_md -->
Fix a rectangle $P$ containing $p$.
The $\ell_i$ eventually pass through $P$.
Thus the Hausdorff limit $L$ (of their closures) contains the leaf $\lambda_p$ of $F \cap P$ containing $p$.
We are now done by Lemma~\ref{Lem:TwoImpliesLeaf}.
<!-- end proof-32 -->
<!-- lemma-29: body_md -->
\label{Lem:CuspLeafImpliesBiLeaf}
Suppose that $L$ contains a cusp leaf $\ell_c$ with cusp $c$.
Then $L$ contains a bi-leaf $k_c$ of $F$ containing $\ell_c$.
<!-- end lemma-29 -->
<!-- proof-33: body_md -->
By Theorem~\ref{Thm:LinkIsLoom} and Definition~\ref{Def:Loom}(\ref{Itm:Cusp}), we have a rectangle $C$ so that 
\begin{itemize}
\item
$c$ lies in the interior of one of the sides of $C$ and 
\item
the interior of $C$ meets the interior of $\ell_c$.  
\end{itemize}
All but finitely many of the $\ell_i$ meet $C$.  
                                                              
See Figure~\ref{Fig:CuspLeafImpliesBiLeaf}.
Passing to a subsequence, either 
\begin{itemize}
\item
the $\ell_i$ are all the same bi-leaf, call it $k_c$, containing $\ell_c$, or
\item
the $\ell_i$ approach $\ell_c$ from one side. 
\end{itemize}
Again, see Figure~\ref{Fig:CuspLeafImpliesBiLeaf}.
In the first case, $L$ contains $k_c$ and we are done.
In the second case, Definition~\ref{Def:Loom}(\ref{Itm:Cusp}) gives a sequence of rectangles $D_i$ so that 
\begin{itemize}
\item
a side of $D_i$ is contained in $\ell_i$,
\item
the opposite side, $s_i$ say, of $D_i$, contains $c$ in its interior, and 
\item
$D_i$ is maximal with respect to the previous two properties.
\end{itemize}
Choose a point $p$ in $\ell_c \cap C$.
Consider the two staircases for $p$ that meet $C$.
Let $m_p$ be the leaf containing $p$ and crossing $\ell_c$. 
By the astroid lemma~\cite[Lemma~4.10]{SchleimerSegerman24}, the projections of the cusps of these staircases to $m_p$ accumulate at $p$.
Thus the two sides of $D_i$ in the same foliation as $m_p$ contain cusps, say $c_i$ and $c'_i$.
See Figure~\ref{Fig:CuspLeafImpliesBiLeaf}.

Applying the astroid lemma again, the projections of $c_i$ and $c'_i$ to the other axes of the staircases exit the ends of a bi-leaf with centre $c$.
We deduce that the ascending union of the sides $s_i$ is a bi-leaf, say $k_c$.
Thus $k_c$ contains $\ell_c$ and is contained in $L$.
<!-- end proof-33 -->
<!-- proof-34: body_md -->
By Lemma~\ref{Lem:OneInteriorImpliesLeaf}, the Hausdorff limit $L$ cannot be a single point of $\mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V})$.
If $L$ is a single point of $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$, we are done.
If $L$ contains at least two points of $\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{V})$ then $L$ contains a leaf, by Lemma~\ref{Lem:TwoImpliesLeaf}.

Suppose that $L$ contains exactly one leaf $\ell$.
By Lemma~\ref{Lem:CuspLeafImpliesBiLeaf}, we deduce that $\ell$ is a non-cusp leaf.
Thus $\ell = L \cap \mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V})$ by Lemma~\ref{Lem:OneInteriorImpliesLeaf}.
Suppose that $x$ is a point of $L - \ell$.
Let $y$ be any point in $\ell$.
By Lemma~\ref{Lem:TwoImpliesLeaf}, we find that $x$ lies in the closure of ${\ell}$.
Thus in this case, $L$ is the closure of ${\ell}$ as desired.

Suppose that $L$ contains at least two distinct leaves $\ell$ and $\ell'$.
Pick $x$ and $y$ to be points in the interiors of $\ell$ and $\ell'$, respectively.
By Lemma~\ref{Lem:TwoImpliesLeaf}, we deduce that there is a cusp $c$ so that $k_c = \ell \cup \{c\} \cup \ell'$ is a bi-leaf. 
Suppose now that $z$ is a point of $L - k_c$.
By Lemma~\ref{Lem:TwoImpliesLeaf}, we find that $z$ lies in the closure of ${k}_c$.
Thus in this case, $L$ is the closure of ${k}_c$ as desired.
<!-- end proof-34 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{Prop:SingleLeaf}
Suppose that $x$ is a point of $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V}) - \Delta_\mathcal{V}$.
Then there is a sequence of non-cusp leaves $(\ell_i)$ so that the half-discs $H(\ell_i)$ give a neighbourhood basis for $x$ in $\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{V})$.
Furthermore, if $x$ is the end of a leaf $m$ then the $\ell_i$ all cross $m$.
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-35: body_md -->
Suppose first that $x$ is an ideal point of a leaf $m$.
By Lemma~\ref{Lem:Extension} we may pick a sequence of points $p_k \in m$ converging to $x$. 
Let $\ell_k$ be the leaf of the opposite foliation to $m$ so that $m \cap \ell_k = p_k$.
Since non-cusp leaves are dense, we may perturb the $p_k$ to ensure that the leaves $\ell_k$ are not cusp leaves.
Pass to a subsequence so that the closures of the $\ell_k$ Hausdorff converge to a set $L$.
Note that $x$ lies in $L$.
By Proposition~\ref{Prop:LimitOfLeaves} and the fact that $x$ is not a cusp, we have that $L = \{ x \}$. 
                                                       
                                                                                        
                                                                                                       
                                                                                      
                                                                    
Fix any oriented embedded polygonal line $\rho$ so that $H(\rho)$ is a neighbourhood of $x$.
Since the $\ell_i$ Hausdorff converge to $x$, all but finitely many are contained in $H(\rho)$.
Thus, for sufficiently large $i$, the neighbourhood $H(\ell_i)$ (with $\ell_i$ oriented appropriately) is contained in $H(\rho)$.

Suppose now that $x$ is a singleton.
Fix a reference point $w \in \mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V}) - \{x\}$.
Choose a sequence $\rho_i$ so that $H(\rho_i)$ is a neighbourhood basis of $x$.
After passing to a subsequence, none of the $H(\rho_i)$ contain $w$.
Thus there is some leaf $\ell_i$ containing a segment of $\rho_i$ so that $H(\ell_i)$ contains $x$ and not $w$.
                       
                                                                    
                                                                      
                                                                      
                                 
By Remark~\ref{Rem:NonCuspLeavesDense} non-cusp leaves are dense.
So we may replace $\ell_i$ by a nearby non-cusp leaf that again separates $x$ from $w$.
                                                                    
                            

As before, we pass to a subsequence so that the closures of the $\ell_i$ Hausdorff converge to a set $L$.
Note that $L$ contains $x$.
Because $x$ is a singleton, it is not contained in the closure of any bi-leaf or non-cusp leaf.
The remainder of the argument is as in the first case.
<!-- end proof-35 -->
<!-- definition-24: body_md -->
\label{Def:Sector}
Suppose that $p \in \mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V}) \cup \Delta_\mathcal{V}$.
Suppose that $S^\circ$ is a component of $\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{V})$ minus the (closures of the) leaves at $p$.
We call the closure of $S^\circ$ a \emph{sector} at $p$.
Two sectors at $p$ are \emph{adjacent} if they share a point other than $p$.
<!-- end definition-24 -->
<!-- lemma-30: body_md -->
\label{Lem:NoneShallPass}
Suppose that $S$ is a sector based at a cusp $d$.
Suppose that $C$ is a clamshell boundary associated to a cusp $c$.
Suppose that $c$ is not in $\partial_\infty S$.
Then we have
\begin{enumerate}
\item
\label{Itm:MeetsOne}
$\partial_\infty C$ meets precisely one of the two components of $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V}) - \partial_\infty S$.
\item
\label{Itm:NoBoundary}
$\partial_\infty C$ does not contain $d$, nor the thorns at the ends of the bounding leaves of $S$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-30 -->
<!-- proof-36: body_md -->
The cusp $c$ lies in one of the two components.
Suppose that $\ell$ and $m$ are the boundary leaves of $S$.
Breaking symmetry, suppose that $\ell$ separates $c$ from $S$.
Any cusp leaf of $c$ crossing $\ell$ cannot cross $m$.
This proves (\ref{Itm:MeetsOne}).
We have that $c \neq d$, which implies (\ref{Itm:NoBoundary}).
<!-- end proof-36 -->
<!-- lemma-31: body_md -->
\label{Lem:IVT}
Suppose that $\ell$ is a leaf and $x$ is a singleton.
Suppose that either
\begin{itemize}
\item $\ell$ is a non-cusp leaf or
\item $\ell$ is a cusp leaf on the boundary of a sector $S$ containing $x$.
\end{itemize}
Then there is a cusp $c$ with cusp leaves $m$, $m'$, and $m''$ so that:
\begin{itemize}
\item $m$ crosses $\ell$,
\item $m$ and $m'$ form a bi-leaf, as do $m$ and $m''$, and
\item exactly one of $m'$ or $m''$ separates $\ell$ from $x$. 
\end{itemize}
<!-- end lemma-31 -->
<!-- proof-37: body_md -->
Breaking symmetry, suppose that $\ell$ belongs to $F^\mathcal{V}$.
Breaking symmetry again, suppose that $x$ is to the right of $\ell$.
Let $R_\ell$ be the set of rays in non-cusp leaves of $F_\mathcal{V}$ emanating from $\ell$ to the right.
Let $C_\ell$ be the closure of the endpoints at infinity $\partial_\infty R_\ell$. 
Note that $C_\ell$ is a Cantor set; the argument is similar to that in~\cite[Lemma~8.24]{FSS22}. 
Let $U$ be the complementary component of $C_\ell$ in $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$ which contains $x$.
Then there is a unique cusp $c$ with the following properties.
\begin{itemize}
\item $c$ lies in $U$ and
\item $c$ has a cusp leaf $m$ that crosses $\ell$.
\end{itemize}
(When $\ell$ is a cusp leaf, this is where we use the sector $S$.)
Let $m'$ and $m''$ be the cusp leaves at $c$ whose endpoints are the endpoints of $U$.
<!-- end proof-37 -->
<!-- corollary-5: body_md -->
\label{Cor:SingletonSingleLeaf}
With hypotheses as in Proposition~\ref{Prop:SingleLeaf}, if $x$ is a singleton then we may choose the sequence $(\ell_i)$ to lie in either foliation.
<!-- end corollary-5 -->
<!-- proof-38: body_md -->
Let $(\ell_i)$ be the sequence provided by Proposition~\ref{Prop:SingleLeaf}.
If the $\ell_i$ lie in both foliations infinitely often then we are done.
Breaking symmetry, suppose that all but finitely many of the $\ell_i$ belong to $F^\mathcal{V}$.
For each $\ell_i$, Lemma~\ref{Lem:IVT} gives a cusp $c_i$.
Let $S_i$ be the sector at $c_i$ which contains $x$.
Let $S'_i$ be the sector adjacent to $S_i$ across a leaf of $F^\mathcal{V}$.
Let $m'_i$ be the bi-leaf boundary of $S_i \cup S'_i$.
Let $m_i$ be a non-cusp leaf sufficiently close to $m'_i$.
Note that $H(m_i)$ is contained in $H(\ell_i)$.
Then $(m_i)$ is the desired sequence of non-cusp leaves.
<!-- end proof-38 -->
<!-- lemma-32: body_md -->
\label{Lem:Perturb}
Every non-cusp leaf $\ell$ is a limit (on either side) of non-cusp leaves $(\ell_k)$ in the same foliation.
Furthermore, the ideal points of $\ell_k$ tend to those of $\ell$ in $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$.
<!-- end lemma-32 -->
<!-- proof-39: body_md -->
By Proposition~\ref{Prop:SingleLeaf} we can pick sequences of non-cusp leaves $(m_k)$ and $(m'_k)$ exiting the two ends of $\ell$.
Fix $k$.
Let $L_k$ be the segment of $\ell$ between $m_k$ and $m'_k$.
Since $\mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V})$ is a loom space, $L_k$ is contained in a rectangle $R_k$.
By Remark~\ref{Rem:NonCuspLeavesDense} non-cusp leaves are dense.
So we can find a non-cusp leaf $\ell_k$ crossing $R_k$ (on either side of $\ell$) which forms a rectangle with $\ell$, $m_k$, and $m'_k$.
<!-- end proof-39 -->
<!-- remark-11: body_md -->
Lemma~\ref{Lem:Perturb} does not hold for cusp leaves.
It holds on the ``non-cusp side'' of a bi-leaf.  
However we will not use this fact.
<!-- end remark-11 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{Prop:LimitOfRectangles}
Suppose that $(R_i)$ is a sequence of skeletal rectangles in $\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{V})$.
Suppose that the closures ${\overline{R}}_i$ Hausdorff converge to a set $L$.  
Then $L$ is one of the following:
\begin{itemize}
\item
a point of $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$,
\item
the closure of a leaf (cusp or non-cusp),
\item
the closure of a bi-leaf, or
\item
the closure of a skeletal rectangle.
\end{itemize}
The last possibility can only occur if the sequence is eventually constant.
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- definition-25: body_md -->
\label{Def:Spans}
Suppose that $Q$ and $R$ are rectangles in $\mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V})$.  
We say that $Q$ \emph{south-north spans} $R$ if $Q \cap R$ contains a leaf of $R \cap F^\mathcal{V}$.
We define \emph{west-east spans} similarly, using $F_\mathcal{V}$.
<!-- end definition-25 -->
<!-- proof-40: body_md -->
Throughout we use the fact that $\mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V})$ is a loom space (Theorem~\ref{Thm:LinkIsLoom}).
If $L$ is a single point of $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$ then we are done.

\begin{claim*}
Suppose that $L$ contains two distinct points $x$ and $y$ of $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$.
Then $L$ contains a point of $\mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V})$.
\end{claim*}

\begin{proof}
We use an (easier) version of the proof of Lemma~\ref{Lem:TwoImpliesLeaf}.
Pick $U$ and $V$ basic open sets about $x$ and $y$, respectively, having disjoint closures.
Passing to a subsequence of $(R_i)$ there are arcs, rays, or lines $m_x$ and $m_y$ in the boundaries of $U$ and $V$, respectively, crossed by all of the rectangles $R_i$.
Let $Q_i \subset R_i$ be the maximal subrectangle having one side in $m_x$ and one in $m_y$.
Let $Q \subset \mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V})$ be the smallest rectangle containing all of the $Q_i$.
Breaking symmetry, we may assume that all of the $Q_i$ south-north span $Q$.
Definition~\ref{Def:Loom}(\ref{Itm:Tet}) gives us a tetrahedron rectangle $R$ containing $Q$.
Thus the Hausdorff limit of the sequence $({\overline{Q}}_i)$ contains a non-trivial segment of a leaf of $F^\mathcal{V} \cap {\overline{R}}$.
Thus $L$ contains a point of $\mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V})$. 
\end{proof}

Suppose that the limit $L$ contains $P$, a rectangle in $\mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V})$.
Shrinking $P$ slightly, and passing to a subsequence, we may assume that all of the $R_i$ contain $P$.
Now~\cite[Lemma~4.16]{SchleimerSegerman24}
tells us that there are only finitely many skeletal rectangles containing $P$.
Thus $L$ is the closure of a skeletal rectangle $R_\infty$ and $R_i=R_\infty$ for sufficiently large $i$.

We are left with the case that $L$ contains a point $p$ of $\mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V})$, but does not contain a rectangle.
Let $P$ be any rectangle containing $p$.
We fix a homeomorphism $f_P \colon (0, 1)^2 \to P$ sending the vertical and horizontal foliations to $F^\mathcal{V}$ and $F_\mathcal{V}$, respectively. 
Passing to a subsequence, we may assume that all of the rectangles $R_i$ meet $P$.
Since $L$ contains no rectangle, we deduce that either the widths or the heights of the preimages $f_P^{-1}(R_i)$ tend to zero.
Breaking symmetry, we may assume that the widths tend to zero.
It follows that the $R_i$ south-north span $P$.

Let $k^W_i$ be the bi-leaf containing the west side of $R_i$ whose divider (see Definition~\ref{Def:BiLeaf}) meets the closure of $R_i$.
We define $k^E_i$ similarly.
Let $L^W$ and $L^E$ be the Hausdorff limits of the sequences $({\overline{k^W_i}})$ and $({\overline{k^E_i}})$, respectively.
Since the widths of the $f_P^{-1}(R_i)$ tend to zero, we find that $L^W$ and $L^E$ contain $p$.
It follows from Proposition~\ref{Prop:LimitOfLeaves} that $L^W$ and $L^E$ contain the closure of $\ell_p$, the leaf of $F^\mathcal{V}$ through $p$.

There are now two subcases, as $\ell_p$ is not, or is, a cusp leaf.
Suppose that $\ell_p$ is not a cusp leaf.
By Proposition~\ref{Prop:LimitOfLeaves} the limits $L^W$ and $L^E$ both equal the closure of $\ell_p$.
Thus $L$ is a subset of the closure of $\ell_p$.
To prove that $L$ is equal to the closure of $\ell_p$, we argue as follows.
Consider the four staircases for $p$.
The rectangles $R_i$ are contained in the union of these staircases.
Since the widths of the $R_i$ go to zero, the astroid lemma~\cite[Lemma~4.10]{SchleimerSegerman24} implies that (the projections of) the north and south sides of the $R_i$ exit the ends of $\ell_p$.
(See Figure~\ref{Fig:Astroid} for an example.)
Thus $L$ is the closure of $\ell_p$.

In the other subcase $\ell_p$ is a cusp leaf.
Suppose that $c$ is the cusp of $\ell_p$.
Breaking symmetry, suppose that $c$ is the southern ideal point of $\ell_p$. 
After passing to a subsequence of the $R_i$ there are two possibilities, as follows.
\begin{itemize}
\item
The cusp $c$ lies on the south side of all of the rectangles $R_i$.
By an argument similar to the one above (applied only to the north sides of the $R_i$), the astroid lemma~\cite[Lemma~4.10]{SchleimerSegerman24} implies that $L$ is the closure of $\ell_p$ and we are done.
\item
The cusp $c$ does not lie in the south side of any of the $R_i$.
Breaking symmetry again, and passing to a further subsequence, we may assume that the rectangles $R_i$ accumulate on $\ell_p$ from the west.
Consider the staircase $\Gamma$ for $p$ so that $p$ is its north-east point.
So $c$ lies in the eastern boundary of $\Gamma$.
Let $\ell_c$ be the cusp leaf lying in the boundary of $\Gamma$ that emanates southward from $c$.
We deduce that $k_c = \ell_p \cup \{c\} \cup \ell_c$ is a bi-leaf.
We next prove that $L$ equals the closure of $k_c$.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\labellist
\small\hair 2pt
\pinlabel $p$      [l] at 585 578
\pinlabel $c$      [l] at 585 267
\pinlabel $\ell_p$ [l] at 583 410
\pinlabel $\ell_c$ [l] at 583 130
\pinlabel $R_i$        at 341 412
\pinlabel $c_i$    [b] at 402 227
\endlabellist
\includegraphics[height=0.7\textwidth]{Figures/sneaky_rectangles}
\caption{A sequence of skeletal rectangles $R_i$, accumulating on $p$ from the west and thus meeting the staircase $\Gamma$. 
We do not draw most of the cusps incident to the $R_i$.}
\label{Fig:SneakyRectangles}
\end{figure}

Recall that the skeletal rectangles $R_i$ accumulate on $p$ from the west.
Thus, after passing to a subsequence, they all meet $\Gamma$.
See Figure~\ref{Fig:SneakyRectangles}.
Let $s_i$ be the southern side of the rectangle $R_i \cap \Gamma$.
Thus $s_i$ meets a (westward) cusp leaf emanating from a cusp $c_i$ in the south-west boundary of $\Gamma$.
The astroid lemma~\cite[Lemma~4.10]{SchleimerSegerman24} tells us that the (eastward projections of the) cusps $c_i$ eventually land in $\ell_c$, and then exit to the south.
We deduce that the $R_i$ accumulate on the cusp $c$ from the west.
Arguing as above we deduce that the Hausdorff limits $L$, $L^W$, and $L^E$ all equal the closure of $k_c$, as desired.
\end{itemize}

This completes the proof of Proposition~\ref{Prop:LimitOfRectangles}.
<!-- end proof-40 -->
<!-- claim--4: body_md -->
Suppose that $L$ contains two distinct points $x$ and $y$ of $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$.
Then $L$ contains a point of $\mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V})$.
<!-- end claim--4 -->
<!-- proof-41: body_md -->
We use an (easier) version of the proof of Lemma~\ref{Lem:TwoImpliesLeaf}.
Pick $U$ and $V$ basic open sets about $x$ and $y$, respectively, having disjoint closures.
Passing to a subsequence of $(R_i)$ there are arcs, rays, or lines $m_x$ and $m_y$ in the boundaries of $U$ and $V$, respectively, crossed by all of the rectangles $R_i$.
Let $Q_i \subset R_i$ be the maximal subrectangle having one side in $m_x$ and one in $m_y$.
Let $Q \subset \mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V})$ be the smallest rectangle containing all of the $Q_i$.
Breaking symmetry, we may assume that all of the $Q_i$ south-north span $Q$.
Definition~\ref{Def:Loom}(\ref{Itm:Tet}) gives us a tetrahedron rectangle $R$ containing $Q$.
Thus the Hausdorff limit of the sequence $({\overline{Q}}_i)$ contains a non-trivial segment of a leaf of $F^\mathcal{V} \cap {\overline{R}}$.
Thus $L$ contains a point of $\mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V})$.
<!-- end proof-41 -->
<!-- definition-26: body_md -->
\label{Def:Collapsing}
Suppose that $Z$ is a compactum with at least three points.
Suppose that $(g_i)_{i\in\mathbb{N}}$ is a sequence of homeomorphisms of $Z$ to itself.
Suppose that $x, y \in Z$ are points (not necessarily distinct).
Suppose that the restrictions $g_i|(Z - \{x\})$ converge uniformly on compact sets to the constant map $(Z - \{x\}) \to \{y\}$.
Then we call $(g_i)$ a \emph{collapsing sequence}.
Also, we call $x$ a \emph{repelling} point, and we call $y$ an \emph{attracting} point, for the sequence.
<!-- end definition-26 -->
<!-- remark-12: body_md -->
Note that collapsing sequences have unique repellers and attractors.
<!-- end remark-12 -->
<!-- definition-27: body_md -->
\label{Def:Convergence}
Suppose that $Z$ is a compactum with at least three points.
Suppose that $G$ is a countable group acting by homeomorphisms of $Z$.  
Then $G$ is a \emph{convergence group} if every infinite sequence of distinct elements of $G$ has a subsequence which is a collapsing sequence.  
We may also say $G\curvearrowright Z$ is a \emph{convergence action}.
<!-- end definition-27 -->
<!-- remark-13: body_md -->
\label{Rem:FiniteIndex}
Suppose that $G$ acts on $Z$.
Suppose that $H < G$ is a subgroup of finite index. 
Suppose that the induced action of $H$ on $Z$ is a convergence action. 
Then the action of $G$ on $Z$ is a convergence action.
<!-- end remark-13 -->
<!-- definition-28: body_md -->
\label{Def:CLP}
Suppose that $G \curvearrowright Z$ is a convergence action.
Suppose that $x, y, z \in Z$ are points, with $y \neq z$.
Suppose that $(g_i)_{i \in \mathbb{N}}$ is a collapsing sequence with $x$ and $y$ as its repeller and attractor, respectively.
Suppose that $(g_i(x))$ converges to $z$.
Then we call $x$ a \emph{conical limit point} of the action.
<!-- end definition-28 -->
<!-- definition-29: body_md -->
Let $f \colon Z \to Z$ be a homeomorphism.
We say that $f$ is \emph{loxodromic} if it is of infinite order and it has precisely two fixed points.
<!-- end definition-29 -->
<!-- definition-30: body_md -->
\label{Def:Parabolic}
Suppose that $G \curvearrowright Z$ is a convergence action.  
Suppose that $x \in Z$ has infinite stabiliser, but no loxodromic fixes $x$. 
Then we call $x$ a \emph{parabolic point} of the action.
                                                                         

Furthermore, suppose that the stabiliser of $x$ acts cocompactly on $Z - \{x\}$.
Then we call $x$ a \emph{bounded} parabolic point.
Finally, we call the stabiliser of any parabolic point a \emph{maximal parabolic} subgroup for the action.
<!-- end definition-30 -->
<!-- definition-31: body_md -->
\label{Def:GeoFinConv}
Suppose that $G \curvearrowright Z$ is a convergence action. 
Suppose that every point of $Z$ is either a conical limit point or is a bounded parabolic point. 
Then we call the action \emph{geometrically finite}.
<!-- end definition-31 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{Thm:HyperbolicGeomFinite}
Suppose that $M$ is a finite-volume cusped hyperbolic three-manifold.
Then the induced action of $\pi_1(M)$ on $\partial_\infty \mathbb{H}^3$ is a geometrically finite convergence action.
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- definition-32: body_md -->
Suppose that $(G, \mathcal{P})$ is a group pair. 
Suppose that $X$ is a connected simplicial graph. 
Suppose that $G \curvearrowright X$ acts via graph automorphisms.
Suppose, moreover, that: 
\begin{enumerate}
\item            
$X$ is Gromov hyperbolic,
\item 
$X$ is \emph{fine}: for any edge $e$ and any $n>0$, there are finitely many embedded edge-circuits of length $n$ containing $e$,
\item               
the action $G \curvearrowright X$ is cocompact, 
\item               
$\mathcal{P}$ is the set of infinite stabilisers of vertices,
\item
every $P \in \mathcal{P}$ is finitely generated, and
\item              
edge stabilisers are finite.
\end{enumerate}
Then we call $(G, \mathcal{P})$ \emph{hyperbolic in the sense of Bowditch}.
<!-- end definition-32 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
\label{Thm:Yaman}
Suppose that $Z$ is a perfect metrisable compactum, with at least three points.
Suppose that $G$ acts on $Z$ via a geometrically finite convergence action.
Let $\mathcal{P}$ be the set of maximal parabolics.
                                                                                      
                                                     
Suppose that every $P$ in $\mathcal{P}$ is finitely generated.
Suppose that $\mathcal{P} / G$ is finite.
Then $(G, \mathcal{P})$ is hyperbolic in the sense of Bowditch.
                                                                                        

Suppose that $Z'$ is another such compactum, equipped with another such action by $G$, having the same set of maximal parabolics.
Then there is a $G$--equivariant homeomorphism from $Z$ to $Z'$. \qed
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label{Prop:Convergence}
Suppose that $M$ is a three-manifold with boundary.
Suppose that $\mathcal{V}$ is a locally veering triangulation on $M$.
The action of $\pi_1(M)$ on the veering two-sphere $\mathcal{S}^2(\mathcal{V})$ is a convergence action.
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- remark-14: body_md -->
\label{Rem:Cover}
We may replace the hypothesis that $\mathcal{V}$ is a locally veering triangulation by the hypothesis that $\mathcal{V}$ is a transverse veering triangulation.
We do this by taking the appropriate number of degree-two covers and appealing to Remark~\ref{Rem:FiniteIndex}.
<!-- end remark-14 -->
<!-- lemma-33: body_md -->
\label{Lem:Diagonal}
There is a subsequence of $(g_i)$ that, after reindexing, gives the following.
\begin{enumerate}
\item Suppose that $c$ is a cusp. 
Then the sequence $(g_i(c))$ converges in~$\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$. 
\item Suppose that $k$ is a bi-leaf.
Then the sequence $\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\left(g_i\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\left({\overline{k}}\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\right)\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\right)$ Hausdorff converges in~$\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{V})$.
\item Suppose that $R$ is a skeletal rectangle.
Then the sequence $\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\left(g_i\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\left({\overline{R}}\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\right)\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\right)$ Hausdorff converges in~$\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{V})$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-33 -->
<!-- proof-42: body_md -->
There are only countably many cusps, bi-leaves, and skeletal rectangles~\cite[Corollary~4.25]{SchleimerSegerman24}.
For each there is a subsequence that (Hausdorff) converges by the compactness of $\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{V})$ (by Theorem~\ref{Thm:Disc}).
Thus, passing to subsequences countably many times and taking a diagonal gives the result.
<!-- end proof-42 -->
<!-- lemma-34: body_md -->
\label{Lem:WellDef}
For any cusp $c$, the point $\lim_i g_i(c)$ lies in $A$.
<!-- end lemma-34 -->
<!-- proof-43: body_md -->
Recall that ${\widetilde{\mathcal{V}}}$ is the induced ideal triangulation of the universal cover.
Since ${\widetilde{\mathcal{V}}}$ is connected there is a chain of tetrahedra glued along faces which joins $c_0$ to $c$.
Recall that the veering tetrahedra of ${\widetilde{\mathcal{V}}}$ are in bijection with the tetrahedron rectangles of $\mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V})$. 
Thus there is a finite sequence $(R_j)_{j=0}^n$ of skeletal rectangles satisfying the following:
\begin{itemize}
\item
${\overline{R}}_0$ meets $c_0$;
\item
$R_j$ meets $R_{j+1}$ (along a face rectangle) for each $j<n$; and
\item
${\overline{R}}_n$ meets $c$.  
\end{itemize}
For each $j$, Lemma~\ref{Lem:Diagonal} implies that the sequence $g_i({\overline{R}}_j)$ Hausdorff converges to some set $L_j$. Proposition~\ref{Prop:LimitOfRectangles} enumerates the possibilities for $L_j$.
Since the $g_i$ are all distinct, the sequence $g_i(R_j)$ is not eventually constant 
                                                                                    
and the limit $L_j$ is either a point of $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$, the closure of a leaf, or the closure of a bi-leaf.  In any of these cases $L_j \cap \mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$ lies in a decomposition element $A_j$.
Let $Q_j = R_j \cap R_{j+1}$.
Applying Proposition~\ref{Prop:LimitOfRectangles} to $g_i({\overline{Q_j}})$, we deduce that $L_j$ meets $L_{j+1}$.  
Hence $A_j$ meets $A_{j+1}$.  
But decomposition elements meet if and only if they are equal.  
Thus $A_n = A_0 = A$.
<!-- end proof-43 -->
<!-- lemma-35: body_md -->
\label{Lem:Direction}
By passing to a subsequence of $(g_i)$ we obtain the following property.  
For any pair of cusps $c, d \in \Delta_\mathcal{V}$ the sequence 
\[
\mathcal{O}_\mathcal{V}( g_i(c), g_i(d), r )
\]
is eventually constant. \qed
<!-- end lemma-35 -->
<!-- definition-33: body_md -->
Let $a\in A$.  
The set $I(a)\subset \Delta_\mathcal{V}$ consists of those cusps $c$ so that $\lim_ig_i(c) = a$.
<!-- end definition-33 -->
<!-- remark-15: body_md -->
\label{Rem:AttractorPartition}
By Lemma~\ref{Lem:WellDef}, the sets $I(a)$ partition the cusps $\Delta_\mathcal{V}$.
<!-- end remark-15 -->
<!-- definition-34: body_md -->
A \emph{collapsing interval} $J$ in $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$ is a closed interval so that, for some $a$ in $A$, the restrictions $g_i|J$ converge uniformly to the constant map $J\to\{a\}$.
In this case we say that $J$ \emph{collapses to} $a$ and we say that $J$ is an $a$--\emph{interval}.
<!-- end definition-34 -->
<!-- lemma-36: body_md -->
\label{Lem:Union}
Suppose that $I$ and $J$ are collapsing intervals.
Suppose that $I$ and $J$ intersect.
Then $I \cup J$ is a collapsing interval.
<!-- end lemma-36 -->
<!-- proof-44: body_md -->
Suppose that $I$ collapses to $a$ and $J$ collapses to $b$.
Since $I$ and $J$ intersect, we deduce that $a = b$.
Choose a neighbourhood $U$ of $a$.
Thus there exists $i_0$ so that for all $i \geq i_0$ we have that $g_i(I) \subset U$.
We define $j_0$ similarly for $J$.
So for $i \geq \max\{i_0, j_0\}$ we have $g_i(I \cup J) \subset U$.
Thus $I \cup J$ converges uniformly to $a$.
However, there is no sequence of homeomorphisms of the circle to itself which converges uniformly to a constant map.
               
Thus $I \cup J$ is an interval and thus is an $a$--interval.
<!-- end proof-44 -->
<!-- lemma-37: body_md -->
\label{Lem:a_interval}
Fix $a \in A$, and suppose $c, d \in I(a)$.
Then exactly one of $[c, d]^{\rotatebox[origin=c]{-90}{\scalebox{0.7}{$\curvearrowleft$}}}$, $[d, c]^{\rotatebox[origin=c]{-90}{\scalebox{0.7}{$\curvearrowleft$}}}$ is an $a$--interval.
<!-- end lemma-37 -->
<!-- proof-45: body_md -->
If both intervals were $a$--intervals then, since their union is $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$, we would contradict Lemma~\ref{Lem:Union}.

Let $(U_j)_{j\in\mathbb{N}}$ be a nested neighbourhood basis of $a$, chosen so that $U_0$ misses the reference point $r$.  
By Lemma~\ref{Lem:Direction}, there is an $n_0$ so that for all $i\geq n_0$, we have $\mathcal{O}_\mathcal{V}(g_i(c), g_i(d), r) = \mathcal{O}_\mathcal{V}(g_{n_0}(c), g_{n_0}(d), r)$.  
Moreover for any $j$ there is an $n_j\geq n_0$ so that $\{g_i(c),g_i(d)\}\subset U_j$ whenever $i\geq n_j$.  
If $\mathcal{O}_\mathcal{V}(g_{n_0}(c), g_{n_0}(d), r) = 1$, then we have $g_i([c, d]^{\rotatebox[origin=c]{-90}{\scalebox{0.7}{$\curvearrowleft$}}})\subset U_j$ for all $i\ge n_j$ and thus $[c, d]^{\rotatebox[origin=c]{-90}{\scalebox{0.7}{$\curvearrowleft$}}}$ is an $a$--interval.  
Otherwise $g_i([d, c]^{\rotatebox[origin=c]{-90}{\scalebox{0.7}{$\curvearrowleft$}}})\subset U_j$ for all $i\ge n_j$ and so $[d, c]^{\rotatebox[origin=c]{-90}{\scalebox{0.7}{$\curvearrowleft$}}}$ is an $a$--interval.
<!-- end proof-45 -->
<!-- corollary-6: body_md -->
\label{Cor:ConnectedI(a)}
For any $a \in A$, the set $I(a)$ is the intersection of $\Delta_\mathcal{V}$ with some connected (possibly empty) subset of $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$. \qed
<!-- end corollary-6 -->
<!-- definition-35: body_md -->
\label{Def:Parting}
We say $p \in \mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$ is a \emph{parting} for $(g_i)$ if it does not lie in the interior of a collapsing interval.
The set $P$ of partings for the sequence $(g_i)$ is called the \emph{parting set}.
<!-- end definition-35 -->
<!-- lemma-38: body_md -->
\label{Lem:Parting}
The parting set $P$ is closed and non-empty.
<!-- end lemma-38 -->
<!-- proof-46: body_md -->
From the definition, the complement of $P$ is open in $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$.
For a contradiction, suppose that $P$ is empty.
Then $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$ is covered by the interiors of collapsing intervals, hence by finitely many.
However, this contradicts Lemma~\ref{Lem:Union}.
<!-- end proof-46 -->
<!-- lemma-39: body_md -->
\label{Lem:AtMostTwo}
For all $a \in A$, the intersection $I(a) \cap P$ has at most two points.
<!-- end lemma-39 -->
<!-- proof-47: body_md -->
Suppose for contradiction that $p$, $q$, and $r$ are distinct cusps of $I(a) \cap P$, ordered anticlockwise.
By Lemma~\ref{Lem:a_interval} and Definition~\ref{Def:Parting} we have that $[p, q]^{\rotatebox[origin=c]{-90}{\scalebox{0.7}{$\curvearrowleft$}}}$ is an $a$--interval.
                                                                    
Similarly $[q, r]^{\rotatebox[origin=c]{-90}{\scalebox{0.7}{$\curvearrowleft$}}}$ is an $a$--interval.
Therefore $[p, r]^{\rotatebox[origin=c]{-90}{\scalebox{0.7}{$\curvearrowleft$}}}$ is an $a$--interval that contains the parting point $q$, a contradiction.
<!-- end proof-47 -->
<!-- lemma-40: body_md -->
\label{Lem:ClosedSubIntervals}
Suppose that $C$ is a component of $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V}) - P$.
Then every closed sub-interval of $C$ is a collapsing interval.
<!-- end lemma-40 -->
<!-- proof-48: body_md -->
Suppose that $c$ and $d$ are points of $C$.
Let $J$ be the interval in $C$ with endpoints at $c$ and $d$.
Since there are no partings in $C$, the interval $J$ is covered by the interiors of collapsing intervals.
Lemma~\ref{Lem:Union} implies that $J$ is a collapsing interval.
<!-- end proof-48 -->
<!-- lemma-41: body_md -->
\label{Lem:I(a)Component}
Suppose that, for some $a \in A$, the set $I(a)$ contains at least two points of $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$.
Then there is a component $C$ of $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V}) - P$ whose closure contains $I(a)$.
Furthermore, $C \cap \Delta_\mathcal{V}$ is contained in the set $I(a)$.
<!-- end lemma-41 -->
<!-- proof-49: body_md -->
Since $I(a)$ has at least two points, Lemma~\ref{Lem:a_interval} implies that $I(a)$ is countably infinite.
By Lemma~\ref{Lem:AtMostTwo}, the difference $I(a) - P$ is non-empty.
So, again using Lemma~\ref{Lem:a_interval}, there is a unique component $C$ of $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V}) - P$ containing $I(a) - P$.
                                                                                                                                               
By Lemma~\ref{Lem:Parting}, the component $C$ is an open interval.
Any points of $I(a) \cap P$ must be boundary points of $C$ by Lemma~\ref{Lem:a_interval} and Definition~\ref{Def:Parting}.
This gives the first half of the lemma.
The second half of the lemma follows from Lemma~\ref{Lem:ClosedSubIntervals}.
<!-- end proof-49 -->
<!-- lemma-42: body_md -->
\label{Lem:AlmostCollapsing}
On $\mathcal{S}^2(\mathcal{V}) - \Psi_\mathcal{V}(P)$, the maps $(g_i)$ uniformly converge on compact sets to the constant map with image $A$.
<!-- end lemma-42 -->
<!-- proof-50: body_md -->
Suppose that $K\subset \mathcal{S}^2(\mathcal{V}) - \Psi_\mathcal{V}(P)$ is compact.  
Then the preimage $\Psi_\mathcal{V}^{-1}(K)$ is compact and misses the closed set $P$.  
                                        
In particular $\Psi_\mathcal{V}^{-1}(K)$ is contained in finitely many closed intervals disjoint from $P$.
Each of the finitely many intervals is a collapsing interval by Lemma~\ref{Lem:ClosedSubIntervals}. 
So for any open neighbourhood $U$ of $A$ in $\mathcal{S}^2(\mathcal{V})$, and for all but finitely many $i$, the set $g_i(\Psi_\mathcal{V}^{-1}(K))$ lies in $\Psi_\mathcal{V}^{-1}(U)$.
                                                                                                   
Thus for all but finitely many $i$, the image $g_i(K)$ lies in $U$.
<!-- end proof-50 -->
<!-- lemma-43: body_md -->
\label{Lem:OrdersAgree}
Suppose that $a_1$, $a_2$, and $a_3$ are distinct elements of $A$, and that $c_j \in I(a_j)$ for each $j$.  
Then $\mathcal{O}_\mathcal{V}(c_1, c_2, c_3) = \mathcal{O}_\mathcal{V}(a_1, a_2, a_3)$.
<!-- end lemma-43 -->
<!-- proof-51: body_md -->
By Remark~\ref{Rem:Cover}, we have that $\mathcal{V}$ is transverse veering. 
Thus the action $\pi_1(M)\curvearrowright\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$ preserves the circular order.
<!-- end proof-51 -->
<!-- lemma-44: body_md -->
\label{Lem:InaccessibleCusps}
Let $a \in A$.  Then $I(a)$ is either
\begin{itemize}
\item empty,
\item a singleton,
\item $J \cap \Delta_\mathcal{V}$ where $J$ is a closed interval in $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$, or
\item all of $\Delta_\mathcal{V}$.
\end{itemize}
<!-- end lemma-44 -->
<!-- proof-52: body_md -->
\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\labellist
\small\hair 3pt
\pinlabel $C$ [r] at 3 140
\pinlabel $\ell$ [bl] at 56 120
\pinlabel $m$ [bl] at 28 110
\pinlabel $c$ [tr] at 34 34
\endlabellist
\includegraphics[width=0.6\textwidth]{Figures/cusp_at_end_of_interval}
\caption{The bi-leaves $\ell$ and $m$ are drawn with thick dashed lines.}
\label{Fig:CuspAtEndOfInterval}
\end{figure}
  
Corollary~\ref{Cor:ConnectedI(a)} tells us that $I(a) = C \cap \Delta_\mathcal{V}$ where $C$ is a connected subset of $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$.  
So $C$ is empty, a point, an interval (closed, open, or half open), or all of $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$.
We claim that ${\overline{C}} - C$ does not meet $\Delta_\mathcal{V}$.  
Given this claim, we may replace $C$ by its closure and the lemma follows.

So, to obtain a contradiction, suppose that $c\in {\overline{C}} - C$ is a cusp.
Since $c \notin C$, we have that $c \notin I(a)$.
Thus $c\in I(b)$ with $b \neq a$. 
Both $F^\mathcal{V}$ and $F_\mathcal{V}$ contain infinitely many bi-leaves with centre $c$ whose endpoints are contained in $C$.  
See Figure~\ref{Fig:CuspAtEndOfInterval}.  
Fix bi-leaves $\ell$ of $F^\mathcal{V}$ and $m$ of $F_\mathcal{V}$, each containing $c$ and two points of $C$.  
By Lemma~\ref{Lem:Diagonal}, the Hausdorff limits $L = \lim_i g_i({\overline{\ell}})$ and $M = \lim_i g_i({\overline{m}})$ both exist.
The limits $L$ and $M$ must both contain $a$ and $b$.   
By Proposition~\ref{Prop:LimitOfLeaves}, and since $a \neq b$, the limits $L$ and $M$ are (closures of) non-cusp leaves or bi-leaves.  
By Corollary~\ref{Cor:OnlyAsymptotics}, since $L$ and $M$ have a common ideal point, they must be closures of bi-leaves $\ell_\infty$ and $m_\infty$, respectively, emanating from a common cusp and sharing a cusp leaf.
In particular, $\ell_\infty$ and $m_\infty$ are in the same foliation.

Since $\ell$ and $m$ are in opposite foliations, so are $g_i(\ell)$ and $g_i(m)$.
                                                             
From the final statement of Proposition~\ref{Prop:LimitOfLeaves}, we deduce that $\ell_\infty$ and $m_\infty$ are in different foliations, a contradiction.
<!-- end proof-52 -->
<!-- lemma-45: body_md -->
\label{Lem:PartingsDecomposeDeltaM}
Suppose that $I(a)$ contains at least two points.
Then there is a component $C$ of $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V}) - P$ so that $I(a) = {\overline{C}} \cap \Delta_\mathcal{V}$.
<!-- end lemma-45 -->
<!-- proof-53: body_md -->
Since $I(a)$ contains at least two points we are in the third or fourth case of Lemma~\ref{Lem:InaccessibleCusps}.
Suppose that $I(a) = \Delta_\mathcal{V}$.
In this case, Lemma~\ref{Lem:a_interval} implies that $P$ is a single point.
Thus ${\overline{C}} = \mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$ and we are done.

Suppose instead that $I(a) = J \cap \Delta_\mathcal{V}$ where $J$ is a closed interval.
We must show that $J \cap P = \partial J$.
We first claim that $P$ misses the interior of $J$.
For a contradiction, suppose that $p \in P$ lies in the interior of $J$.
Since cusps are dense, there are cusps of $I(a)$ on either side of $p$, contradicting Lemma~\ref{Lem:a_interval}.

Now let $C$ be the component of $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V}) - P$ containing the interior of $J$.
Let $q$ be an endpoint of $J$.
Suppose for a contradiction that $q$ lies in the interior of $C$.
Fix a closed sub-interval $I$ of $C$ containing $q$ in its interior.
The interval $I$ contains cusps of $I(a)$ since it meets the interior of $J$.
Also, $I$ contains cusps not in $I(a)$ (and so in some $I(b)$ for $b \neq a$, by Remark~\ref{Rem:AttractorPartition}) by the definition of $J$ and because $I$ meets the interior of $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V}) - J$.
But by Lemma~\ref{Lem:ClosedSubIntervals} the interval $I$ is a collapsing interval.
This is a contradiction.
<!-- end proof-53 -->
<!-- corollary-7: body_md -->
\label{Cor:NotCuspBefore}
Suppose that $P$ has at least two points.
Suppose that $p \in P$ is not an accumulation point of $P$.
Then $p$ is not a cusp.
<!-- end corollary-7 -->
<!-- proof-54: body_md -->
Let $C$ and $C'$ be the components of $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V}) - P$ adjacent to $p$.
Since $P$ has at least two points, $C$ and $C'$ are disjoint.
By Lemma~\ref{Lem:ClosedSubIntervals}, both contain collapsing intervals.
By Lemma~\ref{Lem:PartingsDecomposeDeltaM}, there are points $a$ and $a'$ in $A$ so that $I(a) = {\overline{C}} \cap \Delta_\mathcal{V}$ and $I(a') = {\overline{C}}' \cap \Delta_\mathcal{V}$.
Therefore $a \neq a'$.
By Remark~\ref{Rem:AttractorPartition}, we have that $I(a)$ and $I(a')$ are disjoint.
Note that $p$ is a point of ${\overline{C}} \cap {\overline{C}}'$.
If $p$ were a cusp then $p$ would lie in both $I(a)$ and in $I(a')$, a contradiction.
<!-- end proof-54 -->
<!-- lemma-46: body_md -->
\label{Lem:SingletonGoesToCusp}
Suppose for some $a \in A$, the set $I(a)=\{c\}$ has a single element.  
Then $a$ is a cusp.
<!-- end lemma-46 -->
<!-- proof-55: body_md -->
Suppose that $x \in \mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V}) - \{c\}$ is any point.  
Consider the interval $(c, x)^{\rotatebox[origin=c]{-90}{\scalebox{0.7}{$\curvearrowleft$}}}$.  
Suppose for a contradiction that $I(b)$ meets $(c, x)^{\rotatebox[origin=c]{-90}{\scalebox{0.7}{$\curvearrowleft$}}}$ for only finitely many of the $b$ in $A$.  
Thus $c$ is in the closure of one of the $I(b)$.  
Lemma~\ref{Lem:InaccessibleCusps} (applied to $I(b)$) implies that $a = b$.
Thus $I(a)$ meets $(c, x)^{\rotatebox[origin=c]{-90}{\scalebox{0.7}{$\curvearrowleft$}}}$.  
Thus $I(a)$ is not a singleton, a contradiction.  
We deduce that $A$ is infinite.  
By Definition~\ref{Def:DecompositionElementsCircle} we find that $A$ is the decomposition element for some cusp.
Note that, similarly to the above, the interval $(x, c)^{\rotatebox[origin=c]{-90}{\scalebox{0.7}{$\curvearrowleft$}}}$ also meets infinitely many of the sets $I(b)$ for $b$ in $A$.  

Fix $a_0 \in A - \{a\}$, a thorn so that $I(a_0)$ is non-empty.
Fix $c_0 \in I(a_0)$.
Note that $c_0 \neq c$.
With $c_0$ replacing $x$ above, we find distinct $(a_k)_{k\in \mathbb{Z}}$ in $A$ so that for all $k$
\begin{itemize}
\item the set $I(a_k)$ is non-empty, and
\item there is some $c_k \in I(a_k)$ with $\mathcal{O}_\mathcal{V}(c, c_k, c_0) = \operatorname{sign}(k)$.
\end{itemize}

Lemma~\ref{Lem:OrdersAgree} now implies that $\mathcal{O}_\mathcal{V}(a, a_k, a_0) = \operatorname{sign}(k)$.
Two thorns of $A$ separate the remaining elements of $A$ into a finite set and an infinite set. 
See Figure~\ref{Fig:CuspAtEndOfInterval}.
We deduce that $a$ is a cusp, as desired.
<!-- end proof-55 -->
<!-- corollary-8: body_md -->
\label{Cor:OneSingleton}
For at most one $a\in A$, the set $I(a)$ consists of a single element. \qed
<!-- end corollary-8 -->
<!-- lemma-47: body_md -->
\label{Lem:Case2}
Suppose that the parting set $P$ consists of exactly two points $p$ and $q$.  
Then $P$ is contained in a single decomposition element.
<!-- end lemma-47 -->
<!-- proof-56: body_md -->
By Corollary~\ref{Cor:NotCuspBefore} neither $p$ nor $q$ is a cusp.  
By Proposition~\ref{Prop:SingleLeaf} there is a nested neighbourhood basis $\{ H(\ell_j) \}_{j \in \mathbb{N}}$ of $p$. 
After discarding a finite number of basis elements, the closure of each $\ell_j$ connects a point of some $a$--interval to a point of some $b$--interval.
The Hausdorff limit $L_j = \lim_i g_i({\overline{\ell}}_j)$ contains the points $a$ and $b$.  
By Proposition~\ref{Prop:LimitOfLeaves}, and since $a \neq b$, we find that $L_j$ is the closure of either a non-cusp leaf or a bi-leaf with endpoints $a$ and $b$.  
There is only one such, so the limit $L = L_j$ is independent of $j$. 
There is likewise a nested neighbourhood basis of $q$, say $\{H(\ell_j')\mathbin{\mid} j\in\mathbb{N}\}$, where each $\ell_j'$ connects some $a$--interval to some $b$--interval.  
The limits $\lim_i g_i({\overline{\ell}}_j')$ are also equal to $L$.

Breaking symmetry, suppose that the interior of $L$ lies in $F^\mathcal{V}$.
Choose any non-cusp leaf $m$ in $F_\mathcal{V}$ which crosses $L$.  
For each $j$, there is an integer $N(j)$ so that the leaves $g_i(\ell_j)$ and $g_i(\ell_j')$ cross $m$ whenever $i \geq N(j)$.  
It follows that the leaves $g_i^{-1}(m)$ cross $\ell_j$ and $\ell_j'$ for $i \geq N(j)$.  
In particular, after passing to a subsequence, the Hausdorff limit $M$ of the leaves $g_i^{-1}({\overline{m}})$ must contain the partings $p$ and $q$.  
By Proposition~\ref{Prop:LimitOfLeaves} the interior of $M$ is therefore a non-cusp leaf or bi-leaf connecting $p$ to $q$.  
In either case $P$ is contained in a single decomposition element.
<!-- end proof-56 -->
<!-- lemma-48: body_md -->
\label{Lem:NoCuspsAfter}
Suppose both ${\overline{I(a)}}$ and $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V}) - {\overline{I(a)}}$ have non-empty interior.  Then $a$ is not a cusp.
<!-- end lemma-48 -->
<!-- proof-57: body_md -->
Suppose ${\overline{I(a)}}=[x, y]^{\rotatebox[origin=c]{-90}{\scalebox{0.7}{$\curvearrowleft$}}}$.  We divide into two cases, depending on whether or not $x$ is a cusp. 

\begin{figure}[htbp]

\subfloat[Case: $x$ is not a cusp.]{
\labellist
\small\hair 2pt
\pinlabel {${\overline{I(a)}}$} [r] at 1 125
\pinlabel {$x$} [br] at 38 215
\pinlabel {$y$} [tr] at 38 35
\pinlabel {$\ell$} [tl] at 75 187
\pinlabel {$u$} [tl] at 16 171
\pinlabel {$c'$} [br] at 60 227
\pinlabel {$v$} [b] at 84 240
\pinlabel {$c$} [b] at 114 248
\endlabellist
\includegraphics[width=0.43\textwidth]{Figures/endpoint_of_Ia_non_cusp}
\label{Fig:NoCuspsxNotCusp}
}
\qquad
\subfloat[The limit when $L$ is a leaf (as opposed to a bi-leaf).]{
\labellist

\label{Fig:NoCuspsLimit}
}

\subfloat[Case: $x$ is a cusp.]{
\labellist
\small\hair 2pt
\pinlabel {${\overline{I(a)}}$} [r] at 1 125
\pinlabel {$x$} [br] at 38 215
\pinlabel {$y$} [tr] at 38 35
\pinlabel {$\ell_{j}$} [tl] at 60 129
\pinlabel {$\ell_{j+1}$} [t] at 122 155
\pinlabel {$z_{j}$} [r] at 11 70
\pinlabel {$z_{j+1}$} [l] at 245 141
\endlabellist

\label{Fig:NoCuspsxCusp}
}
\caption{The leaf or bi-leaf $\ell$ is drawn with a dashed line.}
\label{Fig:NoCusps}
\end{figure}

Suppose that one of $x$ and $y$ is \emph{not} a cusp. 
Breaking symmetry, suppose that $x$ is not a cusp.
See Figure~\ref{Fig:NoCuspsxNotCusp}.
In this case Proposition~\ref{Prop:SingleLeaf} gives us a leaf $\ell$ joining a point $u$ in the interior of ${\overline{I(a)}}$ to a point $v$ in the interior of $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V}) - {\overline{I(a)}}$.  
There are cusps $c, c'$ in the interior $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V}) - {\overline{I(a)}}$ which separate $v$ from ${\overline{I(a)}}$; choose them so $\mathcal{O}_\mathcal{V}(c, v, c') = 1$.  
Thus we have $b$ and $b'$, distinct from $a$, so that $c \in I(b)$ and $c' \in I(b')$.  
Passing to a subsequence, the limit $z = \lim_i g_i(v)$ must lie in the (possibly degenerate) interval $[b, b']^{\rotatebox[origin=c]{-90}{\scalebox{0.7}{$\curvearrowleft$}}}$, which does not contain $a$. See Figure~\ref{Fig:NoCuspsLimit}.
Passing to a further subsequence, the limit $L = \lim_i g_i({\overline{\ell}})$ cannot be a point of $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$. 
By Proposition~\ref{Prop:LimitOfLeaves}, the limit $L$ is the closure of either a non-cusp leaf or a bi-leaf.
In either case the endpoints of $L$ are equal to $a$ and $z$.  
No cusp can be the endpoint of a non-cusp leaf or bi-leaf, so $a$ is not a cusp.
                                                         

Suppose that both $x$ and $y$ are cusps.
See Figure~\ref{Fig:NoCuspsxCusp}.
In this case we claim there is a bi-leaf $\ell$ with
\begin{itemize}
\item
centre at $x$,
\item
one endpoint in the interior of ${\overline{I(a)}}$, and 
\item
one endpoint in the interior of $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V}) - {\overline{I(a)}}$.  
\end{itemize}
Given the claim, we argue as above that $a$ is an endpoint of $\lim_i g_i({\overline{\ell}})$, and so cannot be a cusp.  

It remains to find the bi-leaf.  
Let $\{ \ell_j \}_{j \in \mathbb{Z}}$ be the set of cusp leaves of $F^\mathcal{V}$ emanating from $x$.  
Let $z_j$ be the endpoint of $\ell_j$ different from $x$.  
We assume the leaves $\ell_j$ are  indexed so that $\mathcal{O}_\mathcal{V}( z_{j}, z_{j+1}, x) = 1$ for all $j$. 
By Lemma~\ref{Lem:NoDoubleCusps} no $z_j$ is a cusp.  
Thus no $z_j$ is equal to $y$.  
There is thus a unique $j$ so that $\mathcal{O}_\mathcal{V}(z_j, y, z_{j+1}) = 1$.  
Thus $\ell_j \cup \ell_{j+1}$ is the desired bi-leaf.
<!-- end proof-57 -->
<!-- lemma-49: body_md -->
\label{Lem:FiniteImpliesTwo}
Suppose that the parting set $P= (p_1, \ldots, p_n)$ is finite.
Then $n \leq 2$.
<!-- end lemma-49 -->
<!-- proof-58: body_md -->
For a contradiction, suppose that $n\geq 3$.
We assume that the $p_j$ are arranged in anticlockwise order according to their indices, which we take modulo $n$.
Set $C_j = (p_j, p_{j+1})^{\rotatebox[origin=c]{-90}{\scalebox{0.7}{$\curvearrowleft$}}}$.
By Lemmas \ref{Lem:ClosedSubIntervals} and \ref{Lem:PartingsDecomposeDeltaM}, there are distinct $a_j \in A$ so that $I(a_j) = {\overline{C}}_j \cap \Delta_\mathcal{V}$.
No $p_j$ is a cusp by Corollary~\ref{Cor:NotCuspBefore}.
By Lemma~\ref{Lem:OrdersAgree}, the $a_j$ are also circularly ordered consistently with their indices.
Fix $j$.
Proposition~\ref{Prop:SingleLeaf} provides a non-cusp leaf $\ell_j$ separating $p_j$ from $P - \{p_j\}$.
Passing to a subsequence, the Hausdorff limit $L_j = \lim_i g_i({\overline{\ell}}_j)$ exists and contains the points $ a_{j-1}$ and $a_j$.
In particular the intersection in $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$ of $L_j$ and $L_{j+1}$ is non-empty for each $j$.  
Consulting the possible limits in Proposition~\ref{Prop:LimitOfLeaves} we see that this can only happen if each $L_j$ is the closure of a bi-leaf running from $a_{j-1}$ to $a_j$, and all these bi-leaves have centre at a fixed cusp $a$.
By Corollary~\ref{Cor:OnlyAsymptotics}, all of these bi-leaves lie in the same foliation, say $F^\mathcal{V}$.
                                                                                                             

Let $m_j$ be the cusp leaf running between $a_j$ and $a$.
Thus for all $j$, the union $m_{j-1} \cup m_j$ is the interior of $L_j$.  
Re-indexing if necessary, we may assume that $\mathcal{O}_\mathcal{V}(a_n, a ,a_1)=1$.
But then the cusp leaves $m_n$ and $m_1$ are separated by $m_2$; 
thus $L_1$ is not the closure of a bi-leaf, a contradiction.
<!-- end proof-58 -->
<!-- definition-36: body_md -->
A convergent sequence $\{p_j\}\to p$ in $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$ is an \emph{anticlockwise converging sequence} if $\mathcal{O}_\mathcal{V}(p_j,p_{j+1},p) = 1$ for all $j$.
The limit of an anticlockwise converging sequence in $P$ will be called an \emph{anticlockwise accumulation point of $P$}.
We similarly define \emph{clockwise converging sequences} and \emph{clockwise accumulation points}.
<!-- end definition-36 -->
<!-- lemma-50: body_md -->
\label{Lem:AccumulatingPartings}
The parting set $P$ has at most one accumulation point.
<!-- end lemma-50 -->
<!-- proof-59: body_md -->
We first show that there is at most one anticlockwise accumulation point.
Suppose by way of contradiction that there are two anticlockwise converging sequences $p_j\to p$ and $q_j\to q$ in $P$. 
See Figure~\ref{Fig:AntiClockwiseAccumulating}. 
Truncating the sequences if necessary we may assume $\mathcal{O}_\mathcal{V}(p, q_j, q) = \mathcal{O}_\mathcal{V}(q, p_j, p) = 1$ for each $j$. 
For each $j\in\mathbb{N}$ choose cusps $c_j$ and $d_j$ so that $c_j \in [p_j, p_{j+1}]^{\rotatebox[origin=c]{-90}{\scalebox{0.7}{$\curvearrowleft$}}}$ and $d_j \in [q_j, q_{j+1}]^{\rotatebox[origin=c]{-90}{\scalebox{0.7}{$\curvearrowleft$}}}$.
Suppose that $c_j \in I(a_j)$ and $d_j \in I(b_j)$.
By Lemma~\ref{Lem:I(a)Component}, we deduce that $I(a_j)\subset [p_j, p_{j+1}]^{\rotatebox[origin=c]{-90}{\scalebox{0.7}{$\curvearrowleft$}}}$ and $I(b_j)\subset [q_j, q_{j+1}]^{\rotatebox[origin=c]{-90}{\scalebox{0.7}{$\curvearrowleft$}}}$.  
Applying Lemma~\ref{Lem:OrdersAgree}, for any $j$ we have that both $[a_j, b_j]^{\rotatebox[origin=c]{-90}{\scalebox{0.7}{$\curvearrowleft$}}}$ and $[b_j, a_j]^{\rotatebox[origin=c]{-90}{\scalebox{0.7}{$\curvearrowleft$}}}$ have infinite intersection with $A$.  
As in the proof of Lemma~\ref{Lem:SingletonGoesToCusp}, this can only happen if one of $a_j, b_j$ is the cusp, so it can only happen for one $j$, a contradiction.
The argument that there is at most one clockwise accumulation point is similar.

Suppose now there is a clockwise converging sequence $p_j\to p$ and an anticlockwise converging sequence $q_j\to q$.  
Arguing as in the first paragraph, if $I(a) \subset [q,p]^{\rotatebox[origin=c]{-90}{\scalebox{0.7}{$\curvearrowleft$}}}$, then $a$ is the cusp $a_A$.
Thus $p = q$.
<!-- end proof-59 -->
<!-- lemma-51: body_md -->
\label{Lem:AccumulationCusp}
Suppose that $P$ is infinite.
Then $c_P$ is a cusp.
<!-- end lemma-51 -->
<!-- proof-60: body_md -->
For a contradiction, suppose that $c_P$ is not a cusp.
Then Proposition~\ref{Prop:SingleLeaf} provides non-cusp leaves $\ell_k$ determining a nested neighbourhood basis of $c_P$.  
Applying Lemma~\ref{Lem:Perturb}, we may assume that for all $k$, the ideal points $u_k$ and $v_k$ of $\ell_k$ are disjoint from $P$.
We orient $\ell_k$ away from $u_k$, arranging matters so that $\mathcal{O}_\mathcal{V}(v_k, c_P, u_k) = 1$.  
Thus $c_P$ is to the left of $\ell_k$.  

Now suppose that $c_P$ has both a clockwise and an anticlockwise converging sequence.
Passing to a subsequence, we may assume that for $k \neq k'$ the four points $u_k, v_k, u_{k'}, v_{k'}$ lie in distinct components of $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V}) - P$. 
We deduce that $u_k \to c_P$ and $v_k \to c_P$ are clockwise and anticlockwise converging sequences, respectively. 

Let $L_k$ be the Hausdorff limit of $g_i({\overline{\ell}}_k)$.
Since $u_k$ and $v_k$ lie in distinct components of $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V}) - P$, we deduce that $L_k$ meets at least two points of $A$.
Thus, by Proposition~\ref{Prop:LimitOfLeaves} it is the closure of a bi-leaf or a non-cusp leaf.
However, $A$ is an infinite decomposition element and hence contains exactly one cusp, $a_A$, and a collection of thorns.
Non-cusp leaves do not have these as ideal points, thus $L_k$ is the closure of a bi-leaf.

Let $a_k$ and $b_k$ be the thorns of $L_k$, named so that $\mathcal{O}_\mathcal{V}(b_k, a_A, a_k) = 1$.
Since $u_k \to c_P$ is a clockwise converging sequence, by Lemma~\ref{Lem:OrdersAgree} we have that $a_k \to a_A$ is also a clockwise converging sequence.  
Similarly, $b_k \to a_A$ is an anticlockwise converging sequence.  
Thus the endpoints of $L_k$ are separated from $a_A$ by the endpoints of $L_{k+1}$, contradicting the fact that $L_{k+1}$ is the closure of a bi-leaf with centre $a_A$. 
Thus we have proved that $c_P$ is a cusp. 

Now, breaking symmetry, suppose that $c_P$ has an anticlockwise converging sequence in $P$, but no clockwise converging sequence.
We run the above argument again, except that in this case we may assume that $u_k$ and $u_{k'}$ lie in the same component of $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V}) - P$.
Again we have that $u_k \to c_P$ and $v_k \to c_P$ are clockwise and anticlockwise converging sequences, respectively. 
The rest of the argument is the same except that the $b_k$'s all agree, and we reach the same contradiction.
<!-- end proof-60 -->
<!-- lemma-52: body_md -->
\label{Lem:InfiniteCase}
Suppose that $P$ is infinite.
Suppose that $c_P$ is the cusp given by Lemma~\ref{Lem:AccumulationCusp}.
Then $P$ is contained in the decomposition element~$[c_P]_{S^1}$.
<!-- end lemma-52 -->
<!-- proof-61: body_md -->
The point $c_P$ is either an anticlockwise or a clockwise accumulation point (or possibly both).
Breaking symmetry, we suppose that $c_P\in P$ is an anticlockwise accumulation point.  
Index the elements of $P - \{c_P\}$ either by the integers or by the natural numbers so that $\mathcal{O}_\mathcal{V}(p_j, p_{j+1}, c_P) = 1$ for all $j$.  
If $c_P$ is an accumulation point from both sides, we use all the integers; 
otherwise we use only the non-negative integers.

By Lemmas \ref{Lem:ClosedSubIntervals} and \ref{Lem:PartingsDecomposeDeltaM}, for each $p_j\in P - \{c_P\}$, there is some $a_j\in A$ so that $I(a_j) = \Delta_\mathcal{V}\cap [p_j, p_{j+1}]^{\rotatebox[origin=c]{-90}{\scalebox{0.7}{$\curvearrowleft$}}}$.  
By Lemma~\ref{Lem:NoCuspsAfter}, no $a_j$ is a cusp.  
(Note that not every element of $A$ is necessarily given an index here.)
By Corollary~\ref{Cor:NotCuspBefore}, no $p_j$ is a cusp.
By Proposition~\ref{Prop:SingleLeaf}, we can find disjoint non-cusp leaves $\ell_j$ so that $\ell_j$ separates $p_j$ from $P - \{p_j\}$.  
As in the proof of Lemma~\ref{Lem:FiniteImpliesTwo}, the limit $L_j = \lim_i g_i({\overline{\ell}}_j)$ is the closure of a bi-leaf joining $a_{j-1}$ to $a_j$, and passing through the cusp $a_A\in A$.  
Applying Proposition~\ref{Prop:LimitOfLeaves}, it follows that the $\ell_j$ were all in the same foliation.
                                                             
Breaking symmetry, we suppose that the $\ell_j$ are in the foliation~$F^\mathcal{V}$.

\begin{claim}
\label{Clm:GreenThorns}
For each $j$, the point $a_j$ is a non-cusp ideal point of a bi-leaf of $F^\mathcal{V}$.
                                   
\end{claim}

\begin{proof}
Since the $\ell_j$ lie in $F^\mathcal{V}$, by Proposition~\ref{Prop:LimitOfLeaves},  the interior of each $L_j$ is a bi-leaf of $F^\mathcal{V}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{claim}
\label{Clm:AccumulatedBothSides}
The cusp $c_P$ is both an anticlockwise and a clockwise accumulation point of $P$.
\end{claim}

\begin{proof}
Suppose that the elements of $P - \{c_P\}$ are indexed by the natural numbers, starting with $p_1$.
Then $(c_P, p_1)^{\rotatebox[origin=c]{-90}{\scalebox{0.7}{$\curvearrowleft$}}}$ is a component of $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V}) - P$.
By Lemmas \ref{Lem:ClosedSubIntervals} and \ref{Lem:PartingsDecomposeDeltaM} there is some $a_0 \in A$ so that $I(a_0) = \Delta_\mathcal{V}\cap [c_P, p_1]^{\rotatebox[origin=c]{-90}{\scalebox{0.7}{$\curvearrowleft$}}}$.  
Thus the cusp $c_P$ lies in $I(a_0)$.
Note also that, by Lemma~\ref{Lem:NoCuspsAfter}, the point $a_0$ is not a cusp, so it is not $a_A$.

Fix a bi-leaf $\ell$ of $F^\mathcal{V}$ with centre $c_P$ whose other ideal points $p$ and $q$ do not lie in $(c_P, p_1)^{\rotatebox[origin=c]{-90}{\scalebox{0.7}{$\curvearrowleft$}}}$.
Note that $p$ and $q$ do not lie in $P$ because $\ell$ cannot cross the leaves $\ell_j$.
Thus $p$ and $q$ lie in an $a_j$--interval and an $a_k$--interval, respectively, for some $j, k > 0$.
Let $L = \lim_i g_i({\overline{\ell}})$.
Since $L$ contains $a_j$, $a_k$, and $a_0$, it is neither a point, nor the closure of a non-cusp leaf or bi-leaf, contradicting Proposition~\ref{Prop:LimitOfLeaves}.
\end{proof}

Thus the elements of $P - \{c_P\}$ are indexed by the integers.

\begin{claim}
\label{Clm:ForeverAlone}
$\lim_i g_i(c_P) = a_A$.
\end{claim}

\begin{proof}
Since $c_P$ is a cusp, it belongs to $I(a)$ for some $a \in A$ by Remark~\ref{Rem:AttractorPartition}.
By Claim~\ref{Clm:AccumulatedBothSides} and Lemmas \ref{Lem:ClosedSubIntervals} and \ref{Lem:PartingsDecomposeDeltaM}, the set $I(a)$ is a singleton.
By Lemma~\ref{Lem:SingletonGoesToCusp}, the limit $a$ is the cusp $a_A$.
\end{proof}

\begin{claim}
\label{Clm:PurpleThorns}
Suppose that $m$ is a bi-leaf of $F_\mathcal{V}$ with centre $c_P$.
Then the ideal points of $m$ lie in $P$.
\end{claim}

\begin{proof}
Suppose that some ideal point of $m$, say $q$, does not lie in $P$. 
Then $q$ lies in some component of $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V}) - P$.
Thus by Lemma~\ref{Lem:ClosedSubIntervals}, the point $q$ lies in an $a_j$--interval for some $j \in \mathbb{Z}$.
Thus $M = \lim_i g_i({\overline{m}})$ contains $a_A$ and $a_j$.
By Proposition~\ref{Prop:LimitOfLeaves} and Remark~\ref{Rem:Cover}, the interior of $M$ is a bi-leaf of $F_\mathcal{V}$.
However, this with Claim~\ref{Clm:GreenThorns} and Corollary~\ref{Cor:OnlyAsymptotics} gives a contradiction.
\end{proof}

\begin{claim}
\label{Clm:CuspLeaves}
For each $j \in \mathbb{Z}$ there is exactly one bi-leaf of $F^\mathcal{V}$ with centre $c_P$ and other ideal points in an $a_j$--interval and an $a_{j+1}$--interval.
\end{claim}

\begin{proof}
The proof is similar to that of Claim~\ref{Clm:AccumulatedBothSides} but with some key differences.
Suppose that $\ell$ is a bi-leaf of $F^\mathcal{V}$ with centre $c_P$.
Let $m$ be either of the two bi-leaves of $F_\mathcal{V}$ that contain the divider (see Definition~\ref{Def:BiLeaf}) of $\ell$.
Let $q$ and $q'$ be the other ideal points of $\ell$.
Let $q''$ be the ideal point of $m$ which is also the ideal point of the divider of $\ell$.
As in the proof of Claim~\ref{Clm:AccumulatedBothSides}, the points $q$ and $q'$ do not lie in $P$.
Suppose that $q$ and $q'$ lie in an $a_j$--interval and an $a_{j'}$--interval, respectively. 
Let $L = \lim_i g_i({\overline{\ell}})$.
Note that $L$ contains $a_j$, $a_{j'}$, and by Claim~\ref{Clm:ForeverAlone}, the cusp $a_A$.
By Lemma~\ref{Lem:NoCuspsAfter}, neither $a_j$ nor $a_{j'}$ equals $a_A$.

We deduce from Proposition~\ref{Prop:LimitOfLeaves} and Remark~\ref{Rem:Cover} that $L$ is the closure of a bi-leaf of $F^\mathcal{V}$ with centre $a_A$.
Thus $a_j$ and $a_{j'}$ are either identical or consecutive elements of $A - \{a_A\}$.
Thus either $j = j'$ or, by Lemma~\ref{Lem:OrdersAgree}, we have that $j$ and $j'$ are consecutive integers.
Suppose, for a contradiction, that $j=j'$.
Then $q''$ lies in an $a_j$--interval, contradicting Claim~\ref{Clm:PurpleThorns}.

Induction (in both directions) now proves the claim.
\end{proof}

\begin{claim}
For each $p_j\in P - \{c_P\}$ there is a cusp leaf of $F_\mathcal{V}$ joining $c_P$ to $p_j$.
\end{claim}

\begin{proof}
By Claim~\ref{Clm:CuspLeaves}, there is a bi-leaf $\ell$ of $F^\mathcal{V}$ with centre $c_P$ and other ideal points ending in an $a_{j-1}$--interval and an $a_j$--interval.
The divider of $\ell$ has the desired property by Claim~\ref{Clm:PurpleThorns}.
\end{proof}

Thus $P$ lies in the decomposition element $[c_P]_{S^1}$.
<!-- end proof-61 -->

Since the $\ell_j$ lie in $F^\mathcal{V}$, by Proposition~\ref{Prop:LimitOfLeaves},  the interior of each $L_j$ is a bi-leaf of $F^\mathcal{V}$.
