<!-- proposition-5: body_md -->
\label{Prop:FindingB}
There is a unique decomposition element $B \subset \mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$ containing all the partings of $\{g_n\}$.
Furthermore, the sequence of maps $g_n|(\mathcal{S}^2(\mathcal{V}) -\{B\})$ converges uniformly to the constant map $(\mathcal{S}^2(\mathcal{V}) -\{B\})\to \{A\}$. \qed
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- corollary-9: body_md -->
\label{Cor:Collapsing}
The sequence $(g_i)$ is a collapsing sequence. \qed
<!-- end corollary-9 -->
<!-- proposition-6: body_md -->
\label{Prop:Parabolic}
Suppose that $c \in \Delta_\mathcal{V}$ is a cusp. 
Then $[c]_{S^1} \in \mathcal{S}^2(\mathcal{V})$ is a bounded parabolic point for the action of $\pi_1(M)$.
<!-- end proposition-6 -->
<!-- proposition-7: body_md -->
\label{Prop:ParabolicFacts}
\leavevmode
\begin{enumerate}
\item
\label{Itm:ZZ^2}
$\operatorname{Stab}(c) \cong \mathbb{Z}^2$.
\item
\label{Itm:beta} 
There is a primitive element $\beta \in \operatorname{Stab}(c)$ whose fixed-point set in $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$ is $C$. 
\item
\label{Itm:gamma}
If $\gamma\in \operatorname{Stab}(c) - \langle \beta \rangle$, then $\gamma$ preserves $C$ setwise.  
Also 
\[
\lim_{n \to \infty}\gamma^n(x) = c
\]
for any $x \in \mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$. 
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-7 -->
<!-- proof-68: body_md -->
The first item follows from the fact that $c$ is a cusp of ${\widetilde{M}}$ and that the interior of $M$ admits a finite-volume hyperbolic metric. 
See~\cite[Section~7.13]{FSS22}.
The second item is a restatement of~\cite[Lemma~A.8]{FSS22}.
The third item follows from~\cite[Lemma~7.15]{FSS22}.
<!-- end proof-68 -->
<!-- lemma-53: body_md -->
\label{Lem:StabC}
The stabilisers $\operatorname{Stab}(c)$ and $\operatorname{Stab}(C)$ are equal.
<!-- end lemma-53 -->
<!-- proof-69: body_md -->
Note that $\pi_1(M)$ preserves $\Delta_\mathcal{V}$.
By Definition~\ref{Def:DecompositionElementsCircle}, the clamshell boundary $C$ consists of $c$, together with its thorns (none of which are cusps).
By Lemma~\ref{Lem:Laminations}(\ref{Itm:CrownZZ}), the cusp $c$ is the unique accumulation point of $C$.
From this we deduce that $\operatorname{Stab}(C) < \operatorname{Stab}(c)$.
Proposition~\ref{Prop:ParabolicFacts} gives the reverse inclusion.
<!-- end proof-69 -->
<!-- proof-70: body_md -->
Suppose that $C = [c]_{S^1}$ is the decomposition element containing the cusp $c \in \Delta_\mathcal{V}$. 
We first prove that $C$ is a parabolic point, as in Definition~\ref{Def:Parabolic}.

By Proposition~\ref{Prop:ParabolicFacts}(\ref{Itm:ZZ^2}), the stabiliser of $c$ is isomorphic to $\mathbb{Z}^2$.
Applying Lemma~\ref{Lem:StabC}, we have that $\operatorname{Stab}(C)$ is infinite.

We now show that no element of $\operatorname{Stab}(C)$ is loxodromic. 
By Proposition~\ref{Prop:ParabolicFacts}, the stabiliser $\operatorname{Stab}(C)$ contains an element $\beta$ whose fixed set in $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$ is equal to $C$.  
Fix $\delta \in \operatorname{Stab}(C) - \{1\}$.  
If $\delta$ is a power of $\beta$ then its fixed-point set is equal to $C$ in $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$.  
Thus, it acts as a translation on every component of $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V}) - C$.  
If $\delta$ lies in $\operatorname{Stab}(C) - \langle \beta \rangle$ then its powers send every point of $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V}) - c$ eventually to $c$.  
In either case, $\delta$ has no finite orbit in $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V}) - C$.
Thus $\delta$ does not stabilise a singleton or the endpoints of a leaf.

By Corollary~\ref{Cor:CircleDecomposition} the last case we need to consider is that $\delta$ fixes, setwise, some infinite decomposition element $D \neq C$.  
We deduce that $D$ contains a cusp $d$.
By Lemma~\ref{Lem:Laminations}(\ref{Itm:CrownZZ}), the element $\delta$ fixes $d$.  
But then $\delta$ has an orbit of size one, namely $d$ itself.  
This is the desired contradiction. 
We deduce that $C$ is a parabolic point.

We now prove that $C$ is a bounded parabolic point.
Fix some $\gamma \in \operatorname{Stab}(C) - \langle \beta \rangle$.  
By Proposition~\ref{Prop:ParabolicFacts}(\ref{Itm:gamma}), the element $\gamma$ acts as a translation on $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V}) - \{c\}$.
Let $I \subset \mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V}) - \{c\}$ be a fundamental domain for the action, with endpoints in $C$.  
Note that $C \cap I$ is finite.  
We take the closures of the components of $I - C$ to obtain closed intervals $I_1, I_2, \ldots, I_k$.

For each $j$ we choose a closed interval $J_j \subset I_j$ which is a fundamental domain for the action of $\langle \beta \rangle$ on the interior of $I_j$. 
The union $K = \mathbin{\scalebox{1.5}{\ensuremath{\cup}}}_j J_j$ is compact.  
Also  its $\operatorname{Stab}(C)$--translates cover all of $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V}) - C$.  
It follows that the image of $K$ in $\mathcal{S}^2(\mathcal{V})$ under the quotient map $\Psi_\mathcal{V}$ (Definition~\ref{Def:VeeringSphere}) is again compact.
Additionally, the $\operatorname{Stab}(C)$--translates of $\Psi_\mathcal{V}(K)$ cover all of $\mathcal{S}^2(\mathcal{V}) - \{C\}$.  
Thus $\operatorname{Stab}(C)$ acts cocompactly on $\mathcal{S}^2(\mathcal{V}) - \{C\}$.
This proves that $C$ is a bounded parabolic point.
<!-- end proof-70 -->
<!-- proposition-8: body_md -->
\label{Prop:LeafConical}
Suppose that $\ell$ is a non-cusp leaf of either foliation.
Suppose that $x \in \partial_\infty \ell$.
Then the decomposition element $[x]_{S^1} \in \mathcal{S}^2(\mathcal{V})$ is a conical limit point for the action of $\pi_1(M)$.
<!-- end proposition-8 -->
<!-- definition-37: body_md -->
\label{Def:BoxAnatomy}
Let $e$ be an edge of $\mathcal{T}$.
Let $R(e)$ be the associated edge rectangle.
Let $k^W(e)$ be the unique bi-leaf of $F^\mathcal{V}$ which 
\begin{itemize}
\item
contains the west side of $R(e)$ and
\item
is a Hausdorff limit of non-cusp leaves of $F^\mathcal{V}$ meeting $R(e)$. 
\end{itemize}
We define $k^E(e)$ similarly with respect to the east side of $R(e)$. 
The centres of $k^W(e)$ and $k^E(e)$ are the endpoints of the edge $e$.  
The bi-leaf $k^W(e)$ has a northern endpoint $NW^\mathcal{V}(e)$ and a southern endpoint $SW^\mathcal{V}(e)$.  
Similarly, $k^E(e)$ has a northern endpoint $NE^\mathcal{V}(e)$ and a southern one $SE^\mathcal{V}(e)$.  
The \emph{upper product neighbourhood} $P^\mathcal{V}(e)$ is the image of the product 
\[
[SW^\mathcal{V}(e),SE^\mathcal{V}(e)]^{\rotatebox[origin=c]{-90}{\scalebox{0.7}{$\curvearrowleft$}}}\times[NE^\mathcal{V}(e),NW^\mathcal{V}(e)]^{\rotatebox[origin=c]{-90}{\scalebox{0.7}{$\curvearrowleft$}}}
\]
in $\mathcal{M}(\mathcal{V})$. 

We define the bi-leaves $k_S(e)$ and $k_N(e)$, in $F_\mathcal{V}$, with respect to the south and north sides. 
The endpoints $SW_\mathcal{V}(e)$ and $SE_\mathcal{V}(e)$ of $k_S(e)$ and $NE_\mathcal{V}(e)$ and $NW_\mathcal{V}(e)$ of $k_N(e)$ determine the \emph{lower product neighbourhood} $P_\mathcal{V}(e)$ which is the image of the product 
\[
[NW_\mathcal{V}(e),SW_\mathcal{V}(e)]^{\rotatebox[origin=c]{-90}{\scalebox{0.7}{$\curvearrowleft$}}} \times [SE_\mathcal{V}(e),NE_\mathcal{V}(e)]^{\rotatebox[origin=c]{-90}{\scalebox{0.7}{$\curvearrowleft$}}} 
\]
in $\mathcal{M}(\mathcal{V})$.
<!-- end definition-37 -->
<!-- lemma-54: body_md -->
\label{Lem:RectangleBox}
Suppose that $\ell$ is a non-cusp leaf of $F^\mathcal{V}$.
The set of endpoints $\partial_\infty \ell$ lies in $P^\mathcal{V}(e)$ if and only if $\ell$ meets $R(e)$.  \qed
<!-- end lemma-54 -->
<!-- definition-38: body_md -->
Suppose that $U$ and $V$ are subsets of a topological space. 
Then we say that $U$ is \emph{strictly nested} in $V$ if ${\overline{U}} \subset \operatorname{Int}(V)$.
<!-- end definition-38 -->
<!-- lemma-55: body_md -->
\label{Lem:BoxPairsForLeaf}
Suppose that $\ell$ is a non-cusp leaf of $F^\mathcal{V}$.
There is a pair of edges $e$ and $e'$ and a sequence of group elements $(g_i)$ in $\pi_1(M)$ with the following properties.
\begin{enumerate}
\item
\label{Itm:NoCommonCusp} 
The edges $e'$ and $e$ do not share a cusp.
\item
\label{Itm:SNSpan} 
The edge rectangle $R(e')$ south-north spans the edge rectangle $R(e)$.
\item
\label{Itm:StrictlyNested} 
$P^\mathcal{V}(e')$ is strictly nested in $P^\mathcal{V}(e)$.
\item 
\label{Itm:NeighbourhoodBasis}
The products $g_i(P^\mathcal{V}(e'))$ form a nested neighbourhood basis for 
$\partial_\infty \ell \in \mathcal{M}(\mathcal{V})$.
So do the products $g_i(P^\mathcal{V}(e))$. \qed
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-55 -->
<!-- proof-71: body_md -->
Suppose that $\ell$ is a leaf of $F^\mathcal{V}$; the other case is similar. 
Let $e$, $e'$, and $(g_i)$ be as in the conclusion to Lemma~\ref{Lem:BoxPairsForLeaf}.
Recall that $\ell$ crosses $R(e)$ and $R(e')$.
  
Using the notation of Definition~\ref{Def:BoxAnatomy}, set $I(e) = [NE^\mathcal{V}(e), NW^\mathcal{V}(e)]^{\rotatebox[origin=c]{-90}{\scalebox{0.7}{$\curvearrowleft$}}}$ and $J(e) = [SW^\mathcal{V}(e),SE^\mathcal{V}(e)]^{\rotatebox[origin=c]{-90}{\scalebox{0.7}{$\curvearrowleft$}}}$.  
We make the similar definitions for $I(e')$ and $J(e')$.
Let $p$ and $q$ be the points of $\partial_\infty\ell$.
Breaking symmetry, suppose that $p\in I(e')\subset I(e)$ and $q\in J(e')\subset J(e)$.  
By Lemma~\ref{Lem:BoxPairsForLeaf}(\ref{Itm:StrictlyNested}), the products $P^\mathcal{V}(e')\subset P^\mathcal{V}(e)$ are strictly nested.
Therefore, the intervals $I(e')\subset I(e)$ and $J(e') \subset J(e)$ are also strictly nested.  
By Lemma~\ref{Lem:BoxPairsForLeaf}(\ref{Itm:NeighbourhoodBasis}), the products $g_i(P^\mathcal{V}(e))$ and $g_i(P^\mathcal{V}(e'))$ form neighbourhood bases for $\partial_\infty\ell$.

Either infinitely many of the $g_i$ send $I(e)$ into itself, or all but finitely many send $I(e)$ into $J(e)$.
In the first case there is a subsequence so that
\begin{itemize}
\item the intervals $g_i(I(e))$ and $g_i(I(e'))$ form neighbourhood bases for $p$ and 
\item the intervals $g_i(J(e))$ and $g_i(J(e'))$ form neighbourhood bases for $q$.
\end{itemize}
The second case swaps $p$ with $q$ in the above and is handled similarly.
Applying Proposition~\ref{Prop:Convergence}, we pass to a further subsequence and reindex so that $(g_i^{-1})$ is a collapsing sequence for the action of $\pi_1(M)$ on $\mathcal{S}^2(\mathcal{V})$.
 
Let $m$ be a non-cusp leaf of $F_\mathcal{V}$ which crosses $R(e)$ and thus crosses $\ell$.
Let $r = \ell \cap m$. 
                              

\begin{claim*}
The point $r$ lies in $R(g_i(e')) \cap R(g_i(e))$.
\end{claim*}

\begin{proof}
By Lemma~\ref{Lem:BoxPairsForLeaf}(\ref{Itm:NeighbourhoodBasis}), for every $i$, the leaf $\ell$ crosses $R(g_i(e'))$ and $R(g_i(e))$.
We prove the corresponding statement for $m$ by induction.
Since $m$ crosses $R(e)$, it also crosses $R(e')$.
Also $g_0$ is the identity.
This gives the base case.

Suppose that $m$ crosses $R(g_i(e'))$ and $R(g_i(e))$.
Since the neighbourhood bases are nested (Lemma~\ref{Lem:BoxPairsForLeaf}), we find that $R(g_i(e'))$ and $R(g_i(e))$ west-east span $R(g_{i+1}(e))$ and thus west-east span $R(g_{i+1}(e'))$.
Thus $m$ crosses $R(g_{i+1}(e'))$ and $R(g_{i+1}(e))$.
\end{proof}

Thus the point $(g_i^{-1}(r))$ lies in $R(e') \cap R(e)$.
Note that the conclusions~(\ref{Itm:NoCommonCusp}) and~(\ref{Itm:SNSpan}) of Lemma~\ref{Lem:BoxPairsForLeaf} imply that the intersection $R(e') \cap R(e)$ is precompact in $\mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V})$.  
Passing to a subsequence, we have that $(g_i^{-1}(r))$ converges to some point $r_\infty$ in the closure of $R(e') \cap R(e)$.
In particular, $r_\infty$ is in $\mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V})$.

Passing to further subsequences, the following Hausdorff limits exist.
\[
L = \lim_{i\to\infty} g_i^{-1}\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\left({\overline{\ell}}\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\right) \qquad M = \lim_{i\to\infty} g_i^{-1}\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\left({\overline{m}}\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\right)
\]
By Proposition~\ref{Prop:LimitOfLeaves}, the limits $L$ and $M$ are the closures of non-cusp or bi-leaves of $F^\mathcal{V}$ and $F_\mathcal{V}$, respectively.
Since $L$ and $M$ cross at $r_\infty$, they are not bi-leaves for a common cusp.
From Definitions~\ref{Def:DecompositionElementsCircle} and~\ref{Def:DecompositionElementsSphere} we deduce that $\partial_\infty L$ and $\partial_\infty M$ lie in distinct decomposition elements of $\mathcal{S}^2(\mathcal{V})$. 
So define $A = [\partial_\infty M]_{S^1}$ and $B = [\partial_\infty L]_{S^1}$ and note that $A \neq B$.

Suppose that $m' \neq m$ is another non-cusp leaf of $F_\mathcal{V}$ crossing $R(e)$. 
As above, we obtain $A' = [\partial_\infty M']_{S^1}$ with $A' \neq B$.
Since $(g^{-1}_i)$ is a collapsing sequence, we deduce that $A = A'$.
It follows that $\partial_\infty \ell$ is the repelling point.
From this we deduce that $A$ is the attracting point.
Since $A \neq B$ we have verified the properties of Definition~\ref{Def:CLP}.
<!-- end proof-71 -->
<!-- claim--5: body_md -->
The point $r$ lies in $R(g_i(e')) \cap R(g_i(e))$.
<!-- end claim--5 -->
<!-- proof-72: body_md -->
By Lemma~\ref{Lem:BoxPairsForLeaf}(\ref{Itm:NeighbourhoodBasis}), for every $i$, the leaf $\ell$ crosses $R(g_i(e'))$ and $R(g_i(e))$.
We prove the corresponding statement for $m$ by induction.
Since $m$ crosses $R(e)$, it also crosses $R(e')$.
Also $g_0$ is the identity.
This gives the base case.

Suppose that $m$ crosses $R(g_i(e'))$ and $R(g_i(e))$.
Since the neighbourhood bases are nested (Lemma~\ref{Lem:BoxPairsForLeaf}), we find that $R(g_i(e'))$ and $R(g_i(e))$ west-east span $R(g_{i+1}(e))$ and thus west-east span $R(g_{i+1}(e'))$.
Thus $m$ crosses $R(g_{i+1}(e'))$ and $R(g_{i+1}(e))$.
<!-- end proof-72 -->
<!-- proposition-9: body_md -->
\label{Prop:SingletonConical}
Suppose that $x \in \mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$ is a singleton.
Then the decomposition element $[x]_{S^1} \in \mathcal{S}^2(\mathcal{V})$ is a conical limit point for the action of $\pi_1(M)$.
<!-- end proposition-9 -->
<!-- definition-39: body_md -->
Suppose that $u$, $v$, and $w$ are points of $\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{V})$, 
with $v$ in $\mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V}) \cup \Delta_\mathcal{V}$.
Suppose that there are non-adjacent sectors $S$ and $T$ at $v$ so that $u \in S$ and $w \in T$.
Then we say that $v$ is \emph{sector-between} $u$ and $w$.
<!-- end definition-39 -->
<!-- lemma-56: body_md -->
\label{Lem:BetweenTransitive}
Suppose that $u$, $v$, $w$ and $x$ are points of $\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{V})$, 
with $v$ and $w$ in $\mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V}) \cup \Delta_\mathcal{V}$.
Suppose that $v$ is sector-between $u$ and $x$. 
Suppose that $w$ is sector-between $v$ and $x$.
Then $w$ is sector-between $u$ and $x$. \qed
<!-- end lemma-56 -->
<!-- lemma-57: body_md -->
\label{Lem:CuspBetween}
Suppose that $u$, $v_i$, and $w$ are points of $\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{V})$, with $v_i \in \mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V})$.
Suppose that $c$ is a cusp.
Suppose that $u$ and $w$ do not lie on cusp leaves of $c$.
Suppose that the $v_i$ tend to $c$ and that the $v_i$ are sector-between $u$ and $w$.
Then $c$ is sector-between $u$ and $w$. \qed
<!-- end lemma-57 -->
<!-- notation-1: body_md -->
Suppose that $u$ is a point of $\mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V}) \cup \Delta_\mathcal{V}$ and $x$ is a singleton.
We denote the sector at $u$ containing $x$ by $S(u, x)$.
<!-- end notation-1 -->
<!-- lemma-58: body_md -->
\label{Lem:NestedSectors}
Suppose that $c$ and $d$ are distinct cusps and $x$ is a singleton.
Suppose that $d$ is sector-between $c$ and $x$.
Then $S(d, x)$ is a proper subset of $S(c, x)$.
<!-- end lemma-58 -->
<!-- proof-73: body_md -->
We first prove that $\partial S(c, x)$ is disjoint from $\partial S(d, x)$. 
Let $\ell_c$, $m_c$, $\ell_d$, and $m_d$ be the cusp leaves on the boundaries of $S(c, x)$ and $S(d, x)$, respectively.
Leaves from the same foliation do not intersect. 
So, for a contradiction, suppose that $p = \ell_d \cap m_c$.
                          
Consider the initial arc of $m_c$ ending at $p$.
This is entirely contained in some sector $T$ based at $d$, with $\ell_d$ in its boundary.
Thus $T$ contains $c$, and $T$ is adjacent to (or equal to) $S(d, x)$.
Thus $d$ is not sector-between $c$ and $x$, a contradiction.

Since $d$ is sector-between $c$ and $x$, we deduce that $c$ does not lie in $S(d, x)$.
Since the cusp leaves of $S(c, x)$ and $S(d, x)$ are disjoint, we deduce that the sectors either are disjoint or nest as desired.
However, the sectors are not disjoint because both contain $x$.
<!-- end proof-73 -->
<!-- definition-40: body_md -->
\label{Def:Hull}
Suppose that $u, v \in \mathcal{D}(\mathcal{V})$.
The \emph{hull} of $u$ and $v$, written $\textsf{Hull}(u, v)$, is the closure of the set of points of $\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{V})$ that are sector-between $u$ and $v$.
<!-- end definition-40 -->
<!-- corollary-10: body_md -->
\label{Cor:CuspBetween}
Suppose that $c$ is a cusp in $\textsf{Hull}(u, v)$.
Then $c$ is sector-between $u$ and $v$. \qed
<!-- end corollary-10 -->
<!-- definition-41: body_md -->
\label{Def:RectangleTowards}
Suppose that $x$ is a singleton and $c$ is a cusp.
We define the \emph{rectangle at $c$ towards $x$}, denoted $Q(c, x)$, to be the maximal rectangle so that
\begin{itemize}
\item $Q(c, x) \subset S(c, x)$,
\item $c$ is an ideal corner of $Q(c, x)$, and 
\item each point of $Q(c, x)$ is sector-between $c$ and $x$. \qedhere
\end{itemize}
<!-- end definition-41 -->
<!-- lemma-59: body_md -->
\label{Lem:RectangleTowards}
$Q(c, x)$ exists and is unique.
<!-- end lemma-59 -->
<!-- proof-74: body_md -->
Let $\ell_c \in F^\mathcal{V}$ and $m_c \in F_\mathcal{V}$ be the cusp leaves at $c$ bounding $S(c, x)$.
We extend their orientations (namely, away from $c$) to obtain orientations of $F^\mathcal{V}$ and $F_\mathcal{V}$.
With these orientations, $c$ is the south-west corner of $S(c, x)$.

By Lemma~\ref{Lem:IVT} there are cusps $a$ and $b$ with cusp leaves $\ell$, $\ell'$, $\ell''$, $m$, $m'$, and $m''$ so that
\begin{itemize}
\item $\ell$ crosses $m_c$, 
\item $m$ crosses $\ell_c$, 
\item $\ell'$ and $\ell''$ form bi-leaves with $\ell$, and 
\item $m'$ and $m''$ form bi-leaves with $m$.
\end{itemize}
Let $\hat{\ell}$ be the bi-leaf (formed by $\ell$ and either $\ell'$ or $\ell''$) so that $c$ is contained in the sector with boundary consisting of $\ell$ and the divider of $\hat{\ell}$.
We define $\hat{m}$ similarly.

Then $Q(c, x)$ is the rectangle with boundary contained in the union of $\ell_c$, $m_c$, $\hat{\ell}$, and $\hat{m}$.
<!-- end proof-74 -->
<!-- lemma-60: body_md -->
\label{Lem:InHull}
Suppose that $x \neq y$ are singletons in $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$.
Suppose that $c$ is a cusp in $\textsf{Hull}(y, x)$.
Then $Q(c, x) \subset \textsf{Hull}(y, x)$.
<!-- end lemma-60 -->
<!-- proof-75: body_md -->
Suppose that $p = \ell_p \cap m_p$ is a point of the interior of $Q(c, x)$.
With notation as in the proof of Lemma~\ref{Lem:RectangleTowards}, we have that $m_p$ separates $m_c$ from $\hat{m}$.
Thus $m_p$ separates $c$ from $x$.
Similarly $\ell_p$ separates $c$ from $x$.
Thus $p$ is sector-between $c$ and $x$.

By Corollary~\ref{Cor:CuspBetween}, we have that $c$ is sector-between $y$ and $x$. 
Thus Lemma~\ref{Lem:BetweenTransitive} implies that $p$ is sector-between $y$ and $x$.
Thus $Q(c, x)$ is contained in $\textsf{Hull}(y, x)$.
<!-- end proof-75 -->
<!-- definition-42: body_md -->
An edge rectangle $R$ contained in $\textsf{Hull}(u, v)$ is \emph{south-north spanning} if its south and north sides lie in the boundary of $\textsf{Hull}(u, v)$.
<!-- end definition-42 -->
<!-- lemma-61: body_md -->
\label{Lem:ConstructSpanning}
Suppose that $x \neq y$ are singletons.
Suppose that $c$ is a cusp in $\textsf{Hull}(y, x)$.
Then there are cusps $d$ and $e$ of $\textsf{Hull}(y, x)$ as follows.
\begin{itemize}
\item $d$ is sector-between $c$ and $x$,
\item $e$ is sector-between $d$ and $x$,
\item $R = S(d, x) \cap S(e, y)$ is an edge rectangle with cusps $d$ and $e$, and
\item $R$ is south-north spanning.
\end{itemize}
<!-- end lemma-61 -->
<!-- proof-76: body_md -->
From $c$ we will generate a cusp $d$ so that $Q(d, x)$ contains $e$ and thus the desired edge rectangle $R$.
Here we use the same orientation conventions as in the proof of Lemma~\ref{Lem:RectangleTowards}.

To start, if $Q(c, x)$ is as in Figures \ref{Fig:Case0}, \ref{Fig:Case1}, and \ref{Fig:Case3} then we take $d = c$, take $e = a$, and take $R$ to be the edge rectangle with those cusps.
The case in Figure~\ref{Fig:Case2} is more delicate; 
we proceed as follows.

Set $c^0 = c$ and $a^0 = a$.
In general, let $c^{k+1}$ be the cusp labelled $b$ and let $a^{k+1}$ be the cusp labelled $a$ in Figure~\ref{Fig:Case2} as applied to $Q(c^k, x)$.
In all cases, $c^{k+1}$ is sector-between $c^k$ and $x$.
Induction and Lemma~\ref{Lem:BetweenTransitive} imply that $c^{k+1}$ is sector-between $c$ and $x$.

As long as the rectangles $Q(c^k, x)$ are as in case Figure~\ref{Fig:Case2} their northern sides all lie in the leaf $m$ running through the north-west corner of $Q(c, x)$.
Thus the sequence $a^k$ is constant.
The astroid lemma (Section~\ref{Sec:Astroid}) implies that this process eventually terminates with a rectangle $Q(c^N, x)$ in one of the other three cases.
At that point we take $d = c^N$, take $e = a^N = a$ and set $R \subset Q(c^N, x)$ to be the edge rectangle with cusps $d$ and $e$.

In all of the above cases, the first property follows by construction and the second property follows because $e$ lies in the closure of $Q(d, x)$ (Lemma~\ref{Lem:CuspBetween}).
The construction also gives $R \subset S(d, x)$.
Since $d$ is sector-between $y$ and $x$, we have that $S(d, y)$ intersects $S(d, x)$ only at $d$.
Note that $e$ lies in the interior of $S(d, x)$.
Thus, $d$ is sector-between $y$ and $e$.
By Lemma~\ref{Lem:NestedSectors} we have that $S(d, y)$ is a proper subset of $S(e, y)$.
In particular, $d$ lies in $S(e, y)$.
Thus $R \subset S(e, y)$.
The cusp leaves on the boundaries of $S(d, x)$ and $S(e, y)$ run along the sides of $R$ and thus intersect in pairs.
Thus $R = S(d, x) \cap S(e, y)$.

Finally, we show that the rectangle $R$ is a south-north spanning edge rectangle for $\textsf{Hull}(y, x)$.
By Lemma~\ref{Lem:InHull} we have that $R \subset \textsf{Hull}(y, x)$.
We show that the north and south sides of $R$ lie in the boundary of $\textsf{Hull}(y, x)$.
Suppose that $p$ is north of $m$.
Note that $y$ is south of $m$ because if it was north, it would be contained in the union of the two sectors at $d$ to either side of $\ell_d$.
This would mean that $y$ and $x$ would be in the same or adjacent sectors, contradicting the fact that $d$ is sector-between $y$ and $x$.
Moreover, $x$ is (strictly) south of $p$.
(In cases \ref{Fig:Case1} and \ref{Fig:Case3}, the singleton $x$ is south of $m$ thus south of $p$.
In case \ref{Fig:Case0}, the singleton $x$ may be either south or north of $m$, but in both cases $x$ is south of $p$.)
Thus $p$ is not sector-between $y$ and $x$.
A similar argument applies for points $p$ south of $m_d$.
<!-- end proof-76 -->
<!-- lemma-62: body_md -->
\label{Lem:EdgeSpanningInHalfDisc}
Suppose that $\ell$ is a non-cusp leaf so that the half-disc $H(\ell)$ contains $x$ and does not contain $y$.
Then there is a south-north spanning edge rectangle for $\textsf{Hull}(y, x)$ that is contained in $H(\ell)$.
<!-- end lemma-62 -->
<!-- proof-77: body_md -->
Lemma~\ref{Lem:IVT} applied to $\ell$ and $x$ gives us a cusp $c$ with cusp leaves $m$, $m'$, and $m''$ so that 
\begin{itemize}
\item $m$ crosses $\ell$,
\item $m$ and $m'$ form a bi-leaf, as do $m$ and $m''$, and
\item exactly one of $m'$ or $m''$ separates $\ell$ from $x$. 
\end{itemize}

See Figure~\ref{Fig:IVT}.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\labellist
\footnotesize\hair 2pt
\pinlabel $y$ [r] at 11 115
\pinlabel $x$ [l] at 367 118
\pinlabel $c$ [l] at 379 187
\pinlabel $\ell$ [r] at 127 123
\pinlabel $m$ [b] at 217 190
\pinlabel $m'$ [l] at 313 129
\pinlabel $m''$ [l] at 313 245
\pinlabel $\ell'$ [r] at 236 79
\endlabellist
\includegraphics[width=0.45\textwidth]{Figures/IVT}
\caption{The cusp and cusp leaves found in Lemma~\ref{Lem:IVT}. }
\label{Fig:IVT}
\end{figure}

\begin{claim*} 
$S(c, x) \subset H(\ell)$ and $c \in \textsf{Hull}(y, x)$.
\end{claim*}

\begin{proof}
Breaking symmetry, suppose that $m'$ separates $\ell$ from $x$, and therefore separates $y$ from $x$.
It follows that $m'$ separates $S(c, x)$ from $\ell$.
Thus $S(c, x) \subset H(\ell)$.

Furthermore, $m'$ separates $S(c, x)$ from $y$.
Thus $S(c, y)$ is not equal to $S(c, x)$.
Let $\ell'$ be the divider of the bi-leaf containing $m$ and $m'$.
Since $\ell$ and $\ell'$ are in the same foliation, they do not cross.
Since $m$ crosses $\ell$, we deduce that $\ell'$ separates $y$ from $x$.
                                                            
So the sector at $c$ bounded by $\ell'$ and $m'$ also separates $y$ from $x$.
Thus the sectors at $c$ containing $y$ and $x$ are not adjacent.
\end{proof}

From Lemma~\ref{Lem:ConstructSpanning}, we obtain the cusps $d$ and $e$ and their edge rectangle $R$. 
Since $R$ is contained in the sector $S(c, x)$ it is contained in the half-disc $H(\ell)$.
<!-- end proof-77 -->
<!-- claim--6: body_md -->
$S(c, x) \subset H(\ell)$ and $c \in \textsf{Hull}(y, x)$.
<!-- end claim--6 -->
<!-- proof-78: body_md -->
Breaking symmetry, suppose that $m'$ separates $\ell$ from $x$, and therefore separates $y$ from $x$.
It follows that $m'$ separates $S(c, x)$ from $\ell$.
Thus $S(c, x) \subset H(\ell)$.

Furthermore, $m'$ separates $S(c, x)$ from $y$.
Thus $S(c, y)$ is not equal to $S(c, x)$.
Let $\ell'$ be the divider of the bi-leaf containing $m$ and $m'$.
Since $\ell$ and $\ell'$ are in the same foliation, they do not cross.
Since $m$ crosses $\ell$, we deduce that $\ell'$ separates $y$ from $x$.
                                                            
So the sector at $c$ bounded by $\ell'$ and $m'$ also separates $y$ from $x$.
Thus the sectors at $c$ containing $y$ and $x$ are not adjacent.
<!-- end proof-78 -->
<!-- lemma-63: body_md -->
\label{Lem:SpanningEdgeRectangles}
Suppose that $x \neq y$ are singletons.
The hull $\textsf{Hull}(y, x)$ contains a sequence of south-north spanning edge rectangles $(R_n)$ whose closures Hausdorff converge to $x$.
<!-- end lemma-63 -->
<!-- proof-79: body_md -->
Proposition~\ref{Prop:SingleLeaf} provides a sequence of non-cusp leaves $(\ell_n)$ so that the half-discs $H(\ell_n)$ give a neighbourhood basis for $x$ in $\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{V})$.
Pass to a tail so that for all $n$, the leaf $\ell_n$ separates $y$ from $x$.
Applying Lemma~\ref{Lem:EdgeSpanningInHalfDisc} we obtain south-north spanning edge rectangles $R_n$ contained in $H(\ell_n)$.
<!-- end proof-79 -->
<!-- remark-16: body_md -->
In fact the collection of all edge rectangles south-north spanning $\textsf{Hull}(y, x)$ is linearly ordered, from $y$ to $x$, ``along the hull''.
The order has exactly two accumulation points, at $y$ and at $x$.
Curiously, these accumulations may be from one side only.
<!-- end remark-16 -->
<!-- definition-43: body_md -->
\label{Def:SeparatingSectors}
Suppose that the cusps $d$ and $e$, and the rectangle $R$ are as given in Lemma~\ref{Lem:ConstructSpanning}.
We define the \emph{separating sectors} $S$ and $T$, as follows.
Let $\ell_d$ and $m_d$ be the boundary leaves of $S(d, x)$.
If $\ell_d$ separates $y$ from $R$ then let $S$ be the sector at $d$ on the opposite side of $\ell_d$ from $R$.
If instead $m_d$ separates $y$ from $R$ then let $S$ be the sector at $d$ one step further away from $R$ than the sector on the opposite side of $m_d$ from $R$.
We similarly define the sector $T$ at $e$ relative to $x$.
<!-- end definition-43 -->
<!-- lemma-64: body_md -->
\label{Lem:SeparatingSectorProperties}
The separating sectors $S$ and $T$ satisfy the following.
\begin{itemize}
\item $S$ and $T$ are disjoint.
\item $S$ separates $y$ from $T$, while $T$ separates $S$ from $x$.
\end{itemize}
<!-- end lemma-64 -->
<!-- proof-80: body_md -->
Suppose first that $\ell_d$ separates $y$ from $R$ (as in Figures~\ref{Fig:RainbowCA} and~\ref{Fig:RainbowCC}).
Let $m$ be the bi-leaf at $d$ with divider $\ell_d$.
Suppose for a contradiction that $y$ is north of $m$.
Then there is a non-cusp leaf $m'$ close to $m$ so that both $y$ and $x$ are north of $m'$ and $d$ is south.
But then $d$ is not sector-between $y$ and $x$, a contradiction.
It follows that in this case, $S$ separates $y$ from $R$.

Suppose instead that $m_d$ separates $y$ from $R$.
(See Figures~\ref{Fig:RainbowAA} and~\ref{Fig:RainbowAC}.)
Let $S'$ be the sector at $d$ on the opposite side of $m_d$ from $R$.
We saw in the proof of Lemma~\ref{Lem:ConstructSpanning} that no points south of $m_d$ are sector-between $y$ and $x$.
Thus $y$ cannot be in either $S$ or $S'$.

Similar arguments show that $T$ separates $R$ from $x$. 
Finally, any leaf passing through the interiors of the southern and northern sides of $R$ separates $S$ from $T$.
<!-- end proof-80 -->
<!-- proof-81: body_md -->
Lemma~\ref{Lem:SpanningEdgeRectangles} gives us a sequence of south-north spanning edge rectangles $(R_n)$ that Hausdorff converge to $x$.

Recall that there are only finitely many edges in the veering triangulation $\mathcal{V}$.
So pass to a subsequence $(R_n)$ so that the $R_n$ belong to a single orbit under the action of $\pi_1(M)$.
Pass to a further subsequence and reorient the foliations if necessary to ensure that each $R_n$ has its cusps $d_n$ and $e_n$ (provided in Lemma~\ref{Lem:ConstructSpanning}) at its south-west and north-east corners, respectively.
Definition~\ref{Def:SeparatingSectors} gives separating sectors $S_n$ based at $d_n$ and $T_n$ based at $e_n$.
                                                                    
                                              

Pass to a further subsequence and so find group elements $g_n$ so that, for each, we have $g_n(R_0) = R_n$ and $g_n$ preserves the orientations of the foliations.
(Note that we may need to choose a new $R_0$ to arrange this.)
Applying Proposition~\ref{Prop:Convergence}, we pass to a further subsequence so that $(g_n^{-1})$ is a collapsing sequence for the action of $\pi_1(M)$ on $\mathcal{S}^2(\mathcal{V})$.
                                                                                          

We now set $y_n = g_n^{-1}(y)$ and $x_n = g_n^{-1}(x)$.
Pass to a further subsequence so that $y_n \to y_\infty$ and $x_n \to x_\infty$ both converge in $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$.
We now verify the properties of Definition~\ref{Def:CLP} for $\pi_1(M)$ acting on $\mathcal{S}^2(\mathcal{V})$ for the three points $[x]_{S^1}$,  $A = [y_\infty]_{S^1}$, and $B = [x_\infty]_{S^1}$ (in that order).

Let $Y$ be the closure of the component of $\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{V}) - S_0$ that contains $y$.
Let $X$ be the closure of the component of $\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{V}) - T_0$ that contains $x$. 
Note that $y_n$, and thus $y_\infty$ lies in $Y$.
Similarly, $x_n$, and thus $x_\infty$ lies in $X$.

\begin{claim}
No decomposition element of $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$ meets both $\partial_\infty Y$ and $\partial_\infty X$.
\end{claim}

\begin{proof}
By Lemma~\ref{Lem:SeparatingSectorProperties} we have that $Y$ and $X$ are separated by both $S_0$ and $T_0$. 

First, suppose that $p$ is a singleton meeting $\partial_\infty Y$.
Since $\partial_\infty Y$ is disjoint from $\partial_\infty X$, we deduce that $p$ does not meet $\partial_\infty X$.

Next, suppose that $\ell$ is a non-cusp leaf of $F^\mathcal{V}$ so that $\partial_\infty \ell$ meets $\partial_\infty Y$.
(The case when $\ell$ is a non-cusp leaf of $F_\mathcal{V}$ is similar.)
The leaf $\ell$ can cross at most one boundary leaf of the sector $S_0$, namely the leaf that $S_0$ shares with $Y$.
Thus $\partial_\infty \ell$ is contained in $\partial_\infty Y \cup \partial_\infty S_0$.
So again, $\partial_\infty \ell$ does not meet $\partial_\infty X$.

Finally, suppose that $C$ is the clamshell boundary associated to a cusp $c$. 
Let $V$ be the closure of the component of $\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{V}) - S_0$ that does not contain $y$.
Let $W$ be the closure of the component of $\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{V}) - T_0$ that does not contain $x$.
Suppose that some point of $\partial_\infty C$ meets $\partial_\infty Y$.  
There are two (overlapping) cases.
\begin{itemize}
\item 
Suppose that $c$ lies in $\partial_\infty Y$.
In particular, by Lemma~\ref{Lem:SeparatingSectorProperties}, the cusp $c$ is disjoint from $\partial_\infty T_0$.
Applying Lemma~\ref{Lem:NoneShallPass}(\ref{Itm:MeetsOne}), we have that $\partial_\infty C$ meets precisely one of the two components of $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V}) - \partial_\infty T_0$.
Since $c$ lies in $\partial_\infty Y$, we deduce that $\partial_\infty C$ meets $W$.
Thus $\partial_\infty C$ does not meet $\partial_\infty X - \partial_\infty T_0$.
Applying Lemma~\ref{Lem:NoneShallPass}(\ref{Itm:NoBoundary}), we are done in this case.
\item
Suppose that a thorn of $C$ lies in $\partial_\infty Y$. 
If no point of $C$ meets $\partial_\infty V$ then we are done.
Otherwise, by the contrapositive of Lemma~\ref{Lem:NoneShallPass}(\ref{Itm:MeetsOne}), we have that $c$ lies in $\partial_\infty S_0$. 
Thus by Lemma~\ref{Lem:SeparatingSectorProperties} we have that $c$ does not lie in $\partial_\infty T_0$ and we are done as before. \qedhere
\end{itemize}
\end{proof}

We conclude that $A \neq B$.

Suppose that $y' \neq y$ is another singleton separated from $x$ by $S_0$.
The hulls $\textsf{Hull}(y, x)$ and $\textsf{Hull}(y', x)$ are not equal; 
however they coincide on the component of $\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{V}) - S_0$ containing $x$.
Thus $\textsf{Hull}(y, x)$ and $\textsf{Hull}(y', x)$ are both spanned by the edge rectangle $R_n$, for all $n$.
Thus the construction above, applied to $y'$, produces the same collapsing sequence $(g^{-1}_n)$.
Setting $A' = [y'_\infty]_{S^1}$, we find as above that $A' \neq B$.
As in the proof of Proposition~\ref{Prop:LeafConical}, we are done.
<!-- end proof-81 -->
<!-- claim-10: body_md -->
No decomposition element of $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$ meets both $\partial_\infty Y$ and $\partial_\infty X$.
<!-- end claim-10 -->
<!-- proof-82: body_md -->
By Lemma~\ref{Lem:SeparatingSectorProperties} we have that $Y$ and $X$ are separated by both $S_0$ and $T_0$. 

First, suppose that $p$ is a singleton meeting $\partial_\infty Y$.
Since $\partial_\infty Y$ is disjoint from $\partial_\infty X$, we deduce that $p$ does not meet $\partial_\infty X$.

Next, suppose that $\ell$ is a non-cusp leaf of $F^\mathcal{V}$ so that $\partial_\infty \ell$ meets $\partial_\infty Y$.
(The case when $\ell$ is a non-cusp leaf of $F_\mathcal{V}$ is similar.)
The leaf $\ell$ can cross at most one boundary leaf of the sector $S_0$, namely the leaf that $S_0$ shares with $Y$.
Thus $\partial_\infty \ell$ is contained in $\partial_\infty Y \cup \partial_\infty S_0$.
So again, $\partial_\infty \ell$ does not meet $\partial_\infty X$.

Finally, suppose that $C$ is the clamshell boundary associated to a cusp $c$. 
Let $V$ be the closure of the component of $\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{V}) - S_0$ that does not contain $y$.
Let $W$ be the closure of the component of $\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{V}) - T_0$ that does not contain $x$.
Suppose that some point of $\partial_\infty C$ meets $\partial_\infty Y$.  
There are two (overlapping) cases.
\begin{itemize}
\item 
Suppose that $c$ lies in $\partial_\infty Y$.
In particular, by Lemma~\ref{Lem:SeparatingSectorProperties}, the cusp $c$ is disjoint from $\partial_\infty T_0$.
Applying Lemma~\ref{Lem:NoneShallPass}(\ref{Itm:MeetsOne}), we have that $\partial_\infty C$ meets precisely one of the two components of $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V}) - \partial_\infty T_0$.
Since $c$ lies in $\partial_\infty Y$, we deduce that $\partial_\infty C$ meets $W$.
Thus $\partial_\infty C$ does not meet $\partial_\infty X - \partial_\infty T_0$.
Applying Lemma~\ref{Lem:NoneShallPass}(\ref{Itm:NoBoundary}), we are done in this case.
\item
Suppose that a thorn of $C$ lies in $\partial_\infty Y$. 
If no point of $C$ meets $\partial_\infty V$ then we are done.
Otherwise, by the contrapositive of Lemma~\ref{Lem:NoneShallPass}(\ref{Itm:MeetsOne}), we have that $c$ lies in $\partial_\infty S_0$. 
Thus by Lemma~\ref{Lem:SeparatingSectorProperties} we have that $c$ does not lie in $\partial_\infty T_0$ and we are done as before. \qedhere
\end{itemize}
<!-- end proof-82 -->
<!-- theorem-6: body_md -->
\label{Thm:Convergence}
Suppose that $\mathcal{V}$ is a finite locally veering triangulation of a three-manifold $M$. 
Then the action of $\pi_1(M)$ on the veering two-sphere $\mathcal{S}^2(\mathcal{V})$ is a geometrically finite convergence action.  
Furthermore, its parabolic points are exactly the cusps $\Delta_\mathcal{V}$.
<!-- end theorem-6 -->
<!-- proof-83: body_md -->
By Proposition~\ref{Prop:Convergence} the action is a convergence action.
Suppose that $[x]_{S^1}$ is a point of $\mathcal{S}^2(\mathcal{V})$. 
By Proposition~\ref{Prop:Parabolic} if $x = c$ is a cusp, then $[c]_{S^1}$ is a bounded parabolic point for the action.
By Propositions~\ref{Prop:LeafConical} and~\ref{Prop:SingletonConical} if $x$ is the end of a leaf, or a singleton, then $[x]_{S^1}$ is a conical limit point for the action.
By Lemma~\ref{Lem:Laminations} these are all of the points of $\mathcal{S}^2(\mathcal{V})$. 
Thus the assumptions of Definition~\ref{Def:GeoFinConv} are satisfied.
<!-- end proof-83 -->
<!-- corollary-11: body_md -->
\label{Cor:Yaman}
Suppose that $\mathcal{V}$ is a finite locally veering triangulation of a three-manifold $M$. 
Then the veering two-sphere $\mathcal{S}^2(\mathcal{V})$ is equivariantly homeomorphic to $\partial_\infty \mathbb{H}^3$ (as equipped with the action of $\pi_1(M)$ coming from the discrete and faithful representation). \qed
<!-- end corollary-11 -->
<!-- definition-44: body_md -->
\label{Def:CT}
Suppose that $M$ is a finite-volume hyperbolic three-manifold.
Let  $S^2_M \mathrel{\cong} \partial_\infty \mathbb{H}^3$ be the associated two-sphere at infinity, equipped with its canonical action of $\pi_1(M)$.
                                                                                                
Suppose that $S^1_M$ is a circle, equipped with an action of $\pi_1(M)$.
A \emph{Cannon--Thurston map} for $M$ is a continuous equivariant map $\Phi \colon S^1_M \to S^2_M$.
<!-- end definition-44 -->
<!-- definition-45: body_md -->
\label{Def:Equivalence}
                                             
                                                                     
Suppose that $\Phi_M$ and $\Phi_N$ are Cannon--Thurston maps for $M$ and $N$, respectively.
We say that $\Phi_M$ and $\Phi_N$ are \emph{equivalent} if there are homeomorphisms
$f \colon S^1_M \to S^1_N$ and $g \colon S^2_M \to S^2_N$ so that $g \circ \Phi_M = \Phi_N \circ f$.
<!-- end definition-45 -->
<!-- remark-17: body_md -->
\label{Rem:CommensurableEquivalent}
In particular, suppose that $(M, \mathcal{V})$ and $(N, \mathcal{W})$ are commensurable:
they have a common cover.
Then $\Psi_\mathcal{V}$ and $\Psi_\mathcal{W}$ are equivalent.
<!-- end remark-17 -->
<!-- theorem-7: body_md -->
\label{Thm:VeeringCT}
Suppose that $\mathcal{V}$ is a finite locally veering triangulation of a three-manifold $M$. 
Then composing the surjection $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V}) \to \mathcal{S}^2(\mathcal{V})$ and the equivariant homeomorphism given by Corollary~\ref{Cor:Yaman} gives a Cannon--Thurston map $\Psi_\mathcal{V} \colon \mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V}) \to \partial_\infty \mathbb{H}^3$.
<!-- end theorem-7 -->
<!-- proof-84: body_md -->
Taking a finite cover if needed, we obtain a transverse veering triangulation $(M',\mathcal{V}')$.
Since our constructions are insensitive to taking covers, we obtain 
$S^1(\mathcal{V})$, the veering circle, and $S^2(\mathcal{V})$, the veering two-sphere.

Recall from Definition~\ref{Def:VeeringSphere} that $\Psi_\mathcal{V}$ is an equivariant surjection from $S^1(\mathcal{V})$ to $S^2(\mathcal{V})$.
By Corollary~\ref{Cor:Yaman}, we have that $S^2(\mathcal{V})$ is equivariantly homeomorphic to $S^2_M \mathrel{\cong} \partial_\infty \mathbb{H}^3$.
Composing these maps gives the Cannon--Thurston map $\Psi_{\mathcal{V}} \colon S^1(\mathcal{V}) \to S^2_M$ \emph{induced by} $\mathcal{V}$.
<!-- end proof-84 -->
<!-- theorem-8: body_md -->
\label{Thm:Equivalence}
Suppose that $M$ and $N$ are finite-volume hyperbolic three-manifolds.
Suppose that $\mathcal{V}$ is a locally veering triangulation of $M$.
Let $\Psi_\mathcal{V}$ be the Cannon--Thurston map for $M$ induced by $\mathcal{V}$.
Suppose that~$\Phi$ is a Cannon--Thurston map for $N$.
Suppose that $\Psi_\mathcal{V}$ is equivalent to~$\Phi$.
Then $N$ is commensurable with $M$.
Furthermore, there is a locally veering triangulation $\mathcal{W}$ on $N$ so that $\Phi$ is equivalent to $\Psi_\mathcal{W}$ and $(N, \mathcal{W})$ is commensurable with $(M, \mathcal{V})$.
<!-- end theorem-8 -->
<!-- remark-18: body_md -->
That is, up to commensurability, a locally veering triangulation can be recovered from its Cannon--Thurston map.
<!-- end remark-18 -->
<!-- proof-85: body_md -->
As in Theorem~\ref{Thm:VeeringCT}, our constructions are insensitive to taking covers.
Thus we may assume that $M$ and $N$ are oriented.
We can also assume that $\mathcal{V}$ is transverse veering.
The fibres of $\Psi_\mathcal{V}$ are the decomposition elements set out in Definition~\ref{Def:DecompositionElementsCircle}.
From the infinite fibres, and applying Lemma~\ref{Lem:DecompositionElementsRecover}, we recover the upper and lower laminations $\Lambda^\mathcal{V}$ and $\Lambda_\mathcal{V}$ (up to swapping them).

In~\cite[Chapter~10]{FSS22} we construct the link space $\mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V})$ from the laminations $\Lambda^\mathcal{V}$ and $\Lambda_\mathcal{V}$.
By Theorem~\ref{Thm:LinkIsLoom}, the link space is a loom space.
Moreover, the action of $\pi_1(M)$ is by homeomorphisms preserving the loom space structure. 
                                                                                                                            
                                                                                               
Since the Cannon--Thurston maps $\Psi_\mathcal{V}$ and $\Phi$ are equivalent, after transporting the action of $\pi_1(N)$, 
                                           
                                                        
we find that it also acts by homeomorphisms preserving the loom space structure on $\mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V})$.
                                                        
                                                             
                                                                                      
                                                                                                                     
                                                                    

Recall that ${\widetilde{\mathcal{V}}}$ is the induced ideal triangulation of the universal cover.

\begin{claim}
\label{Clm:Faithful}
$\pi_1(N)$ acts faithfully on ${\widetilde{\mathcal{V}}}$.  
\end{claim}

\begin{proof}
Consider $\Delta_\mathcal{V}$, the cusps of ${\widetilde{\mathcal{V}}}$.  
These give a countable dense subset of $S^1(\mathcal{V})$.  
We claim that these can be recovered from $\Psi_\mathcal{V}$ (and thus from $\Phi$).  
To see this, note that the decomposition elements of cusps are exactly the infinite fibres of the map $\Psi_\mathcal{V}$. 
Also, the cusp $c$ is the unique accumulation point in $S^1(\mathcal{V})$ of the decomposition element~$[c]_{S^1}$.

Thus $\Delta_\mathcal{V} \subset S^1(\mathcal{V})$ is also preserved by the $\pi_1(N)$ action.  
Suppose that $\gamma \in \pi_1(N)$ lies in the kernel of the action on ${\widetilde{\mathcal{V}}}$.  
Thus $\gamma$ fixes all of $\Delta_\mathcal{V}$, a dense subset of $S^1(\mathcal{V})$.  
Thus $\gamma$ fixes $S^1(\mathcal{V})$ pointwise.  
We deduce that $\gamma$ fixes $S^2(\mathcal{V})$ and thus $S^2_N$ pointwise.  
By Definition~\ref{Def:CT} we have that $S^2_N = \partial_\infty {\widetilde{N}}$.
However, the only element of $\pi_1(N)$ that acts trivially on $\partial_\infty {\widetilde{N}}$ is the identity.
\end{proof}

Let $\Gamma$ be the group of all combinatorial automorphisms of ${\widetilde{\mathcal{V}}}$.
This contains $\pi_1(M)$ as a finite-index subgroup.
                               
By Claim~\ref{Clm:Faithful}, we have an embedding of $\pi_1(N)$ into $\Gamma$.
Let $\hat\Gamma$ be the intersection of $\pi_1(M)$ and $\pi_1(N)$ inside of $\Gamma$.
Thus $\hat\Gamma$ is finite index in $\pi_1(N)$.
Let $\hat{M}$ and $\hat{N}$ be the induced covers of $M$ and $N$, respectively. 
These are hyperbolic manifolds with identical fundamental groups; 
so they are homotopy equivalent.
Note that $\hat{N}$ is a finite cover of $N$.

\begin{claim}
\label{Clm:Finite}
$\hat{M}$ is a finite cover of $M$.
\end{claim}

Our proof is essentially a combination of~\cite[page~92]{Kapovich10} and~\cite[Section~1]{BieriEckmann78}. 

                                                                      
                                                                    
                                                             
                                                                       
                   

\begin{proof}[Proof of Claim~\ref{Clm:Finite}]
It suffices to prove that the hyperbolic volume of $\hat{M}$ is finite.

Since $M$ is cusped, it deformation retracts to a two-complex.
                                                                   
Lifting, we find that $\hat{M}$ deformation retracts to a two-complex.
So $H_3(\hat{M}) \cong 0$. 
Thus $H_3(\hat{N}) \cong 0$.
We deduce that $\hat{N}$ is not closed.
Since the hyperbolic volume of $\hat{N}$ is finite, we deduce that $\hat{N}$ has (finitely many) cusps.

Let $\mathcal{B}$ be a collection of disjoint closed cusp neighbourhoods $B_i$ in $\hat{N}$, one per cusp of $\hat{N}$.
Set $Q_i = \pi_1(B_i)$.
                                                                  
                                                     
Since $\hat{N}$ is oriented each $Q_i$ is isomorphic to $\mathbb{Z}^2$.
Let $R_i < \hat\Gamma$ be the images of the $Q_i$. 
Set $\mathcal{R} = (R_i)$. 
We note that 
\[
H_3(\hat{\Gamma}, \mathcal{R}) \cong H_3(\hat{N}, \mathcal{B}) \cong \mathbb{Z}
\]
where the first isomorphism follows from~\cite[Theorem~1.3]{BieriEckmann78}. 
                                                                                         
                                                                                                                    

                                                                                                     
                                                              
                      

We transport the groups $R_i$ to $\pi_1(\hat{M})$; 
take $P_i$ to be the image of $R_i$.
Each $P_i$ gives us a parabolic subgroup;
no pair of these is conjugate. 
So we obtain (finitely many) distinct cusps and thus disjoint cusp neighbourhoods $A_i \subset \hat{M}$.
Set $\mathcal{A} = (A_i)$. 

Finally, we have 
\[
H_3(\hat{M}, \mathcal{A}) \cong H_3(\hat{\Gamma}, \mathcal{R}) \cong \mathbb{Z}
\]
Thus $\hat{M}$ is compact relative to a finite set of cusps.
So $\hat{M}$ has finite volume. 
\end{proof}

We apply Mostow-Prasad rigidity~\cite[Theorem~B]{Prasad73} to deduce that $\hat{M}$ is isometric to, thus homeomorphic to, $\hat{N}$. 
(Alternatively, we could use the proof of Claim~\ref{Clm:Finite} to obtain a homotopy equivalence of space pairs; 
then apply~\cite[Theorem~6.1]{Waldhausen68}.)
Thus $M$ and $N$ are commensurable.

Finally, we define $\mathcal{W} = {\widetilde{\mathcal{V}}} / \pi_1(N)$.
<!-- end proof-85 -->
<!-- claim-11: body_md -->
\label{Clm:Faithful}
$\pi_1(N)$ acts faithfully on ${\widetilde{\mathcal{V}}}$.
<!-- end claim-11 -->
<!-- proof-86: body_md -->
Consider $\Delta_\mathcal{V}$, the cusps of ${\widetilde{\mathcal{V}}}$.  
These give a countable dense subset of $S^1(\mathcal{V})$.  
We claim that these can be recovered from $\Psi_\mathcal{V}$ (and thus from $\Phi$).  
To see this, note that the decomposition elements of cusps are exactly the infinite fibres of the map $\Psi_\mathcal{V}$. 
Also, the cusp $c$ is the unique accumulation point in $S^1(\mathcal{V})$ of the decomposition element~$[c]_{S^1}$.

Thus $\Delta_\mathcal{V} \subset S^1(\mathcal{V})$ is also preserved by the $\pi_1(N)$ action.  
Suppose that $\gamma \in \pi_1(N)$ lies in the kernel of the action on ${\widetilde{\mathcal{V}}}$.  
Thus $\gamma$ fixes all of $\Delta_\mathcal{V}$, a dense subset of $S^1(\mathcal{V})$.  
Thus $\gamma$ fixes $S^1(\mathcal{V})$ pointwise.  
We deduce that $\gamma$ fixes $S^2(\mathcal{V})$ and thus $S^2_N$ pointwise.  
By Definition~\ref{Def:CT} we have that $S^2_N = \partial_\infty {\widetilde{N}}$.
However, the only element of $\pi_1(N)$ that acts trivially on $\partial_\infty {\widetilde{N}}$ is the identity.
<!-- end proof-86 -->
<!-- claim-12: body_md -->
\label{Clm:Finite}
$\hat{M}$ is a finite cover of $M$.
<!-- end claim-12 -->
<!-- proof-87: body_md -->
It suffices to prove that the hyperbolic volume of $\hat{M}$ is finite.

Since $M$ is cusped, it deformation retracts to a two-complex.
                                                                   
Lifting, we find that $\hat{M}$ deformation retracts to a two-complex.
So $H_3(\hat{M}) \cong 0$. 
Thus $H_3(\hat{N}) \cong 0$.
We deduce that $\hat{N}$ is not closed.
Since the hyperbolic volume of $\hat{N}$ is finite, we deduce that $\hat{N}$ has (finitely many) cusps.

Let $\mathcal{B}$ be a collection of disjoint closed cusp neighbourhoods $B_i$ in $\hat{N}$, one per cusp of $\hat{N}$.
Set $Q_i = \pi_1(B_i)$.
                                                                  
                                                     
Since $\hat{N}$ is oriented each $Q_i$ is isomorphic to $\mathbb{Z}^2$.
Let $R_i < \hat\Gamma$ be the images of the $Q_i$. 
Set $\mathcal{R} = (R_i)$. 
We note that 
\[
H_3(\hat{\Gamma}, \mathcal{R}) \cong H_3(\hat{N}, \mathcal{B}) \cong \mathbb{Z}
\]
where the first isomorphism follows from~\cite[Theorem~1.3]{BieriEckmann78}. 
                                                                                         
                                                                                                                    

                                                                                                     
                                                              
                      

We transport the groups $R_i$ to $\pi_1(\hat{M})$; 
take $P_i$ to be the image of $R_i$.
Each $P_i$ gives us a parabolic subgroup;
no pair of these is conjugate. 
So we obtain (finitely many) distinct cusps and thus disjoint cusp neighbourhoods $A_i \subset \hat{M}$.
Set $\mathcal{A} = (A_i)$. 

Finally, we have 
\[
H_3(\hat{M}, \mathcal{A}) \cong H_3(\hat{\Gamma}, \mathcal{R}) \cong \mathbb{Z}
\]
Thus $\hat{M}$ is compact relative to a finite set of cusps.
So $\hat{M}$ has finite volume.
<!-- end proof-87 -->
<!-- corollary-12: body_md -->
\label{Cor:NotMadeThere}
Suppose that $M$ and $N$ are finite-volume hyperbolic three-manifolds.
Suppose that $\mathcal{V}$ is a locally veering triangulation for $M$.
Let $\Psi_\mathcal{V}$ be the Cannon--Thurston map for $M$ induced by $\mathcal{V}$.
Suppose that~$\Phi$ is a Cannon--Thurston map for $N$.
Suppose that $\Psi_\mathcal{V}$ is equivalent to~$\Phi$.
Then $\mathcal{V}$ is layered if and only if $\Phi$ is induced by a fibring of $N$. \qed
<!-- end corollary-12 -->
<!-- example-1: body_md -->
\label{Exa:s227}
Suppose that $M$ is the SnapPy~\cite{snappy} census manifold \usebox{\NonfibredSnappy}.
By~\cite[Section~4]{HRST11}, the manifold $M$ is non-fibred. 
Suppose that $\mathcal{V}$ is the veering triangulation \usebox{\NonfibredVeer} of $M$.  
By Corollary~\ref{Cor:NotMadeThere}, the Cannon--Thurston map $\Psi_\mathcal{V}$ is not equivalent to any Cannon--Thurston map arising from a cusped fibred manifold.
<!-- end example-1 -->
<!-- theorem-9: body_md -->
\label{Thm:Isomorphism}
Suppose that $\mathcal{V}$ and $\mathcal{W}$ are finite transverse veering triangulations of a three-manifold $M$.
Suppose that the actions of $\pi_1(M)$ on $S^1(\mathcal{V})$ and $S^1(\mathcal{W})$ are topologically conjugate.
                                                                                                    
Then $\mathcal{V}$ and $\mathcal{W}$ are isomorphic as taut triangulations.
                             
Furthermore, if the topological conjugacy is the identity on $\Delta_M$ then $\mathcal{V}$ is isotopic to $\mathcal{W}$.
<!-- end theorem-9 -->
<!-- definition-46: body_md -->
Suppose that $g \colon S^1 \to S^1$ is a homeomorphism. 
We say that $g$ has \emph{north-south dynamics} if $g$ has exactly two fixed points, with one attracting and the other repelling.
We say that $g$ has \emph{north-south-north-south dynamics} if $g$ has exactly four fixed points, with two attracting and two repelling.
<!-- end definition-46 -->
<!-- proposition-10: body_md -->
\label{Prop:FixedPoints}
Suppose that $\mathcal{V}$ is a finite locally veering triangulation of a three-manifold $M$.
Let $S^1(\mathcal{V})$ be the veering circle.  
Every non-trivial element $\gamma$ of $\pi_1(M)$ satisfies exactly one of the following.
\begin{enumerate}
\item 
\label{Itm:Peripheral}
$\gamma$ is peripheral.
\item 
\label{Itm:NS}
$\gamma$ has north-south dynamics on $S^1(\mathcal{V})$.
Here the fixed points of $\gamma$ are singletons.
                    
\item 
\label{Itm:NSNS}
$\gamma^2$ has north-south-north-south dynamics.
Here the attractors of $\gamma^2$ are the ends of a leaf (of $\Lambda^\mathcal{V}$ or $\Lambda_\mathcal{V}$) and likewise for the repellers.
                                                                     
                                   
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-10 -->
<!-- proof-88: body_md -->
Suppose first that $\gamma$ is peripheral (so satisfies (\ref{Itm:Peripheral})) and thus fixes a cusp.
By Proposition~\ref{Prop:ParabolicFacts} the action of $\gamma$ on $S^1(\mathcal{V})$ has either infinitely many fixed points or has exactly one. 
Thus we do not satisfy (\ref{Itm:NS}) or (\ref{Itm:NSNS}).

Suppose now that $\gamma$ is not peripheral.
By Corollary~\ref{Cor:Yaman}, the action of $\pi_1(M)$ on the veering two-sphere $\mathcal{S}^2(\mathcal{V})$ is topologically conjugate to its action on $\partial_\infty \mathbb{H}^3$.                         
Let $\rho \colon \pi_1(M) \to \operatorname{Isom}(\mathbb{H}^3)$ be the holonomy representation.
Thus $\rho(\gamma)$ is loxodromic. 
                                       
                                                     
(It is possibly a glide reflection, but this does not affect the arguments.)
                                               
Thus the action of $\gamma$ on $\mathcal{S}^2(\mathcal{V})$ has exactly two fixed points;
one, say $A$, is attracting and one, say $B$, is repelling. 
Applying Theorem~\ref{Thm:Convergence} we have that neither $A$ nor $B$ is a cusp. 

We now have various cases as $A$ is a singleton or the pair of ends of a leaf, and similarly for $B$.
If $A$ is a singleton, it contributes one fixed point to the action of $\gamma$ on $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$.
If $A$ is the pair of ends of a leaf, then the ends are either both fixed or are interchanged by the action of $\gamma$ on $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$.

First suppose that $A = \{x\}$ and $B = \{y\}$ are singletons.  
Since $A$ is attracting for the action of $\gamma$ on $S^2(\mathcal{V})$, the continuity of the Cannon--Thurston map $\Psi_\mathcal{V}$ implies that $x$ is attracting for the action of $\gamma$ on $S^1(\mathcal{V})$.
                                                                                                
                                                                           
Similarly, $y$ is repelling.
Thus we satisfy (\ref{Itm:NS}).

Replacing $\gamma$ by $\gamma^{-1}$ if needed, we next suppose that $A = \{x, y\}$ where $x$ and $y$ are the ends of a leaf in the veering circle.  
Squaring $\gamma$ if necessary, we can assume that $\gamma$ (as it acts on $S^1(\mathcal{V})$) fixes $x$ and $y$ individually.  
Similar to the above,
                                                                                                
                                
                                
                                                                                  
                                               
                                               
                                                            
   
                    
   
                                                         
                                                                         
                       
    
                                                                        
                                           
                                           
                                          
                       
we deduce that $x$ and $y$ are attracting fixed points for the action of $\gamma$ on $S^1(\mathcal{V})$.  
We deduce that $\gamma$, acting on $S^1(\mathcal{V})$, has (at least)
two more fixed points: one in $(x, y)^{\rotatebox[origin=c]{-90}{\scalebox{0.7}{$\curvearrowleft$}}}$ and one in $(y, x)^{\rotatebox[origin=c]{-90}{\scalebox{0.7}{$\curvearrowleft$}}}$.  
Thus by the above it has precisely four fixed points.
So $B$ is also the ends of a leaf, and we are done.
<!-- end proof-88 -->
<!-- proof-89: body_md -->
By Proposition~\ref{Prop:FixedPoints} and Proposition~\ref{Prop:ParabolicFacts}, an element of $\pi_1(M)$ has infinitely many fixed points as it acts on $S^1(\mathcal{V})$ if and only if it is a non-trivial power of $\beta$ for some cusp $c$.
Applying Lemma~\ref{Lem:DecompositionElementsRecover}, we recover the upper and lower laminations $\Lambda^\mathcal{V}$ and $\Lambda_\mathcal{V}$.
In~\cite[Chapter~10]{FSS22} we construct the link space $\mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V})$ from the laminations $\Lambda^\mathcal{V}$ and $\Lambda_\mathcal{V}$.
We do the same for $\mathcal{W}$.
We deduce that the link spaces of $\mathcal{V}$ and $\mathcal{W}$ are isomorphic.
Furthermore, the conjugacy takes the action on the link space $\mathsf{L}(\mathcal{V})$ to that on $\mathsf{L}(\mathcal{W})$.
This gives a bijection of orbits of tetrahedron rectangles as well as their adjacencies. 

Suppose that the conjugacy is the identity on $\Delta_M$.
In this case, the isomorphism of link spaces built in the previous paragraph is in fact the identity.
                                                                                   
The resulting isomorphism of triangulations induces a homeomorphism $h \colon M \to M$.
The isomorphism preserves all cusps of $\Delta_M$.
Thus $h$ sends homotopy classes of edges to themselves.
Using the hyperbolic geometry on $M$, we straighten $h$ and find that it is homotopic to the identity.
Applying~\cite[Theorem~7.1]{Waldhausen68}, we find that $h$ is isotopic to the identity.
<!-- end proof-89 -->
<!-- lemma-65: body_md -->
Suppose that $M$ is a cusped hyperbolic three-manifold.
Suppose that $\mathcal{T}$ is a layered triangulation of $M$.
Suppose that $L^\mathcal{T}$ has internal singularities.
Then $\mathcal{O}_\mathcal{T}$ is not equal to $\mathcal{O}_\mathcal{V}$ for any veering triangulation $\mathcal{V}$ of $M$.
<!-- end lemma-65 -->
<!-- proof-90: body_md -->
We prove the contrapositive.
Suppose that $\mathcal{O}_\mathcal{T} = \mathcal{O}_\mathcal{V}$ for some veering triangulation $\mathcal{V}$ of $M$.
Thus their order closures agree, giving $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$.
By Proposition~\ref{Prop:FixedPoints}, the action of $\pi_1(M)$ on $\mathcal{S}^1(\mathcal{V})$ recovers the decomposition elements of cusps.
Applying Lemma~\ref{Lem:DecompositionElementsRecover}, we recover the upper and lower laminations $\Lambda^\mathcal{V}$ and $\Lambda_\mathcal{V}$.

By~\cite[Theorem~4]{Thurston88}
                                                                                                    
                                                                                    
                                                                                                                                   
we can recover the boundary $\partial L^\mathcal{T}$ from the action of (the various lifts of) $f$ on $\partial {\widetilde{S}}$.
Since $\partial {\widetilde{S}}$ is naturally homeomorphic to the order completion of $\mathcal{O}_\mathcal{T}$, and since $f$ appears as an element of $\pi_1(M)$, we have that 
\begin{itemize}
\item $\partial L^\mathcal{T} = \Lambda^\mathcal{V}$ and $\partial L_\mathcal{T} = \Lambda_\mathcal{V}$ or 
\item $\partial L^\mathcal{T} = \Lambda_\mathcal{V}$ and $\partial L_\mathcal{T} = \Lambda^\mathcal{V}$.
\end{itemize}
By Corollary~\ref{Cor:CircleDecomposition}, we find that $L^\mathcal{T}$ has no finite-sided ideal polygons.
Thus $L^\mathcal{T}$ has no internal singularities.
<!-- end proof-90 -->
<!-- remark-19: body_md -->
Suppose that the manifold $M$ has a layered veering triangulation $\mathcal{V}$.
Suppose that $D$ is any disc carried by the horizontal branched surface (as is the case in Thurston's examples of punctured torus bundles).
Then there is a continent $C$ whose cusps include the ideal points of $D$, in the same circular order.
Thus if we choose the continent appropriately, we exactly recover Thurston's examples.
<!-- end remark-19 -->
<!-- remark-20: body_md -->
We can estimate $\epsilon$ by the maximal distance between consecutive vertices.
Thus $\epsilon$ in Figure~\ref{Fig:Thurston} seems to be smaller than a pixel.
Note that there are some visible line segments near the lower left corner.
These happen at leaves of the search tree that hit maximal depth before hitting minimal feature size.
Thurston seems to have removed this part of the stopping criterion in his more recent image of the Cannon--Thurston map for the figure eight knot~\cite[Figure~2]{Thurston98}.
<!-- end remark-20 -->
<!-- theorem-10: body_md -->
\label{Thm:Terminates}
The continent algorithm terminates.
<!-- end theorem-10 -->
<!-- proof-91: body_md -->
Suppose for contradiction that it does not terminate.
Then there is a sequence $(e_n)$ of distinct hyperbolic edges whose projections to $\partial_\infty \mathbb{H}^3$ have length greater than or equal to $\epsilon$. 
Since $\partial_\infty \mathbb{H}^3$ is compact we may pass to a subsequence, again denoted $(e_n)$, where the projections converge.
Thus for any $\delta$ we may find a point $p$ of $\mathbb{H}^3$ so that infinitely many of the $e_n$ intersect the $\delta$--ball about $p$.
This contradicts the local finiteness of the (geometric) triangulation ${\widetilde{\mathcal{V}}}$.
<!-- end proof-91 -->
<!-- remark-21: body_md -->
\label{Rem:DiscVsContinent}
Figure~\ref{Fig:CT_fig8_intro} shows two approximations to the Cannon--Thurston map associated to the figure-eight knot complement.
The curve produced by Thurston's algorithm is in black;
it consists of 835,774 arcs and uses a feature size of $0.00265752$.
The curve produced by our algorithm is the common boundary of the green and purple regions;
it consists of 83,576 arcs and uses a feature size of $0.04$.
Note that our curve has one-tenth the arcs and uses a feature size that is (a bit more than) fifteen times larger.
Nonetheless, our curve fills the sphere much more evenly.
<!-- end remark-21 -->
<!-- lemma-66: body_md -->
\label{Lem:InjectivityRadius}
Suppose that $\mathcal{V}$ is geometric.
Suppose that $0 < \epsilon \leq \pi/2$. 
Suppose that $\psi_\mathcal{V}$ is the approximation produced by the continent method.
Then the complement of $\psi_\mathcal{V}$ in $\partial_\infty \mathbb{H}^3$ has injectivity radius at most $\epsilon$.
<!-- end lemma-66 -->
<!-- proof-92: body_md -->
Since $\mathcal{V}$ is geometric the ideal hyperbolic tetrahedra of ${\widetilde{\mathcal{V}}}$ have shapes with positive imaginary part.
Set ${\overline{\mathbb{H}}}^3 = \mathbb{H}^3 \cup \partial_\infty \mathbb{H}^3$;
this is a closed three-ball in $\mathbb{R}^3$. 
Positivity of the shapes ensures that $C$, the continent, is a three-ball embedded in ${\overline{\mathbb{H}}}^3$. 
(The embedding is almost proper, in the sense that the preimage of $\partial_\infty \mathbb{H}^3$ is only a finite subset of $\partial C$:
the ideal vertices of the tetrahedra in $C$.)
Thus $\partial C$, the boundary of the continent, is a topological two-sphere embedded in ${\overline{\mathbb{H}}}^3$. 

Recall that $p_0$, our basepoint, lies in the edge $e_0$ connecting $0$ to $\infty$. 
The spherical distance between $0$ and $\infty$ is $\pi$.
Since $\epsilon \leq \pi/2$ all triangles meeting $e_0$ lie in the interior of $C$.
Thus the basepoint $p_0$ also lies in the interior of $C$.
It follows that the outward radial projection of $\partial C$ to $\partial_\infty \mathbb{H}^3$ is a degree-one map.
                                    
                                                                                    
In particular, every point of $\partial_\infty \mathbb{H}^3$ lies in the image of some ideal hyperbolic triangle of $\partial C$.
Also, the approximate Cannon--Thurston map $\psi_\mathcal{V}$ meets every ideal vertex of $C$.

Now, all faces of $\partial C$ are disjoint from $p_0$.
Fix one such.  
Its outward radial projection is a spherical triangle $t$ with edges of length at most $\epsilon$.
Since $\epsilon \leq \pi/2$, we find that $t$ is contained in some hemisphere.
We deduce that the (closed) $\epsilon$--disc about any one vertex of $t$ contains $t$.
                                                                      
                                                        
                                                                    
                                                                   
                                                                     
                                                                 
                                                                    
                                                                     
                                                          
This implies that the vertices of the approximation $\psi_\mathcal{V}$ are $\epsilon$--dense in $\partial_\infty \mathbb{H}^3$, as desired.
<!-- end proof-92 -->
<!-- question-1: body_md -->
In all of the examples we have produced (using the algorithm of Section~\ref{Sec:OurAlgorithm}), our approximate Cannon--Thurston maps are embedded. 
In particular, this happens even when the veering triangulation is not geometric. 
Are these approximate maps embeddings?
<!-- end question-1 -->
<!-- question-2: body_md -->
Give useful bounds for the injectivity radius of Thurston's algorithm at feature size $\epsilon$.
<!-- end question-2 -->
<!-- question-3: body_md -->
\label{Que:ThurstonWork}
Estimate the amount of work done by Thurston's algorithm at feature size $\epsilon$. 
(And so justify the quote given in Section~\ref{Sec:ThurstonAlgorithm}.)
<!-- end question-3 -->
<!-- question-4: body_md -->
\label{Que:OurWork}
Estimate the amount of work done by the continent algorithm at feature size~$\epsilon$.
<!-- end question-4 -->
<!-- question-5: body_md -->
Estimate how close the disc method and continent method come (as measured by the work done) to the true Cannon--Thurston map in $C^0$.
<!-- end question-5 -->
<!-- theorem-11: body_md -->
\label{Thm:Schoenflies}
Suppose that $\Sigma \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ is a Jordan curve (Jordan line).  
Then there is an orientation-preserving homeomorphism of $\mathbb{R}^2$ taking $\Sigma$ to the unit circle $S^1$ (to the $x$--axis).
\qed
<!-- end theorem-11 -->
<!-- definition-47: body_md -->
\label{Def:PeanoSpace}
A topological space $P$ is a \emph{Peano space}~\cite[page~76]{Wilder49} if it is non-degenerate~\cite[page~2]{Wilder49}, perfectly separable~\cite[page~70]{Wilder49}, normal~\cite[page~49]{Wilder49}, locally compact~\cite[page~29]{Wilder49}, connected~\cite[page~7]{Wilder49}, and locally connected~\cite[page~40]{Wilder49}.
<!-- end definition-47 -->
<!-- definition-48: body_md -->
\label{Def:PeanoContinuum}
A Peano space $P$ is a \emph{Peano continuum}~\cite[page~76]{Wilder49} if it is compact.
<!-- end definition-48 -->
<!-- theorem-12: body_md -->
\label{Thm:Zippin}
Suppose that $D$ is a Peano continuum containing a circle $C$.
Suppose that we have the following.
\begin{enumerate}
\item
\label{Itm:Exists}
$D$ contains an arc that spans $C$.
\item
\label{Itm:All}
Every arc of $D$ that spans $C$ separates $D$.
\item
\label{Itm:None}
No closed proper subset of an arc spanning $C$ separates $D$.
\end{enumerate}
Then there is a homeomorphism of pairs $(D, C) \mathrel{\cong} (D^2, S^1)$. \qed
<!-- end theorem-12 -->
<!-- definition-49: body_md -->
\label{Def:ClosedEquiv}
An equivalence relation on a topological space $X$ is \emph{closed} if it is closed as a subset of $X \times X$.
<!-- end definition-49 -->
<!-- theorem-13: body_md -->
\label{Thm:Moore}
Suppose that $E$ is a closed equivalence relation on $S^2$ with at least two classes.  
Suppose that, for all $x$, the class $[x]_E$ is closed, connected, and non-separating.  
Then the quotient $S^2/E$ is homeomorphic to $S^2$. \qed
<!-- end theorem-13 -->
